lawyer:
Md. Ashfaqul Islam, Advocate ----- For the Petitioners. 
Dewan AMS Zaman, Deputy-Attorney-General ----- For the Opposite Party
parties:
Jasimuddin (Md) and another ------ Petitioners
vs.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
The petitioners obtained this Rule against judgment and order passed by the Assistant Judge, 3rd Court Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 8 of 1991 on 18.5.92, restoring Title Suit No. 19 of 1991.

2. The petitioners filed Title Suit Nd. 787 of 1978 against the Government Opposite Party which was decreed ex parte on 6.3.84 declaring title of the petitioners in 0041 acres of land of dagh No. 549 of mouza Meradia, Dhaka. The Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh instituted Title Suit No. 138 of 1990 in the court of Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka, for setting aside the ex parte decree dated 6.3.84 made in title suit No.787 of 1978. The petitioners contested the suit. The suit was subsequently transferred to the court of Assistant Judge, Additional3rd Court Dhaka. The Government appeared in that court and filed hazira and received copy of the written statement on 5.3.91. The suit, however, was dismissed for default on 30.3.91. The Government opposite party thereafter instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 8 of 1991 for setting aside the ex parte decree dismissing the suit and restoration of the suit on the ground that it had no knowledge of transfer of the suit to the court of Additional Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka.

3. The petitioner contested the said Miscellaneous case on the assertion that transfer of suit was notified on the doors of the shertaders of the transfer courts regarding the transfer of the present suit and the transfer of the suit was within knowledge of the Government. On 5.3.91, the date fixed for serving copy of the written statement, the Government appeared but the defendants were absent. It also appears from the order of that date that Government took copy of the written statement filed by the petitioner before me.

4. This Rule although is opposed by the learned Deputy Attorney-General Mr. Dewan AMS Zaman but no affidavit-in-opposition has been filed by the Government controverting material statements made in the revisional application.

<u>5. Mr. Ashfaqul Islam vehemently submits that the impugned order in the application under Order IX rule 9 for setting aside ex parte decree dismissing the suit of the Government has been made without application of judicial mind inasmuch as from the order dated 5.3.91 on the ground upon which application for setting aside the ex parte decree of dismissing the suit was made palpably shows that the learned Judge did not apply his mind in making the impugned order. Mr. Ashfaq has drawn my attention to order of the transferer court made on 5.3.91. On perusal of the same it appears that the Government filed hazira on that date before the transferer court, the Additional Assistant Judge 3rd Court, Dhaka and also received written statement filed by the defendant. Thus, in view of such position it appears that the Government had knowledge about the transfer of the suit. In view of such facts how the learned Assistant Judge passed the impugned order is not understandable to me. For, this conduct of the Government in proceeding with the suit it was proper on the part of the learned Judge also to take into consideration the ground upon which the case has been filed while making the order sought to be set aside. But in this case statement made in the application by Government through his agent exposes it to criticism by the court of law. The Government and his agent should be careful in making statement against the order of the Court for making out the case for the Government. The ground upon which the government sought to set aside decree of the dismissal of the suit seems to be unfounded. In order to set aside an order made ex parte the party which seeks such order should be clear in making the ground for setting aside the order and the court should not exercise its jurisdiction in allowing such application without application of its mind to the facts of the case. This material aspect unfortunately, was not noticed by the court in making the impugned order and this has caused failure of justice. Accordingly, I set aside the order. In the result, the Rule is made absolute with cost of Taka 500.00 (five hundred) only.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Md Fazlul Karim, Advocate ------ For the Petitioners.
Bakhtear Hossain, Advocate ------ For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Gajendra Nath Mondal and others ------ Petitioners
vs.
Motia Begum and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: This Rule arises out of an application filed under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act and is directed against the judgment and order dated 22-6-86 passed by the then Munsif and SCC Judge Of Serajganj in Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1985 reversing those of the Judgment and decree dated 18-9-85 passed by the same Court in SCC Suit No.1 of 1983.

2. The opposite party Nos. 1-6 as plaintiffs filed SCC Suit No.1 of 1983 in the then Court of Munsif, 2nd Court and the SCC Judge at Serajganj against the defendant-petitioner for ejectment of the defendant-petitioner from the suit premises alleging' that the defendant-petitioner had been in possession of the suit premises as monthly tenant under Satish Chandra and others from whom the plaintiffs have purchased the suit land. After their purchase the plaintiffs asked the defendant No.1 to deliver possession of the suit shop to them for pucca construction and the defendant No. 1 agreed to such proposal, but subsequently refused to deliver possession and also to pay rents to the plaintiffs. It is also alleged that defendant No.1 sub-let part of the suit premises to one Saber Ali. Thus they filed the aforesaid suit for ejectment of the defendant petitioner from the suit premises.

3. The defendant petitioners contested the suit by filing a written statement. The case of the defendant petitioners is that the original owner of the suit premises left for India in 1946 and their tenant also left for India in 1952. Thereafter one Saber Ali took possession of a portion of the suit premises and another Nagendra Nath took over possession of the remaining part of the suit premises. Nagendra left for Kushtia in 1956 in the said year and since then he has been carrying on Homeopathic business thereon. The suit property was declared as Enemy Property and the defendant No.1 and late Saber Ali took lease of the same. The plaintiffs prayed for releasing the said property but that was rejected initially but ultimately on appeal the property was released from the list of vested property. But a review application is pending against that order.

4. After the closing of the pleadings issues were framed and parties led their evidence. The learned SCC Judge by a judgment and decree dated 18-9-85 dismissed the suit. Against the said judgment and decree the plaintiffs filed Miscellaneous Case No. 54 of 1985 under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the learned SCC Judge by his judgment and order dated 22-6-86 set aside the judgment and decree dated 18-9-85 and decreed the suit against the defendants and ordered for khas possession of the suit premises by evicting the defendants therefrom. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order the defendant petitioners preferred this application and obtained the instant Rule.

5. Mr Md Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant petitioners, submits that against the judgment and decree dated 18-9c85 passed in SCC Suit No.1 of 1983 there was specific provision for revision under section 25 of the Small Causes Courts Act and review application before the same court under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was misconceived and the learned SCC Judge committed an illegality by entertaining the same. The learned Advocate further submits that there was no decision on a reference from the court of Small Causes and, as such, the learned SCC Judge exercised. power and jurisdiction not vested in him by law.

6. Mr Bakhtiar Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiffs opposite parties, submits that if section 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure is read with Order 50 of the Code it would be clear that I the Small Cause Courts have the power of review under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate further submits that J the review application in question was a competent one and the learned SCC Judge legally exercised the jurisdiction and rightly reviewed the order dated 18-9-85 as it came within the ambit of Order 47 rule 1 of the Code.

7. This Rule raises a pure question of law as to whether the Court of Small Cause exercising  jurisdiction under the Small Causes Courts Act. 1887 I has jurisdiction to entertain an application for review under section 114 read with rule 1 of Order 47 of the Civil Procedure Code (for short called "the Code").

8. Now it is well settled that the power to review is not an inherent power. It must be conferred by law either specifically or by necessary implication. It will, therefore, be necessary to trace the source of power either in the Small Cause Courts Act or some other provision of law under which the Court of Small Cause, exercising jurisdiction in proceedings under the Small Causes Court Act could exercise powers of review.

9. Section 17 of the Small Cause Court Act provides that the procedure prescribed in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, shall, insofar as is otherwise provided by that Court or by this Act, be the procedure followed in a Court of Small Causes in all suits cognizable by it and in all proceedings arising out of such suits. Thus in all Courts of Small Causes the procedure as laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, shall be followed subject to the exceptions provided by the Code of Civil Procedure or the Small Cause Courts Act.

10. The Code of Civil Procedure in section 7 and Order 50 has specified the provisions which shall not extend to the court constituted under the Small Cause Courts Act, IX of 1887. Section 7 is intended to apply to Small Causes Court established with exclusive jurisdiction to try Small Cause Suits and also to other Civil Courts of ordinary jurisdiction specially empowered to exercise small cause jurisdiction in respect of specified classes of suits. Order 50, rule 1 excludes only so much of provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure as is enumerated in the Order. The proviso to sub-section 17 of the Small Cause Courts Act further provides that in case of an application for setting aside an ex parte decree or for review the applicant.

i) must either deposit the amount in court due under the decree or judgment.

(ii) or give security to the court for the amount so due. These are the relevant provisions as are found both in the Code as well as the Small Cause Courts Act. It is therefore, obvious that section 114 and Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure is applicable to the Small Cause Courts section 114 and Order 50 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and section 17 of the Small Cause Courts Act invest the Court of Small Causes the jurisdiction to entertain and decide a review application.

<u>11. On a, consideration of the provisions of the Small Cause Courts Act and the Code of Civil Procedure it would appear that the Small Cause Court has power of review in the proceedings under the Small Cause Courts Act. From a reading of the Act and the Code it can be said that the Small Cause Court is invested with the jurisdiction to entertain an application for review as contemplated under section 114 read with Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It would, therefore, follow that the review application filed by the landlord in the Small Cause Court is competent and maintainable. The view taken by me gets support from the decision reported in ILR 5 Cal 699.</u>

12. The second submission of Mr Karim is that, a review lies only against a decision on a reference from a Court of Small Cause and since there was no decision on a reference from the Court of Small Cause the learned SCC Judge in the instant case exercised jurisdiction not vested in him. This submission is also absolutely misconceived and devoid of any substance.

13. Since Mr Karim did not argue on merits, I need not enter into the same but suffice it to say that on a perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the learned Small Cause Court on valid and legal grounds reviewed its earlier judgment and decree dated 18-9-85 passed by the same Court in SCC Suit No.1 of 1985.

The Rule is accordingly discharged without any order as to cost.

End.

lawyer:
Abdul Quayum with Swapan Kumar Dutta, Advocates -----For the Petitioners.
Fazlul Karim with Md Abdullah, Advocates -----For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Mizanur Rahman Khan (Md) and another ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Jinnatul Ferdous and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the order dated 19-10-97 passed by the Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, 4th Court, Dhaka in Title Execution Case No. 20 of 1997 rejecting the application of the petitioners under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of possession on the ground that no executable decree was passed.

2. Short facts relevant for the purpose of the case are that, the predecessor-in-interest of opposite party Nos. 1-8 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 52 of 1986 under section 14 of the Arbitration Act to make the award dated 28-12-1985 rule of the Court. It has been stated that on the basis of an arbitration agreement dated 31-5-85 the parties appointed Mr. MA Rashid as the sole arbitrator to adjudicate the dispute in respect of the land mentioned in the agreement as to the shares of the parties thereto in the light of the different deeds of transfer. Reference was made to the arbitrator to ascertain the share of the four parties in the land under dispute whereupon the arbitrator ultimately made the following award:

1.	The first party is entitled to 0.4550 acre of land

2.	The 2nd party is entitled to 0.2250 acre of land

3.	The 3rd party is entitled to 0.2475 acre of land

4.	The 4th party is entitled to 0.4325 acre of land

Total=	1.3600 acre

3. Title Suit No. 52 of 1986 was originally filed in the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka but subsequently it was transferred to the Court of the Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, 4th Court, Dhaka and it was renumbered as Title Suit No. 224 of 1992. The learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 30-11-96 made the award the Rule of the Court on hearing the contending parties.

4. Thereafter opposite party Nos. 1-8 filed Title Execution Case No. 20 of 1997 in the Court of The Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 4, Dhaka praying for execution of the decree, following which the learned Executing Court appointed an Advocate Commissioner for the purpose and issued writ of delivery of possession to the Advocate Commissioner for execution of the award in 45-1/2 acre of unascertained land. It appears that in pursuance of the aforesaid writ the learned Advocate Commissioner along with a contingent of police force all on a sudden went to the spot on 18- 6-97 and on the showing of the petitioner forcibly evicted the petitioners' tenants who were living there and demolished the tin-shed structures. The learned Advocate Commissioner thereafter filed the report before the Court stating, inter alia, that he delivered possession to the petitioner of Title Execution Case No. 20 of 1997 in 18 acre of land but he could not deliver the - possession in the remaining portion of the suit property due to apprehension of tough resistance by the judgment- debtors and prayed for a larger contingent of police force for delivering possession to the decree-holder in the remaining portion of the suit property. It also appears that the present petitioners filed an application before the learned Execution Court under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for restoration of possession in the suit property from where they were allegedly dispossessed by the learned Advocate Commissioner.

5. The opposite parties contested the aforesaid application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure contending, inter alia, that the learned Executing Court rightly issued the writ of delivery of possession for giving physical possession of the suit property to the decree holder and the learned Advocate Commissioner in pursuance of the writ issued to him under Order 21 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure duly executed the writ and delivered possession to the decree-holder and, as such, the petitioners are not entitled to get any relief under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It was also contended that if any illegality was committed by the Executing Court, the petitioners had remedy before that Court but without availing the opportunity they are not entitled to invoke the application of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of possession and, as such, the application is liable to be rejected as being a misconceived one.

6. The learned Subordinate Judge on hearing the contending parties at length, has been pleased by the impugned order dated 19-10-97 to reject the petitioners' application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid impugned order, the petitioners moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that in view of the fact that the award, which was subsequently made Rule of the Court, merely determined the entitlement of the parties in respect of their shares in the disputed property without any reference to possession therein, the award decree are essentially a preliminary decree and it could not be executed without making the decree a final one in accordance with law and consequently all actions taken by the learned Advocate Commissioner in pursuance of the order of the Execution Court in forcibly evicting the petitioners' tenants from an unspecified portion of the suit property and demolition of the tin-sheds standing therein and delivering possession to the decree-holder are in clear violation of the provision of law and, as such, the petitioners are entitled under the law to restoration of possession in the suit property from where - they were illegally and arbitrarily dispossessed by the action of the Court. The learned Advocate for the petitioners further submits that in view of the fact that the impugned decree is not such a decree as in a partition suit and the award, which was not a registered one, was not evidently executable per se and consequently the action of the learned Advocate Commissioner in dispossessing the petitioners from the suit property in exercise of the purported power given to him by the Execution Court is illegal and consequently the petitioners have no other efficacious remedy available to them for redress of their grievance and, as such, they are entitled to get relief by way of restoration of possession by resorting to the provision of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate further submits that in view of the fact that the action of the learned Advocate Commissioner dispossessing the petitioners from their suit property causing them irreparable loss and injury and the writ of delivery of possession was evidently an error of law committed by the learned Execution Court in purported execution of an inexecutable decree, the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in refusing relief to the petitioners under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Subordinate Judge also erred in law in not properly appreciating the scope of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in asking the petitioners to initiate independent proceedings for redress of their grievance on an erroneous view of law and the same has occasioned a failure of justice.

8. Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties, on the other hand, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge was perfectly justified in passing the impugned order on assigning cogent and sound reasons and consequently the impugned order does not suffer from any illegality occasioning failure of justice so as to justify interference by this Court exercising revisional jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Fazlul Karim further submits that in view of the provision of Order 21 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure the executing Court has ample power to appoint Commissioner for executing a decree and if the petitioners really feel aggrieved by the action of the learned Advocate Commissioner, they are required to place the matter before the learned. Court by challenging the decree itself but instead of doing so, they invoked the application of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which is not maintainable in law. Mr. Fazlul Karim submits that on detailed discussion and proper appreciation of the materials on record, the learned Subordinate Judge rightly passed the impugned order as in the facts of the case there is no scope for giving any relief to the petitioners under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and consequently the petitioners are not entitled to get any relief in the case.

The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners has placed before me the impugned order as well as the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for restoration of the suit property from where they were admittedly dispossessed by the learned Advocate Commissioner on 18-6-97 it is seen from the report of the learned Advocate Commissioner that he delivered possession to the opposite parties on 18-6-97 in 0.18 acre of land from plot No. 989 but he could not deliver possession in the remaining portion of the suit property due to tough resistance put by the present petitioners, for which he asked for a larger contingent of police force. It is found from the report of the learned Advocate Commissioner that he delivered possession to the opposite party in 0.18 acre of land on the showing and choice of the opposite parties. It appears that 3 plots are involved in the award' decree but the learned Advocate Commissioner gave possession to the opposite parties only from plot No. 989 by evicting the petitioners' men therefrom, who were residing in the sheds, which were subsequently demolished in the process, although there was no specific order for demolition of any structure. This action of the learned Advocate Commissioner prima facie betrays a sense of over zealousy on his part.

9. An award decree is nothing more thana preliminary decree as is usually made in a partition suit. Before an award decree can be executed it is necessary to make it final by initiating necessary proceedings. But in this case it appears that no such steps were taken by the opposite parties. The award decree simply determines the shares of the parties in the joint property without allotting specific sahams to them and there is nothing in the award in respect of actual possession in the disputed property. The learned Executing Court straightaway issued the writ of delivery of possession at the instance of the decree holder without complying with the provision of Order 21 rule 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

10. Order 26 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure authorizes the Court to issue commission to make partition of undivided properties according to the rights declared by the Court in favour of the contending parties. Rule 14 Order 26 of the Code provides the procedure for the Commissioner for preparation and allotment of sahams to the contending parties and thereafter to submit a signed report to the Court which, after hearing any objections by an aggrieved party, shall vary or set aside the report on the merit of the objection. In this case no such exercise appears to have been made by the learned Execution Court as well as the learned Advocate Commissioner. What happened in this case is that, on receiving the application for execution of the award decree from the opposite parties, the learned Execution Court straightaway issued writ to the learned Advocate Commissioner for delivery of possession to the opposite parties without making the preliminary decree final and without preparing sahams for the respective parties in accordance with law. It is obvious that the petitioners had no opportunity to place their case either before the learned Executing Court or before the learned Advocate Commissioner before they were summarily dispossessed on 18-6-97 from the suit property by the learned Advocate Commissioner. Between the passing of the award decree and execution of decree there ensued a big gap and obviously the procedures adopted by the learned Execution Court are not contemplated in law. So, the action of the learned Advocate Commissioner in pursuance of the order of the learned Executing Court in effecting delivery of possession to the opposite parties in an undivided and unspecified joint property at the instance of the opposite parties cannot be sustained as being illegal and arbitrary, for which the petitioners have suffered irreparable losses and injury.

11. The submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite parties that the petitioners had other remedy available to them for redressing their grievance and as such they are not entitled to get any relief under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not amenable to reason, justice and good conscience.

12. It is well-settled that no party to a proceeding should suffer due to the act of the Court. One of the first and highest duties of all Courts is to take care that the act of the Court does not cause any injury to any of the suitors. It will be quite equitable if the illegal and arbitrary action of the learned Advocate Commissioner in pursuance of the writ issued by the learned Executing Court in violation of the provision of law is allowed to stand, driving the petitioners to have recourse to other arduous costly and time consuming exercises for getting back their lost possession in suit property from which they have been illegally dispossessed. Under such circumstances, I am of the view that this is an appropriate case where relief under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is clearly available to the petitioners and the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in rejecting the petitioners' application under section. 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on an erroneous view of law occasioning failure of justice

<u>13. Mr Fazlul Karim has cited before me the case of Abdul Hamid vs Abdul Jabbar; reported in 34 DLR (AD) 208 in which it has been held that by restitution the parties are to be put in the position which they would have occupied but for the erroneous decision. It has also been held that the distinction between restitution under section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is that action under the former is mandatory whereas action under the latter is discretionary. It is needless to say that this discretion has to be exercised according to sound and established judicial principles and not fancifully. The cited decision does not help the petitioners in any way rather it lends support to the opposite parties. Mr Fazlul Karim then refers to the case of Devaki Amma Mookambi Amma vs Meenakshy Amma Vijayama and another, reported in AIR 1990 Kerala 37. The cited decision is also of no assistance to the opposite parties as the facts and circumstances of the cited decision are quite distinguishable from the present case.</u>

<u>14. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, has cited before me the case of Mababala Hegde vs Meenakshi Heggadithi and others reported in AIR 1960. Mysore 198. In this case the nature and scope of an award decree has been elaborated. Mr Quayum also cited before me the case reported in 43 DLR 207 and 539, AIR 1922 (PC) 269, 5 BCR (AD) 346 and 12 BLD (AD) 245 in support of his submission.</u>

<u>15. In all these cases the scope of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been enunciated. The consistent trend of judicial decisions is that a Court cannot remain silent about the sufferings of a party for no fault of its own by not resorting to the exercise of the inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and pushes him to take independent, time consuming and costly proceedings. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record, I am of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in rejecting the petitioners' application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure illegally and arbitrarily, occasioning failure of justice.</u>

16. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs and the impugned order dated 19-10-97 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat Court No. 4, Dhaka in Title Execution Case No. 20 of 1997 rejecting the petitioners' application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of possession in the suit land is set aside. Accordingly, the petitioners' application for restoration under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is allowed. In view of the fact that the petitioners were dispossessed from the suit property by the learned Advocate Commissioner in pursuance of the order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in Title Execution Case No. 20 of 1997, I find no difficulty in restoration of possession to the petitioners. The learned Subordinate Judge is accordingly directed to restore to the petitioners possession of the suit property from where they were dispossessed by the learned Advocate Commissioner on 18-6-97 in execution of the writ issued to him by the learned Executing Court.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

lawyer:
Syed Mahmud Hossain with Shahana Hoque, Advocates------ For the Petitioner.
Md. Latifur Rahman, Advocate------For Opposite Party No. 11 (C).
parties:
Sabirannessa and others ----- Petitioners
Vs
Kabir Ahmed and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-12 to show cause why the order dated 22-2-93 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Comilla Sadar in Partition Suit No. 150 of 1964 shall not be set aside.

2. The short fact leading to this Rule is that, opposite parties 1 and 2 as plaintiffs instituted Partition Suit No. 150 of 1964 in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Comilla against the present petitioners and others and the same was decreed in preliminary form on 13-6-67 and thereafter final decree was passed on 10-11-87 which was subsequently set aside. On 6-1-1993 the learned Assistant Judge accepted the commissioner's report and the preliminary decree was made final which was subsequently sealed and signed on 21-11-1993 and then Title Execution Case No.1 of 1993 was initiated for getting possession in the land and that execution proceeding is still pending. Thereafter defendants 8Ka-8Cha and 121 and defendants 67, 37, 1 Cha, 2 and the plaintiffs filed a petition under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure alleging, that the newly appointed commissioner has not distributed the saham in accordance with the preliminary decree and he has also not given to the defendants and allotted more land than some of the parties are entitled to. The learned Assistant Judge then after hearing the parties by his order dated 22-2-93 set aside, the final decree. The  petitioner then being aggrieved by the impugned order moved this court and obtained the present Rule.

3. Mr. Syed Mahmud Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submits that when the final decree was sealed and signed by the trial Court a petition filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not maintainable. He further submits that if the final decree is to be questioned the aggrieved party may move the appellate Court and the same cannot be set aside under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Assistant Judge failed to appreciate the provision of law and illegally passed the order dated 22-2-93.

4. Mr. Md. Latifur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 11(c), on the other hand, submits that the final decree must be in accordance with the terms of the preliminary decree and if the same is found to be not in terms and if there is illegality in distribution of the proceeding land this may be interfered with and the learned Assistant Judge has not committed any illegality in passing the impugned order.

5. Admittedly, the trial Court accepted the Commissioners report and final decree was drawn up and the same was sealed and signed by the trial Court on 21-1-1993. Thereafter a petition was filed by the aforesaid parties under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for setting aside the decree on the ground that it has not been drawn up in accordance with the preliminary decree and some of the parties have not been given any land.

<u>6. There is nothing before this Court at this stage to hold that any of the parties preferred any appeal against the preliminary decree and admittedly previously another Commissioner was appointed for distribution of the Saham which was subsequently cancelled and a new Commissioner was appointed who submitted his report and there was no objection from either side against that Commissioner report and, as such, the report was accepted and the final decree was drawn up which was duly sealed and signed by the trial Court. It appears that against that final decree neither party moved any higher court in appeal; though there may be an appeal against the final decree, on the ground that the decree was not drawn up in accordance with the terms of the preliminary decree and also on the ground of non-distribution of land in terms of the preliminary decree. When the suit has been finally disposed of, with the signing and sealing of the final decree there cannot be any petition filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that decree cannot be interfered with under this provision of the Code. When the aggrieved party has other remedy available, the inherent power of the Court under section 151 of the Code cannot be invoked. The learned Assistant Judge committed illegality in interfering with the final decree under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It further appears that the trial Court interfered with the decree of the ground that when the commissioner submitted his report, the matter was not brought to the notice or the parties in the litigation and, as such, they failed to file any objection. But it is well-settled that when parties are aware that the matter has been referred to a Commissioner they must be vigilant. It appears that in the present case the parties were not vigilant and they took no steps in filing any objection against the Commissioner's report and their indolent act cannot be ground to set aside the final decree drawn up after long and arduous litigations. In arriving at this decision reliance is placed in the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 51 (Abdur Rahman & ors. vs. Sultan @ Sultan and ors).</u>

7. Having given my anxious consideration to the materials on record and hearing the learned Advocates of both the sides I hold that the learned Assistant Judge committed illegality in setting aside the decree by order dated 22-2-93 and it requires interference.

8. The Rule is made absolute. The order dated 22-2-93 passed by the learned Assistant Judge in the aforesaid suit is hereby set aside. The order of stay passed earlier is hereby vacated.

The parties will bear their respective costs.

End.

lawyer:
Mahfuzur Rahman, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Q Akhtar Hossain, Asstt. Attorney-General ----- For the Respondent No. 2.
parties:
Rahela Khatun ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Chairman, Court of Settlement, Bangladesh Abandoned Buildings, Segunbagicha, Ramna, Dhaka and ors. ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Jalil J: This Rule calls in question a judgment and order dated 23.2.89 passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No. 1043 of 1987.

2. The petitioner's case is that she filed a case, under section 7 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985(Ordinance No. LIV of 1985) praying for exclusion of Holding No. 2/10, Block-F, Joint Quarter, Mohammadpur, (Kha-20) from the 'Kha' list of abandoned buildings published on 23.9.86 in Bangladesh. Gazette (Extraordinary) contending that the said holding was allotted to one Qumrul Hoque, an immigrant from India as a lessee by the Government and possession was delivered to him on 4.2.63. The said Qumrul Hoque executed a bainapatra in favour of Mosammat Rahela Khatun, the petitioner, on 20.11.70 agreeing to sell the said holding to her at a consideration of Tk. 8,000.00 on receipt of Tk. 6,500.00 as earnest money and thereafter the petitioner paid further amount of Tk. 1000.00 later on and there was a balance of Tk. 500.00 only to be paid at the time of registration of the kabala as per terms of the contract. The said vendor having failed to execute and register the necessary Deed, the petitioner filed. Title Suit No. 67 of 1975 against said Qumrul Hoque and obtained a decree for specific performance of contract and in execution of the said decree obtained a kabala through court on 25.9.79 and thereby the petitioner became the absolute owner of the said holding. In the said suit the Secretary, Ministry of Works and the Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka were added as defendants, but none contested the suit. The Government filed Miscellaneous Case No. 217 of 1986 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for setting aside the said ex parte decree under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was also dismissed for default. Thereafter the said holding was included in the 'Kha' list of the abandoned buildings on 23.9.86 published in the Bangladesh Gazette and, as such, the petitioner had to file the said case.

3. The respondent-Government did not file any written statement but contested the case by way of making verbal submissions contending that the whereabouts of the petitioner's vendor were not known and he left the house uncared and, as such, it vested in the Government under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and was allotted to one Mariam Begum on 1.4.72 and that the petitioner's Bainapatra is a concocted one executed by fictitious person other that the lessee and the transfer through Court is the outcome of the fraudulent decree and is void ab initio.

4. The Court of Settlement after hearing dismissed the case by the impugned judgment and order dated 23.2.89 as aforesaid.

5. Being aggrieved by the said order, the petitioner filed an application under Article 102 of the Constitution in this Court on which the aforesaid Rule was issued calling upon the respondents, namely, the Chairman, Court of Settlement and the Secretary, Ministry of Works to show cause why the said judgment and order passed by the Settlement Court, Dhaka on 23.2.89 in case No. 1043 of 1987 should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

6. The respondent No. 2 Government of Bangladesh, filed an affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the writ petition and contending, in substance, that the petitioner's sale deed is a fictitious document and the agreement and all other papers in that connection are forged but he obtained the decree by practicing fraud upon the Court which is hit by Articles 6, 14(1), 23 and 24 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and by section 44 of the Evidence Act. It was further stated that the original lessee Qumrul Hoque was not present in Bangladesh after liberation but the petitioner showed his appearance in the suit by false presentation and that during liberation movement said Qumrul Hoque left Bangladesh with members of his family and did not return back and so the holding in question vested in the government as an abandoned property.

7. Mr. Mahfuzur Rahman, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the learned Court of Settlement acted without lawful authority in discarding the decree of the competent Court followed by execution and registration of the sale deed and that the Court of Settlement has no jurisdiction to do so. He further submits that the Government is estopped from questioning the propriety of the decree and the document executed in execution thereof as the Government was a party to that suit and that the holding in question was never an abandoned property within the definition of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972.

8. Mr. Quazi Akhtar Hossain, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 2, on the other hand, submits that the alleged agreement although executed in 1970 was not acted upon till the suit was filed and the petitioner did not acquire any title before the decree and, as such, in 1972 Qumrul Hoque remained the owner and he having left the place, it was rightly taken over as an abandoned property and still continuing as abandoned property and all subsequent acts are void as no suit lies touching an abandoned property. He further submits that the learned Court of Settlement acted with lawful authority in rejecting the case.

9. The petitioner has filed the agreement dated 20.11.70, a Photostat copy of the plaint of Title Suit No. 67 of 1975, a copy of the decree, a copy of the application for execution of the decree and the sale deed executed through Court as Annexure 'A' respectively to the petition. The copy of the impugned judgment has been filed as Annexure I to the petition.

10. It appears that the agreement was executed on 20.11.70 and on the basis of that agreement a decree was passed for specific performance of contract and a deed of sale was executed and registered through Court in execution of the said decree. It further appears that the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Housing and Settlement, Government of Bangladesh and the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka were defendant Nos. 2 and 3 in the said suit.

11. The learned Court of Settlement came to the finding that the bainapatra was executed by a fictitious person other than the lessee and that the lessee was absent possibly because he left the country as alleged by the Government and the petitioner could not establish the whereabouts and presence of the lessee and, as such, the holding fell within the mischief of Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. It was further held that the transfer is subject to Articles 6, 14(1) of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 read with section 44 of the Evidence Act and Article 5(2) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985.

<u>12. We have already observed that on the basis of the agreement dated 30.11.70 a decree for specific performance of contract was passed and in execution of the decree a deed of sale was executed and registered and the Government was a party to that suit. Hence, the said decree is binding on the Government unless and until the said decree is set aside or declared void by any court of competent jurisdiction. A party to the suit cannot say that an agreement is forged which was the basis of the decree. The Court of Settlement has no power to set aside a decree of the Civil Court but it has the jurisdiction only to decide the matter on the basis of the papers produced and so the decree stands against the Government. It further appeared that the Government filed a case under Order, 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the said ex parte decree but it was rejected.</u>

13. Now turning to the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 it may be said that the observations of the learned Court of Settlement about the application of Articles 6 and 14(1) of the said Order would have been held valid had the said holding been an abandoned property.

It appears that before the said President's Order came into being, the owner of the property, namely the lessee from the Government entered into an agreement in 1970 and by that agreement the petitioner acquired a valuable right on the property. Had this agreement been not acted upon, it could have been struck down, but, in fact, on the basis of the said agreement a decree was passed followed by execution and registration of a deed of sale. So, in this view of the matter, there is no reason to hold that the said holding is an abandoned property. It may be managed by the Government treating it as an abandoned property but unless it is covered by the definition of abandoned property in terms of Article 2 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972, the possession and management of the Government will not make the property an abandoned property and the Government is liable to release the property in favour of the petitioner.

14. As to the assertion of the Government that the owner Qumrul Hoque left the country and did not turn up and the property was accordingly taken over as an abandoned property, no paper nor any evidence was produced before the Court of Settlement save and except the verbal submission of the learned Advocate appearing for the state.

15. Be that as it may, without entering into the disputed question of facts, it may be said that even not a scrap of paper showing that the said property was taken over as an abandoned property was produced by the Government either before the Court of Settlement or in this Court, It is the case of the petitioner that by virtue of the agreement he has been in possession of the same. However, we have already observed that we are not going to enter into the disputed question of facts as to whether the petitioner or the Government is in possession of the holding in question.

<u>16. The learned Court of Settlement also referred to section 44 of the Evidence Act in this connection.</u>

<u>For proper appreciation, we quote the section as under:—</u>

<u>"44. Any party to a suit or other proceeding may show that any judgment, order or decree which is relevant under sections 40, 41, or 42 and which has been proved by the adverse party, was delivered by a Court not competent to deliver it, or was obtained by fraud or collusion."</u>

<u>17. So, this section goes against the respondents as the petitioner produced a judgment and decree. The burden is on the adverse party, namely, the Government in this case, to show that the Court was not competent to pass the decree.</u>

18. In the facts and circumstances as discussed above, we are of the opinion that the learned Court of Settlement acted without lawful authority in dismissing the case.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without, however, any order as to costs and the judgment and order dated 23.2.89 passed by the Court of Settlement in case No. 1043 of 1987 as evidenced by Annexure Ito the petition is declared to have been made without any lawful authority.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and order dated 26-10-92 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar in Other Execution Case No. 70 of 1964 allowing the application filed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and directing restoration of possession of the suit land in favour of the judgment debtors.

2. Facts that have given rise to this Rule, in brief, are that the plaintiff brought Title Suit No. 173 of 1961 in the Court of the then Munsif, Cox's Bazar against the defendants for declaration of his title to the suit land and for khas possession after demolition of the structures standing thereon. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1-3 by filing a written statement. After hearing the trial Court decreed the suit of the plaintiff by his judgment and decree dated 14-1-1964. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendants 1-3 preferred Title Appeal No. 86 of 1963 in the Court of the District Judge, Chittagong. On transfer the appeal was heard by the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong who by his judgment and decree dated 10-2-1964 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. After disposal of the aforesaid Title Appeal the plaintiff put the decree to execution by starting Execution Case No. 70 of 1964 in the Court of the Senior Assistant Judge (then Munsif), Cox's Bazar. Defendant-appellants 1-3 preferred Second Appeal No. 583 of 1964/Civil Rule No. 213(S) of 1964 before the then East Pakistan High Court and the High Court was pleased to stay all further proceedings of other Execution Case No. 70 of 1964 passed in Civil Rule No. 213(S) of 1964 on 4-12-1964 till disposal of the second appeal. The Second Appeal No. 583 of 1964 was dismissed for default on 4-8-78. As the decree holder Md Abul Quashem, and the judgment debtor-defendants 1-3 died leaving behind their legal heirs, the said legal heirs were duly substituted in the Execution Case No. 70 of 1964 by the Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar. On 27-5-1992 the heirs of the decree holder filed an application for proceeding with the execution case and the Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar allowed the prayer of the decree holders by his order dated 27-5-1992 and fixed 3-6-1992 for taking necessary steps in the case. By an order dated 3-6-1992 the Assistant Judge directed the decree holders to deposit Taka 300.00 as fee of the Nazir. On the prayer of the Judgment debtors the Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar appointed an Advocate Commissioner for local inspection of the suit land to ascertain if there were huts standing on the suit land and the Advocate Commissioner accordingly inspected the suit land on 28-4-1964 and submitted his report on the following day stating that there was no shop house and valuable goods on the suit land. The Nazir of the Court delivered possession of the suit land to the decree holders on 9-6-1992 and submitted his report before the Assistant Judge accordingly. The judgment debtors thereafter filed a written objection against the report of the Nazir on 10-6-1992 and 29- 6-1992 was fixed for hearing of the objection. On 29-6-1992 the judgment debtors filed an application before the Assistant Judge under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure stating, inter alia, that the starting of the execution case on 20-5-1992 was not intimated to the judgment debtors or their Advocate and that the schedule of the decree is vague and indefinite and that the execution case in question is barred by limitation and that their possession in the suit land be restored to them.

3. The decree holders contested the said application of the judgment debtors by filing a joint written objection on 19-8-1992 wherein they denied all material allegations made in the application. It is asserted by the decree holders that the judgment debtors or their engaged lawyer had knowledge of the execution case right from 20-5-1992 and that notices were duly served upon the substituted heirs of the original judgment debtors, that the execution proceeding is not barred by limitation and that, as such, the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure as filed by the judgment debtors is liable to be rejected. The Senior Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar heard both sides on 26-10-1992 and allowed the application of the judgment debtors and directed restoration of possession of the suit land in favour of the judgment debtor upon a finding that the execution proceeding is barred by limitation.

4. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order dated 26-10-1992 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar the decree holders moved this Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule.

5. The Rule is opposed by the opposite party Nos. 1-6. From the impugned order it appears that the executing Court has held that the Other Execution Case No. 70 of 1964 is barred by limitation as per the provisions of Article 181 of the Limitation Act for having revived the case after about 14 years since the dismissal of the Second Appeal No. 583 of 1964 on 4-8-1978. This finding of the executing Court necessitates the consideration of Article 181 of the Limitation Act. Article 181 provides for a limitation of 3 years with respect to applications for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere in the schedule or by section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure as mentioned in Article 181 provides for a limitation of 12 years in a case where an application is made to execute a decree. Neither in Article 181 of the Limitation Act nor in section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure the term 'revival' occurs. The language couched in Article 181 of the Limitation Act and section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure do not refer to pending execution case. The golden principle of interpretation of statute lays down that a statute is to be interpreted in its plain and ordinary meaning and no word can be imported which is not found there. Admittedly, the decree holder petitioners started the instant execution case on 18-4-1964 which is well within the period of limitation of three years from the decree. The present case seems to have had a chequered history after its filing in the year 1961. It culminated in the dismissal of the Second Appeal being No. 583 of 1964 on 4-8-78 and this second appeal was taken by the judgment debtors. So, it is clear that the judgment debtors-opposite parties were not altogether in the dark about the proceedings of the case till receipt of the records by the lower Court. It appears from Annexure-A, an application filed on behalf of the judgment debtor-opposite parties that they prayed for passing an order to the effect that the execution proceeding is barred by limitation and that possession of the suit property be restored to them. So, Annexure-A shows that the judgment debtor-opposite parties were aware of the execution proceeding at least on the date on which they made such an application. Now the central point that calls for determination is whether the execution proceeding is barred by limitation for not having proceeded with for a period of about 14 years and whether the period of limitation will be guided and governed by either Article 181 of the Limitation Act or under section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

<u>6. The provisions of Article 181 of the Limitation Act or section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure, in my opinion, will be applicable in the case of an application made for execution of a decree for the first time. It is submitted by Mr. Shafique Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioners that in the instant case the executing Court has committed gross illegality in holding that execution proceeding is barred by limitation under Article 181 of the Limitation Act. He further goes on to argue that the unfortunate part of the impugned order is that the executing Court has gone to the extent of giving direction for restoration of possession of the suit property in favour of the judgment debtors in the case where the petitioners obtained the decree after much hardships. It is argued by the learned lawyer of the petitioners that Other Execution Case No. 70 of 1964 is not barred by limitation and in this connection he refers to the decision reported in AIR 1964 (Assam) 64 in the case of Smt. Akani Das and others vs Muhiram Bharali and others. It is submitted by the petitioner's learned lawyer that while giving decisions in the aforesaid reported case, G Mehrotra, CJ relied upon the decision reported in AIR 1940 (Allahabad) 151 (FB). In the instant case the application of the petitioners for vacating the order of stay has been filed on 27-5-92. In my opinion, this application of the petitioners will be deemed to be an application for proceeding with the pending Other Execution Case No. 70 of 1964. It is not to be construed as a fresh application for execution. From the facts reported in AIR 1964 (Asaam) 54, it appears, that execution case was started in the year 1947 and the proceeding of the execution of the execution case was stayed pending disposal of a suit filed by a 3rd party and the said suit by that party was dismissed in 1955 and after dismissal of that suit execution proceeding which was stayed so long was started. It was held in the aforesaid reported case that the execution case or the execution proceeding is not barred under section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure or under Article 181 of the Limitation Act. From the facts in AIR 1940 Allahbad151 decision, it is revealed, that a mortgage suit was decreed on the 5th January, 1928 and a final decree under Order 34 rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure was passed in favour of the mortgagees on the 9th August, 1928. The decree holders applied for execution of their decree on the 19th December, 1930. The matter passed through several stages and the decree holders applied for execution of the mortgage decree against the judgment debtors on the 25th July, 1935. The judgment debtors raised objection contending that it was barred by limitation. In the course of arriving at the decision by the Full Bench several decisions were referred to and relied upon and it was the considered view of their Lordships in the AIR 1940 Allahabad 151 case that the decree holders are not required to file an application for proceeding with the pending execution case and it is the duty of the Court to proceed with the same suo-moto. The Full Bench of the Allahabad High Court considered the provisions of Article 181 of the Limitation Act. So, from the above decision it is clear that responsibility lay with the executing Court to proceed with the execution case suo-moto after dismissal of second Appeal No. 583 of 1964. After receipt of the records by the executing Court from the High Court Division it ought to have proceeded with the execution case and directed the decree holders to take steps, if any, and in the event of failure of the decree holders to take any step in the execution proceeding, the executing Court could either dismiss the case, strike it off or otherwise could dispose it of but in the instant case the executing Court did not do either of these three. In my opinion, the executing Court wrongly has held that the execution case in question is barred by limitation as per the provisions of Article 181 of the Limitation Act. As the Execution case is a pending case it is not hit by Article 181 of the Limitation Act. In this view of the matter the impugned judgment and order is not legally sustainable.</u>

7. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 26-10-1992 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar in Other Execution Case No. 70 of 1964 is hereby set aside.

Stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the pre-emptee directed against the judgment and order No.26 dated 21-6-87 passed by Assistant Judge, Dumuria, District Khulna in Miscellaneous Case No. 83 of 1986.

2. The opposite party a pre-emptor filed case under section 96 of EBSA and Tenancy Act in the Court of Assistant Judge, being Miscellaneous Case No. 37 of 1986 on 11-8-86 against the present petitioner and other opposite parties. Said Miscellaneous Case No. 37 of 1986 was decreed ex parte on 11-12-86. Thereafter the pre-emptee petitioner filed an application under Order 9 rule 13 of Civil Procedure Code which is the subject-matter of Miscellaneous Case No. 83 of 1986 on 27-12-86 alleging, inter alia, that the show cause notice and registered notice of the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case No. 37 of 1986 were not duly served upon him which were suppressed in collusion with the process server and thereby the pre-empter who in collusion with the process server and the simultaneous issue of registered letter under Order 5 rule 19B was not received by the petitioner rather received by one Nur Mohammad who is own man of the pre-emptor. The petitioner came to know the said miscellaneous Case No. 37 of 1986 from one Asaduzzaman only on 23-12-86 at his residence and thereafter learnt about the Miscellaneous Case No. 37 of 1986 and the ex parte decree; accordingly filed the Misc. Case No. 83 of 1986 under Order 9 rule 13 CPC for setting aside the ex parte decree on 27-12-86 well within 30 days. The certified copy of the said petition and Misc. Case No.83 of 1986 is made annexure C of this petition and certified copy of show cause notice with service return is filed as Annexure-D of this petition.

3. The present opposite party No.1 appeared in this Misc. Case No. 83 of 1986 and filed written objection on 25-2-87 denying all the allegations of the petitioner alleging due service and further asserting that Mokabila witness regarding service of show cause notice are relative of petitioner. It was also asserted that registered letter was duly served. The certified copy of said written objection is filed as annexure E of this petition. But he did not appear at the hearing of miscellaneous case.

4. The learned Assistant Judge by the impugned order rejected the said miscellaneous case.

5. Mr. MA Jabbar, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the opposite party No.1 has failed to discharge his onus to prove service inasmuch mokabila witness deposed denying service. and there was an initial error regarding service in the absence of non-examination of process server by the court before recording due service of notice upon the party and on the same day the case was set for ex parte hearing on 1-12-86. The learned Advocate further submits that in view of the fact that the service was under rule 17 of Order 5 the court has a duty to ascertain by enquiry as to whether summon has been duly served or not.

6. I have perused the service return and it appears that the process server has served the notice upon the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 by hanging at the door of the their residence and has filed a rubber stamp verification on 19-10-86 which was accepted as a valid service.

The report of the process server is as follows:

নিজ অনুসন্ধানে ও মোকাবিলাগণের পরিচয়মতে শরাপপুর সাকিনে আসিয়া উক্ত ১/২ নংপ্রতিপক্ষদ্বয়ের  বাড়িতে যাইয়া ডাকামতে ২নং প্রতিপক্ষ গরহাজির থাকায় উহার  পক্ষেকার্য্য কারক স্বামী ও স্বয়ং

১নং প্রতিপক্ষকে হাজির পাইয়া উহাতে ১নং উহার নিজ নামীয় ও ২নং উহার স্ত্রীর নামীয় নোটিশাদাদির মর্মজ্ঞাত করাইয়া রশিদ দিয়া লইতে বলায় তিনি রশিদ দিয়া না লওয়ায় উহাদের নামীয় নকল নোটিশাদী উহাদের বাটির ধারে লটকাইয়া দিয়া জারী করিলাম। মোকাবিলাগণ স্বাক্ষর না করায় উহাদের নাম লিখিয়া লইলাম।

7. It appears from the order sheet of the Miscellaneous Case No. 37 of 1986 that the case was filed on 11-8-1986 and 20-8-1986 was fixed for filing challan, on 20-8-86 notices of the case was ordered to be issued upon the opposite parties fixing 5-11-1986 for return and on that date that case was adjourned to 12-11-86 for return of AID, on 12-11-86 the court recorded the order as under;

ছায়েল হাজিরা দিয়াছেন। নোটিশ জারী হয়। এডি ফেরৎ সে। তখনি কেহ হাজির হইয়া আপত্তি দাখিল দেন নাই। ইং ১-১২-৮৬ তারিখ একতরফা নিস্পত্তির জন্য দিন রহিল।

on 1-12-1986 the petitioner therein prayed for time and the case was adjourned to 11-12-1986 for ex parte hearing, on 11-12-1986 the case was heard and decreed ex parte.

<u>8. The relevant provisions regarding service of summons notices involved in this case are rules 17, 19 and 19A of Order V of CPC. In view of the service of notice under rule 17 Court has a duty to examine the serving officer on oath touching his proceeding and to ascertain by enquiry in the matter as to whether the summons have been duly served or not and declare that the summons/notices have been served. Rule 19A thereof goes to show that any declaration by the process server should be received as a piece of evidence on making necessary inquiry by examining the process server on oath or making any such further enquiry.</u>

9. In the case of Johara Begum vs. Rafiqul Kader 25 DLR 91 it has been held that Rule 19A cannot be read to take away the responsibility of the court as provided in Rule 19, nor can it be read to justify recording in the order sheet as a matter of routine that summons was duly served.

10. In the case of Santosh Kumar Chakraborty and ors vs. MA Motaleb Hossain & on, 36 DLR AD 248 it has been held that it was incumbent upon the court to make an enquiry and to record a declaration of due service in spite of the fact that the return accompanied a declaration as to service in which case the examination of the process server is not mandatory.

11. In view of the above, when the service has been effected by hanging the notice on the door of the house of the petitioner, a duty is cast upon the court to be satisfied on enquiry that notice has been duly served.

12. In the instant case the learned Munsif having recorded in his order dated 12-11-86 that নোটিশ জারী হয় is not the requirement of law as to due service of notice and, as such, there was no due service of notice in the case.

<u>13. Accordingly, the learned Munsif erred in law in fixing the case for ex parte hearing by the same order dated 12-11-86 and disposing of the case ex parte by order dated 11-12-86 is illegal and, as such, the said impugned order is liable to be set aside and accordingly the same is set aside as the same was passed in the absence of any due service of notice upon the petitioner.</u>

14. The pre-emptor has claimed pre-emption in respect of kabala dated 1-6-86 and the alleged transfer was effected on 21-12-1986 even after the ex parte decree dated 11-12-86. The ex parte decree dated 11-12-1986 has been impugned in this proceeding and the pre-emptee had interest in the case which accrued on' 11-12-1986 and, as such, even after transfer on 21-12-86 the pre-emptee petitioner has a right to proceed with the ex parte decree and as such the case is maintainable and the proceeding under Order 9 rule 13 CPC do not become infructuous by the alleged transfer on 21-12-1986.

15. In view of the above, the impugned judgment and order dated 21-6-87 passed by the learned Assistant Judge are set aside and the Miscellaneous Case No. 83 of 1986 is hereby allowed and the Miscellaneous Case No. 37 of 1986 is restored to its original file and number setting aside the exparte decree dated 11-12-86.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Mahfuzur Rahman J: This Rule under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against an order passed by Subordinate Judge, 3rd, Court, Dhaka on 30-11-97 in Partition Suit No.176 of 1995 staying all further proceeding of Execution Case No. 16 of 1995 pending in the Court of the Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka till the disposal of the suit.

2. The short facts relevant are that, the petitioners being plaintiff instituted SCC Suit No. 8 of 1994 before the SCC Judge and Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka for eviction of the tenant opposite party No. 1 from the shop room No. 2 in the ground floor of holding No. 20 Islampur Road within PS Kotwali, Dhaka on the ground of default in payment of monthly rent claiming opposite party No. 1 to be their monthly tenant. The petitioners also filed SCC Suit No. 9 of 1994 in the same Court for eviction of the opposite party No. 1 from shop room No. 9 in the 1st floor of the same holding. The opposite party No. 1 did not enter appearance in SCC Suit No. 9 of 1994 and the same was decreed ex parte on 25-9-94.

Thereafter the opposite party No. 1 filed an application for restoration of the suit after setting aside the ex parte decree in Miscellaneous Case No. 66 of 1994 which was dismissed by the judgment and order dated 28-10-96 and then the petitioner started Execution Case No. 16 of 1995.

3. The opposite party No. 1 filed written statement in SCC Suit No. 8 of 1994 admitting that he was a tenant under the petitioners but he purchased the portion of the suit premises from Mrs Akhtar Banu, another co-sharer of the suit premises by registered sale deed dated 3-8-85 and the suit was decreed against him. Opposite party No. 1 filed revisional application against the aforesaid judgment and order under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act before the High Court Division which was numbered as civil order No. 659 of 1996 and the Rule was discharged on 7-3-96 in limine. The opposite party No. 1 moved the Appellate Division by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 276 of 1996 which was rejected by their Lordships' judgment and order dated 7-7-96 holding that:

"it is established that as a person is a tenant he cannot be permitted during the continuance of the tenancy to resist a suit for eviction by his landlord as a subsequent purchaser from a co-sharer without surrendering his possession to his landlord. As, in the instant case, it is found that the petitioner was a tenant under the respondents to whom he paid rents upto December, 1990, he is debarred from setting up a claim of title in himself to resist the decree for eviction."

During the pendency of the aforesaid SCC Suit No. 8 of 1994 the opposite party filed a Partition Suit No. 175 of 1995 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka impleading the petitioners as defendants and opposite party No. 2 claiming partition of the alleged purchased shop of the aforesaid holding No. 20, Islampur Road, Dhaka:

4. On the application by opposite party No. 1 in Partition Suit No. 176 of 1995 under Order 21rule 29 of the Code the learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 24-7-96 stayed further proceedings of SCC Suit No. 8 of 1994 pending in the Court of the Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka. The petitioners also on 11-8-96 filed an application for setting aside the stay order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in Partition Suit No. 176 of 1995 and the opposite party No. 1 filed another application on 27-11-96 under Order 21 rule 29 of the Code before the learned Subordinate Judge in the same suit for stay of the proceedings of SCC Suit No. 9 of 1994 and the Execution Case No. 16 of 1995 pending before the Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka. Both the applications filed by the petitioners dated 11-8-96 and the application filed by opposite party No. 1 dated 27-11-96 were heard by the learned Subordinate Judge who by his order dated 30-11-96 allowed the petition dated 27-11-96 filed by the opposite party No. 1 praying for stay of further proceeding of Execution Case No. 16 of 1995 and dismissed the petition dated 11-6-96 filed by the petitioners for setting aside the order dated 24-7-96 staying the further proceeding of SCC Suit No. 8 of 1994.

5. As against that the petitioners moved this Court and obtained this Rule.

<u>6. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that in view of the established legal position as enunciated by the Appellate Division in the case of Md Atiqullah vs Mrs Sanawara Begum and others, reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 260, the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law resulting in his decision occasioning serious failure of justice in passing the impugned order. He further submits that in the aforesaid case the Appellate Division clearly held that a tenant cannot be permitted during the continuance of the tenancy to resist a suit for eviction by his landlord without surrendering his possession to his landlord, the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law in his decision resulting in an error of law occasioning serious failure of justice. He lastly, contends that both the suits are not in the same Court and Order 21 rule 29 of the Code has got no manner of application in this case when the proceedings as stayed are not pending in the same Court.</u>

7. None appears to oppose the Rule.

<u>8. We have perused the application and the relevant law. Admittedly both the SCC Suits are in the Court of the Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka and another in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 3d Court, Dhaka who passed the impugned order. Order 21 rule 29 provides as follows:</u>

<u>"29.-Where a suit is pending in any Court against the holder of a decree of such Court, on the part of the person against whom the decree was passed, the Court may, on such terms as to security or otherwise, as it thinks fit, stay execution of the decree until the pending suit has been decided."</u>

<u>Admittedly both the suits are not in the same Court and the impugned order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is absolutely illegal and has got no manner of application in this case. In the decision referred by Mr. Islam reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 260 their Lordships have also referred:</u>

<u>"This consistent view of the Appellate Division is that once it is found that a person is a tenant he cannot be permitted during the continuance of the tenancy to resist a suit for eviction by his landlord as a subsequent purchaser from a co-sharer without surrendering his possession to his landlord. In the instant case, the petitioner was found as a tenant under the respondents to whom he had paid rent and as such, he is debarred from setting up a claim-of title in himself to resist the decree for eviction."</u>

9. In view of the discussions and the decision referred above we are of the view that the impugned order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge cannot be sustained in law and is liable to be set aside.

10. In the result the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka on 30-11-97 staying the Execution Case No. 16 of 1995 of the Court of the Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka is hereby set aside.

The stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated. Communicate the order to the Court below at once.

End.
