full_judgment:
Md. Ansar Ali J : This Rule comes out of application by the plaintiff petitioner under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and is directed against an order dated 10.5.94 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka in Money Suit No. 1 of 1992 allowing an application by the defendant under Order 37 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure and also the subsequent orders dated 23,7.94 and 30.7.1994 passed by him allowing time to the defendant for filing written statement and fixing the date of hearing of the suit respectively.

2. Short facts relevant for the dismissal of the Rule may be stated as follows:

3. The plaintiff petitioner instituted the above suit against the defendant opposite party praying for a decree of Taka 8,00,000.00 with interest thereon i.e. a total sum of Taka 9,00,000.00 on the basis of a promissory note as executed by defendant opposite party in favour of the plaintiff petitioner. The said suit was admitted for hearing under Order 37 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the learned District Judge vide order dated 15.3.1992 with direction to issue summons upon the defendant asking him to appear within 10 days from the date of service thereof and to defend the suit according to law. The defendant-opposite party received the summons on 16.2.92 and thereafter entered appearance in the suit through his duly engaged lawyer and filed an application on 24.3.1992 praying for time to file written statement. The said application was posted for hearing on 8.4.1992. On 8.4.1992 the defendant filed another application supported by an affidavit with a prayer for leave to appear and file written statement within a month but the plaintiff also filed an application on that day for passing a decree in her favour according to law as the defendant failed to seek leave to appear and defend the suit in accordance with rule 2(2) of Order 37 CPC, The learned District Judge fixed 15.4.1992 for hearing both the applications and accordingly on 15.4.1992 after hearing both the sides, the learned District Judge found that the defendant had disclosed no defence and also did not seek leave to appear and defend the suit in due course; hence in pursuance of  the provisions of rule 2(2) of Order 37 CPC he passed the decree in favour of the plaintiff and rejected the application of the defendant by his order dated 15.4.1992. Thereafter the defendant-opposite party filed an application by affidavit under Order 37 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 25.4.1992, for setting aside the ex parte decree dated 15.4.1992 and praying for leave to appear and defend the suit. It was alleged, inter alia, in the application under rule 4 of Order 37 CPC that the plaintiff is an adopted daughter of one Meherunnessa Begum, wife of Late Nowab Ali Ashgar Khan and that she did not inherit any property and she used to live with her said mother having no means of her own; that the defendant's sons purchased 6 kathas of land from the said Meherunnessa Begum and paid Taka 1,00,000.00 on the date of agreement for sale of 61-Purana Paltan holding and promised to pay Taka 8,00,000.00 after execution and registration of the sale deed and accordingly she executed and registered it on 28.8.86 in the name of the 3 sons of the defendant. It was further alleged that the plaintiffs mother obtained a signature from the defendant on a document for payment of Taka 8,00,000.00 on 24.8.86 and the same has now been treated as promissory note and further alleged in the application that the defendant paid the entire amount of Taka 8,00,000.00 through Nusrat Ali and obtained receipt from the mother of the plaintiff on 4.4.87 and as such nothing is due to the mother of the plaintiff from the defendant and now on a false plea, the aforesaid document is being used as a promissory note against the defendant petitioner and that the stamp of the so-called promissory note has been purchased in the name of Meherunnessa Begum mother of the plaintiff and that on the ill advice of some interested persons for the purpose of illegal gains this false suit has been started against the defendant Hence it was contended that the defendant made out a good defence in his application and also made up special circumstances and accordingly prayed for setting aside the ex parte decree and for leave to appear and contest the suit. The plaintiff decree-holder seriously opposed the application under rule 4 of Order 37 CPC. The learned District Judge after hearing both the sides was pleased to reject the application by his judgment and order dated 15.4.1992 holding inter alia that the decree was not a ex parte decree, rather it was a contested one; hence application under Order 37 rule 4 was not maintainable. The defendant being aggrieved by the said order of the learned District Judge moved this court in revision and obtained a Rule being Civil Revision No. 1381 of 1992 and the same was heard by a Division Bench of this Court which however found that the learned District Judge passed the order on a misconception of law and facts to the effect that the decree was a contested one but without considering the merit of the application, rejected the same most illegally and accordingly the said Bench set aside the impugned order dated 2.5.1992 of the learned District Judge and directed him to re-hear and dispose of the application of the defendant under Order 37 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure on merit within certain time vide judgment and order dated 7.3.94. Thereafter the learned District Judge heard the application again from both the sides on 10.5.1994 and passed the following order:

"Heard the learned advocates of both the sides in full Seen the order dated 7.3.1994 passed by the Honorable High Court Division by which the order dated 2.5.1992 of this court has been set aside. Perused the petition dated 25.4.1992 under Order 37, rule 4 CPC, grounds stated therein and the affidavit sworn by Ali Ahmed Patwari. Grounds seem to be acceptable. Hence ordered that the petition is admitted and allowed, the order and decree dated 15.4.92 is hereby set aside leave is given to the defdt to defend the suit. Execution is stayed until further orders, defdt. to file WS within 3 weeks."

4. Thereafter, it appears that the defendant filed a written statement in the suit on 30.7.94 without serving copy of the same on the other side. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order dated 10.5.1994 of the learned District Judge, the plaintiff petitioner moved the present application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule and also an order of stay of all further proceeding of the Money Suit pending in the Court of the learned District Judge, Dhaka.

5. Mr. MI. Faruqui with Mr. M Saleemullah, the learned Advocates appeared for the plaintiff-petitioner in support of the Rule and Md. Abdus Sobhan with Mr. Md. Ahsanullah Chowdhury the learned Advocates appeared for the defendant opposite party to oppose the Rule.

<u>6. Mr. MI Faruqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, seriously assails the impugned order of the learned District Judge on various grounds. His first contention is that the learned District Judge without applying his judicial mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the relevant provisions of law has passed the impugned order and thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and, as such, the impugned order is liable to be set aside. Referring to rules 2 and 3 of the Order 37 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the learned Advocate submits that a special procedure has been laid down for adjudication of the present kind of suit and the aforesaid rules provided that on receipt of the summons defendant is first required to seek leave to appear and to defend the suit, but in the instant case the defendant on receipt of the summons at once engaged a lawyer who entered appearance and filed an application on behalf of the defendant for time to file W/S. as done in normal suits. Subsequently he filed another application with affidavit for leave to appear and for time to file WIS but without disclosing any plausible defence from the side of the defendant The learned District Judge considering the above application rejected the prayer of the defendant and in view of sub-rule (2) of rule 2 of Order 37 passed the ex parte decree against the defendants on 15.4.92, hence there is no illegality in passing the said decree and the learned District Judge by an earlier order rightly rejected the application of the defendant under Order 37 rule 4 for setting aside the decree. Mr. Faruqui thereafter contends that from the application of the defendant-petitioner it is apparent that it was due to ignorance of law, the defendant could not take proper step in accordance with law to seek leave and to defend the suit and as such ex parte decree was liable to be set aside. But Mr. Faruqui the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner on the other hand contends the ignorance of law is no excuse and the same cannot constitute a special circumstance as required under rule 4 of Order 37 CPC. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has relied on a decision in the case of Kokarmal Gurudayal, vs. Sagarmal Bengani reported in AIR 1972 (Calcutta) 430, in relevant paragraph 74. Mr. Faruqui thereafter contends that the special circumstances as required under rule 4 of Order 37 CPC are not like sufficient cause as under Order 9 rule 13 CPC for setting aside the ex parte decree. Special circumstance is something more than ordinary and general circumstance. In support of his contention he has relied on a decision in the case of Mohan Lal vs. Om Prakash reported in AIR 1989 (Rajasthan) 132 where the meaning of special circumstance as distinguished from sufficient cause in Order 9 rule 13 has been given. In the said decision in paragraph 9 it has been held as follows :</u>

<u>"Under rule 13 of Or. 9 the court has power to set aside the ex parte decree if the defendant succeeds in satisfying the court that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing in the court Under rule4 of Or. 37 it is necessary for the defendant to show that "special circumstances" exist to set aside the decree. Mere "sufficient ground" cannot be equated with "special reason". "Sufficient cause" and "special circumstances" appearing in rule 13 of Or. 9 and rule 4, Or. 37 respectively are not synonymous. Legislature in its wisdom has used the words "special circumstances in rule 4 of Or. 37. The gravity of the reasons is more high in case of "special circumstances as provided under rule 4 of Or. 37. It will not be out of place here to mention that the words sufficient cause" and "special reasons" carry different meanings. The word "cause" cannot be equated with 'reasons' and similarly the word "sufficient" cannot be equated with "special". Special circumstances ordinarily mean that the defendant was prevented to appear in the Court on account of unavoidable circumstances beyond his control.</u>

<u>In such circumstances, I hold that the meaning assigned to the words sufficient cause" under rule 13 of Or. 9 cannot be given to the words used in rule 4 of Or. 37 to the words special reasons In this connection the learned Advocate has also referred to a decision in the case of Allied Bank of Pakistan Ltd. vs. VC Khilnani and 2 others reported in PLD 1984 (Karachi) 127 (131). In the aforesaid decision it has been held:</u>

<u>"Under rule 13 again the same words sufficient cause, have been used for setting aside an ex parte decree. Under Order XXXVII neither of these words have been used. The words used are "special circumstances" which seem to be different from "sufficient" or "good cause" and are comparatively narrower in their applicability. Special circumstances exclude ordinary circumstances or circumstances which may happen every day. They indicate such circumstances which may be rare, exceptional and are not of common occurrence. Therefore heavy burden is cast on the defendant to show that circumstances had arisen which besides being good cause or sufficient cause were of special nature due to which he was unable to appear or fulfill the condition laid down in the order."</u>

7. The last contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that the impugned order of the learned District Judge is not a speaking order and he has illegally allowed the application of the defendant petitioner under rule 4 Order XXXVII CPC without coming to any exclusive finding as to special circumstance which prevented the defendant from seeking leave and defending the suit and without coming to such a finding as to special circumstances, the impugned order setting aside the ex parte decree obtained by the plaintiff petitioner cannot be sustained in law and, according to him, it is in fact again a case of remand of the application under Order 37 rule 4 ere to the court of the learned District Judge for rehearing.

<u>8. Mr. Md. Abdus Sobhan, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant opposite party, on the other hand, submits that in the application for setting aside the ex parte decree under rule 4 Order 37 special circumstances have been specifically narrated and the defendant made out a plausible defence in his said application. Therefore his submission is that the learned District Judge rightly allowed the application under Order 37 rule 4 and set aside the ex prate decree and granted leave to the defendant to appear and contest the suit by filing written statement. The learned Advocate further submits that allowing an application under Order 37 rule 4 CPC is a discretion of the court and the learned District Judge has rightly exercised his discretion in the facts and circumstances of the case and set aside the ex parte decree as the defendant opposite party has been able to show plausible defence in his application. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has relied on a decision in the case of Fine Textile Mills Ltd. Karachi vs. Haji Umar reported in 15 DLR (SC) 86 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"In a suit filed under the provisions of Order XXXVII of the Civil Procedure Code where the defendant discloses upon his affidavits facts which may constitute a plausible defence or even show that there is some substantial question of fact or law which needs to be tried or investigated into, then he is entitled to leave to defend. What is more is that even if the defence set up be vague or unsatisfactory or thereby a doubt as to its genuineness, leave should not be refused altogether but the defendant should be put on terms either to furnish security or to deposit the amount claimed in court."</u>

<u>The principles upon which the provisions of Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure should be applied are that at the stage when leave to defend is sought the judge is not to try the action; he is to .see that there is a bonafide allegation on a triable issue, which is not illusory; he need not be satisfied that the defence will succeed: it is enough that such a plausible defence is verified by affidavit.</u>

<u>Where the allegations are not merely illusory leave to defend should be granted.</u>

<u>9. The next contention of Mr. Sobhan is that there is no laches or negligence on the part of the defence to seek leave and to defend the suit. As it was a special kind of suit having a special procedure for its adjudication, it is in fact due to mistake of law proper steps could not be taken in due course by the defendant in spite of his diligence. He therefore contends that the mistake of law committed by the learned Advocate of the defendant was a bonafide one and it was not accompanied with any negligence or inaction and, as such, the same may be considered also as one of the special circumstances in this case. It is further submitted that ignorance of law may not be constituted as a sufficient cause or special circumstance but mistake of law may be constituted as special circumstance if the same is a bonafide one and not accompanied with any negligence or inaction. It is further submitted that a client should not suffer for the fault of his lawyer and the bonafide mistake of law by the lawyer of the defendant in the facts and circumstances of the case may be constituted as special circumstances as required under Order 37 rule 4 CPC. In this regard the learned Advocate has relied on the same decision in the case of Komarmal Gurudayal, vs. Sagormal Bergani reported in AIR 1972 (Calcutta) 430 relevant page 442 paragraph 74 wherein it has been observed that ignorance of law may not be an excuse to constitute sufficient cause but mistake of law if bonafide and not accompanied by negligence or inaction may constitute sufficient cause.</u>

<u>10. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the impugned orders particularly the order dated 10-5-94 setting aside the ex parte decree and granting the defendant opposite party leave to appear and contest the suit. From a reading of the same it appears that the learned District Judge without considering the facts alleged in the application of the defendant under Order 37 rule 4 CPC and without coming to any finding as to whether those constitute special circumstance or circumstances justifying setting aside the impugned ex parte decree and giving the defendant leave to appear and to defend the suit wrongly allowed the application and set aside the impugned decree dated 15-4-1992 and granted leave to the defendant to defend the suit. In our view, the impugned order is not at all a speaking order in conformity with rule 4 Order 37 CPC as stated hereinafter. Order 37(4)</u>

<u>"After decree the Court may, under special circumstance, set aside the decree, and, if necessary, stay or set aside execution, and may give leave to the defendant to appear to the summons and to defend the suit, if it seems reasonable to the Court so to do, and on such terms as the Court thinks fit."</u>

<u>Hence, special circumstances must be found by the court concerned before setting aside an ex parte decree under Order 37 CPC.</u>

11. In view of our above observation and finding we are of the opinion that in the interest of justice, the learned District Judge should again be directed to hear the application of the defendant under rule 4 Order 37 CPC and pass necessary order in accordance with law, keeping in view the provisions of Order 37 particularly rules 2, 3 and 4 therein. The impugned order dated 10.5.94 therefore cannot be sustained in law and the same is liable to be set aside.

12. The Rule is therefore made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned order dated 10.5.94 is accordingly set aside and the learned District Judge is directed to rehear the application of the defendant under rule 4 Order 37 of the Code of Civil Procedure and write out a proper judgment and order in accordance with law and dispose of the same within 2(two) weeks from the date of receipt of this judgment and order. The order of stay of all further proceedings of the suit shall continue till disposal of the application of the defendant under Order 37 rule 4 afresh in accordance with law. The other 2 orders namely, orders dated 23-7-94 and 30-7-94 passed in the said suit will follow the consequences of the result of the application under Order 37 rule 4 CPC after re-hearing.

Communicate this order and send down the records to the court below at once.

End.
