case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 30 October 1992 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in First Miscellaneous Appeal from Original Order (Award) No. 224 of 1990).
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, C.J.: Government is the appellant in this appeal by special leave. The main question raised here is whether the limitation for filing an appeal against a decree will run from the date of the decree or from the date on which the decree has been amended on an application under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure, briefly the "Code". Contention of the learned Additional Attorney-General is that when a decree has been amended, the original decree does not exist and the decree that has been amended is the only decree in the eye of law and hence limitation will start from the date of the amendment. But reply to this contention given by Mr. Giasuddin Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate for the respondents, is that on application under section 152 of the Code the original decree remains intact but only some clerical mistakes or accidental omissions are corrected, and as such, this date of correction, whether it is called an amendment or correction, cannot be the date of the decree for the purpose of challenging it in appeal. Facts leading to this question are given below.

2. In LA Case No. 41/64-65 the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, requisitioned the respondents land measuring about 1.23 acres along with lands of some other persons, on 25 May 1967 under section 3 of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948—Act XIII of 1948, briefly the "Act", and later on acquired it for extension of the Second Capital at Sher-e-Bangla Nagar. Case of the appellant-government is that by serving a notice under section 5(1)(a) of the Act on 6 June 1967 they proceeded to acquire the land the possession of which has already been taken. The LA Collector assessed compensation for the land at Taka 1.10 lakh (and some odd) out of which the respondents-land owners-received Taka 1.08 lakh (and some odd) in the period between 1968 and 1973. The Government issued a Notification on 26 July 1983, which was published in the Gazette on 11 August 1983, under section 5(7) of the Act finally acquiring the land. The land owners not being satisfied with the amount of compensation as assessed by the Collector prayed for arbitration; accordingly, the matter went to the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, who was an Arbitrator appointed by the Government under section 7(b) of the Act. Thus Arbitration Case No. 333 of 1984 started. The Arbitrator, after hearing the parties, gave his award on 28 May 1985. In this award compensation determined was Taka 37.71 lakh and some odd in addition to the amount already paid. Respondents-land owners filed Execution Case No. 24 of 1986 for realisation of the amount of compensation and in that execution proceedings the appellant appeared and prayed for time to pay the decretal amount. But on 5 May 1987 the appellant filed an application to the Arbitrator for correction of the decree (award) under section 152 of the Code pointing out that in the judgment of the Arbitrator, the area of the land acquired was shown to be 1.35 acres instead of 1.23 acres, and, as such, the award needed to be corrected by reducing the amount. The Arbitrator, by an order dated 10 March 1990, corrected the award reducing the amount of compensation by about four lakh of taka, that is, to Taka 33,63,958.22 (thirty-three lakh and odd). The appellant then filed an appeal-FMA No. 224 of 1990-before the High Court Division on 26 May 1990. The High Court Division found that the appeal was barred by limitation since it was not filed within 60 days from the date of the decree that is, 28 May 1985, and dismissed the appeal on this ground, by a judgment dated 29 October, 1992.

3. Leave was granted by us to consider the question, as already stated at the beginning, whether the limitation will start from the date of the original decree (28.5.85) or from the date of its correction (10.3.90), and also to consider whether the second contention of the appellant that the decree itself is void and nullity, in that it was made in violation of the mandatory provision of section 7(e)(i) of the Act. This section provides that the Arbitrator in making an award shall, among other things, take the average market value of the land of similar description and with similar advantages in the vicinity "during the twenty-four months preceding the date of service of notice under section 5(1)(a)" of the Act; but in this case the Arbitrator had taken the average value of land during the twenty-four months preceding the date of the Notification under section 5(7) of the Act for final acquisition of the land.

<u>4. As it has been stated hereinbefore, the decree that is, the award in this case, was made on 28 May 1985 and this decree is appealable. If any appeal challenging this decree was to be filed, it should have been filed within 60 days; but it was filed about 4½ years beyond this period. The learned Additional Attorney-General has argued that since the government filed an application under section 152 of the Code for amendment of the decree and accordingly the decree was amended on 10 March 1990, this date should be the date of the decree as it stood amended and computing the limitation from this date excluding the period spent in receiving a copy of the amended decree from the Arbitrator the appeal was within time But the question; is what has been done Or What can at all be done on an application under section 152 of the Code. The scope and purpose of this section are very limited and the decision on a successful application under this section cannot materially affect the decree except correcting some insignificant errors or accidental omissions having nothing to do with the merit of the decree itself.</u>

<u>This section reads thus:</u>

<u>"152. Amendment of judgments, decrees or orders—Clerical or arithmetical mistakes in judgments, decrees or orders or errors arising therein from any accidental slip or omission may at any time be corrected by the Court either of its own motion or on an application by any of the parties."</u>

<u>In their application under this section the appellant simply pointed out that by mistake 12 decimals of land had been shown to have been acquired in excess of the actual area of 1.23 acres, and hence the compensation for this excess land should be deducted; and this was actually done by correcting the decree that is, by reducing the amount to Taka 33.66 lac (and some odd). But the appeal is not directed against this order of correction; it is directed against the whole decree challenging its very foundation on the ground that it is a nullity because it has been passed on the average value of land during the twenty-four months preceding the date of final acquisition in 1983, whereas, the law says that the period of twenty-four months shall precede the date of notice under section 5(1) which is, in this case, 6 June 1967. This ground as to nullity of the decree itself cannot be a matter for determination on an application under section 152 of the Code, nor any such ground was taken in the application under section 152 in this case. The only remedy against this decree dated 28 May 1985 on the ground of nullity was by way of an appeal and that appeal should have been filed within 60 days. In that appeal the ground as to clerical error or accidental omission in the decree could have also been taken.</u>

<u>5. There are other aspects of the matter which are also heavily against the appellant-government. According to their own statement, the appellant received a copy of the award on 16 November 1985 and the period of 60 days started since then. If they wanted to have the decree corrected in respect of the amount of the decree only, they could have filed the application under section 152 within this period of 60 days; but they did not; they rather filed it after about one year seven months that is on 6.5.87. By this time an execution proceeding, which had been instituted by the decree holder, was going on. In the execution proceeding the appellant prayed for time to pay up the decretal amount. There was nothing to prevent the appellant from filing the appeal in time and then from getting the operation of the decree stayed, and if the execution process had already started, to have that process stayed. The learned Additional Attorney-General contends that there is no limitation for filing an application for correction of a decree under section 152. Yes, there is no such limitation, and an application for correcting a decree may be filed even when an appeal is pending against the decree, or even when appeal has been disposed of without noticing the clerical or accidental error in the decree. But by filing such an application for correction the statutory period for filing an appeal against the decree cannot be got extended. If such a practice is allowed, execution of a decree may be forestalled for years together under the camouflage of an application for correction of a clerical mistake.</u>

<u>6. A similar question arose in the case of Kedar Nath Vs. Golam Hossain, 40 CWN 83, and in that case a Single Judge of the Calcutta High Court held that "when a decree is amended under section 152 of the Civil Procedure Code, the amendment does not give a fresh start of limitation to file an appeal from the date of the amendment; the point remains as before the date of the decree". It was also observed that when an appeal is filed beyond time, time can only be extended on an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act.</u>

<u>7. In the instant case before us the question of extension of the period of limitation for filing an appeal cannot arise in view of section 29 of the Limitation Act. This is because the proceedings in which this appeal has arisen are governed by a special law namely, Act XIII of 1948, which has prescribed the period of limitation and, as such, section 5 of the Limitation Act is not applicable here. This question has been already decided by us in the case of Ishaque Vs. Bangladesh 43 DLR (AD) 28.</u>

<u>8. The learned Additional Attorney-General has referred to the case of Tincowri Halder Vs. Nani Gopal Mondal, AIR 1960 Cal. 258. This case was decided by a a Division Bench and the question raised in that case was whether the limitation for appeal against a decree would start from the date on which it was amended under section 151 or section 152 of the Code or from its original date. The decision in the earlier case of Kedar Nath Vs. Golam Hossain 40 CWN 83 was also considered in that case and the decision therein was modified instead of being overruled. The decisions of the Division Bench are the following: (1) If the decree is amended on an application under section 151 or section 152 and the appeal is confined to the amended portion only the starting point would be the date of amendment. (2) If the appeal is directed against the decree as it stood prior to the amendment, the starting point would be the date of original decree.</u>

9. The learned Additional Attorney-General has made half-hearted attempts to show that the instant appeal is directed against the amended portion of the decree and, as such, limitation will start from the date of amendment. This is a futile attempt, for, the appeal is found directed against the very foundation of the original decree, that is, the compensation has been determined on the basis of the value of land during the twenty-four months prior to the date of the final acquisition in 1983 and not prior to the date of the notice under section 5(1) in 1967. Whether the decree was corrected or not in respect of the decretal amount under section 152, the ground for the appeal, the very basis of determination of the compensation, could not be gone into on an application under section 152. Therefore, the decision in this later case as cited does not help the appellant in any way.

10. In this case as cited by the learned Additional Attorney-General, it was observed that in the case of a re-hearing on a successful application for review, the starting point of limitation would be the date of the new decree drawn up after the review, whether the original decree is modified or reaffirmed. We find nothing to disagree with this view, for in the case of review of a decree under Order 47 of the Code the date of the decree will always be the date on which the decree is reviewed. For, the scope of an application for review under Order 47 is quite different from, and much wider than, that of an application under section 152. In exercise of power of review the Court which has made a decree may amend or modify it in any way and to any extent which it thinks proper on the basis of the record of the case, but in the case of an application under section 152 the Court's power is limited only to correction of any clerical error or accidental omission.

<u>11. The learned Additional Attorney-General has referred to the case of Ramji Lal and ors. Vs. Giani and another, AIR 1921 Lah 250, in which it has been found that the trial Court, though it purportedly acted under section 152, it in fact, acted under Order 47; he has therefore submitted that in the instant case we should treat the appellant's application under section 152 before the Arbitrator as an application for review under Order 47. Our answer is clearly in the negative. In the Lahore case he application for correction of clerical errors was not limited to mere correction, but "the whole system of calculation adopted by the Court in its judgment" was challenged. We do not understand how an application for the correction of mere arithmetical error or any accidental slip can be treated as an application for review. However, facts of that case are quite distinguishable from that in the instant case. The learned Additional Attorney-General has also referred to section 151 of the Code and has argued that in the case of a successful application thereunder for correction of a decree, the date of amendment of the decree under this section will be the date of the decree and not its original decree. But how these two sections, 151 and 152, can be taken as synonymous? Section 151 simply confirms the Court's inherent power and this power cannot be exercised where alternative remedies, such as remedies by way of appeal, revision or review are available. An application under section 151 in such a case is not maintainable. In the instant case, the ground taken in the appeal could not have been taker in the application for mere correction under section 152. From whichever angle the question is considered, we are firmly of the view that the date of correction or amendment of the decree under section 152 cannot be the starting point of limitation for the purpose of filing an appeal against the decree, and that we find that the High Court Division rightly decided the question holding that the appeal is badly barred by limitation of about four years six months.</u>

<u>12. The second question is whether the award is a nullity and void ab initio in that the Arbitrator while determining the value of the land took into consideration the average value of land during the twenty-four months preceding the date of final acquisition in August 1983, whereas according to section 7(e) of the Act, this period of twenty-four months shall precede the date of notice under section 5(1), in this case 6 June, 1967. The law is very clear on this point and it is that the period of twenty-four months shall be the period preceding the date of notice under section 5(1). But the Arbitrator has given reasons for not doing so. He has taken into notice this position of law, but has observed that the appellant could not show or produce any copy of the notice under section 5(1) of the Act. The respondents challenged the appellant's claim that any notice was published under section 5(1) or served under section 5(3) of the Act. But it has been admitted that the land was requisitioned and possession thereof was taken over some time in 1967 and that the Deputy Commissioner (sometimes referred to as Collector) made an assessment of compensation at Taka 1.10 lakh, out of which Taka 1.08 lakh was received by the respondents. But neither the government, nor the land-owners stated before us on what date the Deputy Commissioner had made this assessment except stating that out of the total amount assessed, Taka 1.08 lakh was received in the period from 1968 to 1973. No paper was produced to show whether this assessment was a provisional one under section 5B of the Act. If it were provisional, when the final assessment was made also could not be ascertained. From the papers submitted by the appellant, we find only one assessment was made, out of which the major part was received by installments in the four years following the requisition and possession. If it were the full and final assessment, how could it have been made long before the final acquisition by Notification No. DA-37/80/530 Acqn dated 26 July 1983. In these circumstances, the learned Arbitrator took the average value of the land during the twenty-four months preceding the date of actual acquisition in 1983. Considering the fact that the value of the land increased at very high rates since the requisition in 1967, the Arbitrator had taken this period for determining the compensation. It has been submitted by the respondents that from ill-motive the concerned officials of the Land Acquisition Department of the appellant kept the matter pending neither filing any appeal in time, nor producing the necessary documents including the notice under section 5, if any, and for this delay they (respondents) had filed a writ petition-WP No. 1004 of 1983-seeking a direction upon the appellant to issue notice for acquisition. The result of this writ petition was that the Rule issued thereon was made absolute by an order on 11 March 1984 and the appellant was directed to issue notice for acquisition of the land. This fact has not been denied by the appellant. It is thus found that though some compensation was paid to the respondents in the years following the requisition for the purpose of acquisition the matter of acquisition was not finalised, and that, for finalisation of the matter of acquisition, the respondents had to file a writ petition. In these circumstances, the Arbitrator, in the absence of any copy of the notice under section 5(1) and also in the absence of any evidence that the notice was published under section 5(1) or served under section 5(3), took the average of the value during the twenty-four months preceding the date of acquisition. Legally, this action is not defendable; in a previous case, Abdul Gafur Vs. Bangladesh 42 DLR (AD) 100, we also made it clear that the period of "twenty-four months" would precede the date of notice under section 5(1). But the question is whether, in the circumstances of this case, the award can be held to be null and void. Our answer is clearly in the negative. In this case, the notice for acquisition under section 5(1) was issued in 1967 as found from a copy of the notice which has been produced before us at the time of hearing of this appeal. The learned Additional Attorney-General has explained that this copy was not traceable when the matter was dealt with by the Arbitrator and then by the High Court Division. Be that as it may, when compensation was assessed whether provisionally or not, the bulk of the money of compensation was received in the years following 1968. It can be presumed that notice was issued under section 5(1) sometime in 1967-68. But final acquisition was made when the notification dated 26 July 1983 was issued and published under section 5(7). In the previous case of 42 DLR, we observed that though there is no time limit prescribed for final acquisition under section 5(7) but there should be some proximity between the date of notice under section 5 (1) and that under section 5(7). In that case, the Arbitrator had taken the average value of the land at the point of time in-between the date of notice under section 5(1) and the date of final acquistion under section 5(7), and on that basis made the award which was not challenged by either of the parties. In these circumstances, this Court did not interfere with the award when it was brought to this Court in appeal from the High Court Division's order maintaining the award.</u>

13. Result of these discussions is that the impugned award before us is not a nullity and the contention of the learned Additional Attorney-General in this respect is rejected.

14. The learned Additional Attorney-General has lastly referred to Article 104 of the Constitution of Bangladesh which provides for doing "complete justice in any cause or matters pending before it" and has submitted that the impugned award for Taka 33.66 lakh (and odd) is very excessive. We find the bulk of the amount of compensation as assessed in the years 1967-68 was received within 3 or 4 years. So it cannot be said that the respondents were totally deprived of their right to compensation. Had the acquisition been finalised and the matter been brought ultimately to the Arbitrator during the period, the balance due to the respondents would not have been a big amount. But whatever the balance might have been, the respondents were deprived of it for about 16 years when the final acquisition was made and the appellant, instead of filing appeal against the award, adopted dilatory tactics and thereby passed about five years time more, during which the respondents remained deprived of their dues. Taking all these facts and circumstances into consideration and though both the grounds taken by the appellant before us have failed, we think that ends of justice of the matter will be met if the amount of compensation given by the Arbitrator, and upheld by the High Court Division, is reduced by 50%. We, therefore, reduce the amount of the award to Taka 17 (seventeen) lakh, minus the amount already drawn by the respondents. The amount must be paid to the respondents within three months from the date, failing which, this amount will carry interest at the rate of 10% till it is realised. Subject to this reduction in amount and direction for payment, the appeal is dismissed without, however, any cost.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Order No. 98 of 1996.
lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam, Advocate -----For the Appellant. 
Kh Mahbubuddin Ahmed with S M Munir, Advocates -----For the Respondents.
parties:
Fatema Khatun ------Appellant
Vs.
Wach Khatun and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
This First Miscellaneous appeal is directed at the instance of the plaintiff appellants challenging the judgment and order dated 19-5-96 passed by Mr. Md Muniruzzaman, Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Feni in Miscellaneous Case (Review) No.55 of 1995 setting aside the Judgment and decree dated 4- 5-95 passed by Mr. AKM Salimullah, Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Feni in Title Appeal No.54 of 1986 thereby affirming the judgment and decree passed on 30-9-85 by Assistant Judge Chhagalnaya in Title Suit No.21 of 1984.

2. Facts, in brief, are that the appellant as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 21 of 1984 in the 1st Court of the learned Munsif, Feni (now Assistant Judge) for partition of the suit properties stating, inter alia, that the suit property belongs to Monsur Ali who died leaving behind Bonde Ali and Rahim Box, two sons who owned the property in equal shares of 8 annas each and that Rahim Box died leaving son Kona Mia and that during the survey, Rahim Box being dead and Bonde Ali being entrusted to supervise the recording, he fraudulently suppressed the names of the heirs of Rahim Box and instead put his name but as heirs of the original owner Monsur Ali, being entitled to the suit property, the plaintiff claimed partition of her share in the suit property but in vain and hence was the suit.

3. The defendant No.1 contested the suit filing written statement denying material allegations made in the plaint and stated, inter alia, that the suit property did not belong to Monsur Ali and the property in fact was owned by Bonde Ali and that Rahim Box was never son of Monsur Ali and the suit property was not the property of Rahim Box and, as such, the plaintiff nor her co-sharer had been in possession of the suit property and, as such, the plaintiff had no locus standi to file the suit and the suit was therefore liable to be dismissed.

4. The further case of the defendant was that without filing the suit for declaration the present suit for partition simpliciter was not maintainable.

5. After hearing the parties the trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 30-9-85 decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff and the lower appellate Court by the judgment and decree dated 4-5-95 dismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

6. The defendant respondents thereafter filed an application under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 9-7-95 praying the learned Subordinate Judge in Title Appeal No.54 of 1986.

7. The learned Subordinate Judge by the impugned Judgment and order dated 19-5-96 allowed the review application and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the same court in Title Appeal No.21 of 1985 (by his predecessor in office) and sent the suit on remand directing the trial Court to dispose of the suit after giving chance to the parties to adduce further evidence.

8. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order dated 19-5-96 passed in the Review Case the plaintiff preferred this appeal.

9. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellant, submits that the plaintiff being successful to prove that Rahim Box and Bonde Ali were brothers and that both the courts below earlier coming to the finding on this issue on the basis of evidence on record, this question could not be decided again in a review application filed by the defendants and the learned Subordinate Judge passed in the impugned Judgment, which is beyond his jurisdiction as the application was not filed following the provisions of Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, hereinafter referred to as the Code.

10. The learned Advocate further submits that on the basis of the documents both the courts below by the concurrent finding came to the opinion that the suit land appertains to khatian No.123 and there was no scope for any doubt as to identity as to the land in question and in such view of the matter the lower appellate Court while deciding the review application found fault with the judgment of both the courts below for not framing an issue on the point and for not deciding the identity of the suit property through an Advocate Commissioner. He further submits that the courts below considered the point of hotchpotch but the lower appellate Court held that the said point was not considered, the said learned Advocate finally submits that the grounds advocated in the review application are not grounds coming within the purview of Order 47 rule 1 of the Code and, as such, the impugned judgment suffers from the illegality and so is liable to be set aside.

11. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant respondent, on the other hand, submits that in view of the materials on record including the proceeding of criminal case section 145 CrPC an issue ought to have been framed as to maintainability of the suit inasmuch from the findings of the aforesaid criminal proceeding it will appear that the suit as framed was not maintainable. He further submits that the failure to decide the first issue framed in the suit as to the maintainability gives rise to the cause of action for the application under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code. He also submits that the matter as to relationship between Rahim Box and Monsur Ali has not been decided legally and, as such, there is cause of action for filing the application for review of the judgment of the lower appellate Court.

12. It appears from the application filed by the defendant respondent under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code that judgment passed in Title Appeal No.54 of 1986 was sought to be reviewed on the grounds which included, amongst others, that the impugned judgment and decree were bad for its patent error apparent on the basis of evidence and that the documents marked as Exhibits 4 and 5 has been erroneously admitted into evidence and that Ext.4 and 8 had not been properly considered and that there being a serious dispute regarding title, ownership and possession of the plaintiff and the plaintiff totally failing to prove right, title of ownership and possession and the suit ought to have been dismissed. He further submits that the impugned Judgment of both courts below arc passed on surmises and conjectures and, as such, the defendants felt constrained to file the Review petition and there being no illegality in allowing the petition, the appeal is liable to be dismissed.

13. The said application for review was resisted by the plaintiff appellant filing written objection stating, inter alia, that the application was not maintainable and that the appeal being heard and disposed of previously by the learned court of appeal below on consideration of evidence on record and there being discovery of no new or important matter nor any evidence being not available, which was not available previously, the application does not lie within the purview of Order 47 rule 1 of the Code and, as such, it was liable to be rejected.

14. It appears that challenging the legality of the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif (now Assistant Judge) the defendant respondent preferred Title Appeal No.54 of 1986 which was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Feni and the appeal was dismissed on contest by the judgment and decree dated 4-5-95. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, his successor-in- office passed the impugned judgment and order dated 19-5-96 allowing the application filed under Order 47 rule 1 read with section 151 of the Code. Order 47 rule 1 of the Code runs as fallows:

"Order XLVII

Review

1-(1) Any person considering himself aggrieved-

(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is allowed but from which no appeal has been preferred.

(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is allowed, or

(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of Small Causes, and who, from the discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence, was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when the decree was passed or order made, or on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or for any other sufficient reason, desires to obtain a review of the decree passed or order made against him may apply for a review of judgment to the court which passed the decree or made the order."

From the above provision of law it appears that in order to maintain application under Order 47 rule I of the Code the following requirements are necessary (a) discovery of new and important matter or evidence which was not within the knowledge of the petitioner or could not be produced by him at the time when the judgment was passed in spite of exercise of due diligence, (b) mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, (c) for any other sufficient reason. The circumstances mentioned in (a) and (b) are almost self-speaking but the circumstances mentioned in (c) above are natters to be interpreted. Any other sufficient reason, provided in the law, must be like mature of the other grounds mentioned in (a) and (b). In other words, the ground of any sufficient reason should be read with other grounds mentioned in (a) and (b).

15. As stated above the ground as taken in the review application filed before the same court passing a judgment on contest after hearing the parties included the ground that the impugned Judgment was bad in law and certain documents were illegally admitted and both the courts below did not apply judicial mind to the statutory mandatory provision of law and furthermore, the judgment of both the courts below have been vitiated by surmises and conjectures These grounds apparently are available in the language of filing an appeal before any higher forum.

<u>16. Be that as it may, it appears from the impugned judgment that the learned Subordinate Judge while allowing the review petition held that the plaintiff was not entitled to any relief in the instant suit which he filed for partition simpliciter without seeking declaration of title too. This defect, if any, in the framing of the suit cannot be said to be set within the knowledge of the defendant respondents at the time of trial of the suit, may be at the time of hearing of the appeal in question. Moreover the defendants raised the objection as to maintainability of the suit on the ground that the plaintiff being not co-sharer in the suit property, she could not claim partition. Entering into the controversy as to whether the contention of the parties was correct or not, was one of the points for determination in the suit, may be of the appeal and in fact the 1st issue framed in the suit was as to maintainability of the suit and after discussing other issues along with the said issue the trial Court decreed the suit. And it appears that the said issue was also taken up before the appellate Court. The lower appellate Court after lengthy discussion of the facts and circumstances and evidence in support of the possession of the plaintiff found that the suit for partition was validly filed and was maintainable and he agreed on the point with the trial Court. In deciding this appeal I do not like to embark upon the legality or otherwise of the said finding as to maintainability of the suit. There being specific finding and decision by the appellate Court on this point after considering the materials and submissions of both the parties I am of the opinion that this cannot be a ground for review of the said judgment as none of the ingredients of an application for review have been invoked in the matter.</u>

<u>17. It appears that the defendant-respondent praying for review alleged that the trial Court and lower appellate Court did not consider the evidence and facts and circumstances of the case and thus committed error. This error apparently is the cause of action of the application for review. The court of the Subordinate Judge being a court of appeal and the said court deciding the appeal on merit the prayer made by the defendant respondent to review the judgment on the aforesaid cause of action before the same court cannot be justified in law. From the impugned judgment it appears that while deciding the case of the respondent the learned Subordinate Judge describes the case of the respondent stating</u>

<u>“বিজ্ঞ নিম্ন আদালত ও অন্য আদালত পক্ষ গণের সাক্ষ্য  প্রমান সঠিকভাবে পর্যালোচনা করনে নাই এবং করিতে গিয়ে আইনগত ভুল করিয়াছেন।</u>

<u>This being the cause of action for the Review petition, it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge was not within his jurisdiction to entertain or decide the said petition since he was not the appellate authority.</u>

18. While allowing the review application the learned Subordinate Judge observed that from the documents marked as Ext. 4 and 5, it could not be said that Rahim Box was son of Monsur Ali and that from Ext. 'Kha', it appears that Rahim Box was shown as son of one Borket Ullah and, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge passed the judgment and order of remanding the suit to ascertain the parentage of Rahim Box. The learned Subordinate Judge also directed an investigation by an Advocate Commissioner to ascertain the identity of the suit plot. In this connection the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff appellants submits that if the two documents-Ext. 4 and 8 are taken together it will appear from those documents that assertion of the plaintiff that Rahim Box was son of Monsur Ali was proved as the documents executed by Kona Mia son of Rahim Box mentioned the father of the vendee Madov Bibi to be his Jhetha (father's brother) and from the document marked as Ext. 8, the identity of the suit land was also clearly revealed and more so, Ext.8 was attested by Kala Mia admitted son of Bonde Ali. The learned Advocate appearing for the defendant however assails this claim stating that Jhetha also not necessarily means that he was brother of the father of executant. This matter being absolutely a point of fact has been decided by both the courts below making specific finding in favour of the plaintiff. I do not like to embark upon this point again while adjudicating the appeal as to the propriety or otherwise of the order allowing review of the judgment of the appellate Court. This is sufficient to say that in any view of the matter this being point of fact and there being decision by lower appellate Court, on the basis of evidence, no review lies seeking set at naught the said finding made by the selfsame court.

<u>19. It appears further that the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the review application giving directions to give the parties chance for deciding whether the suit was bad for defect for hotchpotch observing that the trial Court did not frame any issue on the point of hotchpotch and as the suit should be sent on remand for framing an issue on hotchpotch and give decision on the point. But it appears from the judgment of the lower appellate Court that the said appellate Court specifically discussed and considered the points on defect of party and hotchpotch in the suit and after considering the facts and circumstances and materials on record found that the suit was not bad for defect of parties or on point of hotchpotch vide page 205 of the Paper Book 11. Order of allowing the review application sending the suit on remand for framing an issue on the point therefore appears to be unjustified in view of the definite finding of the lower appellate Court on this point though there was no issue, framed by the trial Court in the matter. Moreover, non-framing of an issue on any point cannot invalid the judgment if it appears that there was judicial consideration of the said point and on sufficient reasoning decision was arrived at. It is however correct to say that the finding arrived at could be challenged by the aggrieved party before higher forum and, in any case, the same court being not a court of appeal was not authorized in law to sit upon his own judgment and set it aside. The learned Advocate appearing for both the parties submitted at length for and against the findings arrived at by the lower appellate Court referring to various materials. As I have already stated that the learned Subordinate Judge being not court of appeal, the legality or otherwise of the findings was not within the lookout in the petition filed under Order 47 of the Code. I do not like to embark upon the legality of the findings or otherwise of the same which, according to me, shall be an useless exercise so far as disposal of this appeal before me is concerned.</u>

<u>In this connection a decision in the case of Nurul Hossain vs Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 49 DLR (AD) 108 may be referred to. Their Lordships held.</u>

<u>"It is well known that a review was never meant and allowed to be utilised as another opportunity for rehearing the matter which is already closed by a final judgment. The points raised by Mr. Nurul Hoque have already been considered while dismissing the leave petition and the petitioner cannot be permitted to raise the same question in different form. There is no occasion for review."</u>

20. Appears that the grounds taken in the review application in the instant case in fact are meant for an opportunity for rehearing the matter which is already closed by a final judgment passed by the lower appellate Court. The points raised by the learned Advocate for the defendant respondent are matters which may be considered at the time of disposal of the appeal. Following the decisions of the case reported in 49 DLR 1 am of the opinion that the grounds taken in the Review Petition are aimed at taking another opportunity for rehearing the matter which cannot be allowed. In such view of the matter the impugned judgment allowing the application under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure appears to be illegally passed and hence it should be knocked down.

21. In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The impugned Judgment and order dated 19-5-96 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge 1st Court, Feni in Miscellaneous Case (Review) No. 55 of 1995 is set aside.

Send down the LC records at once.

End.

lawyer:
Gour Gopal Saha with Goutam Kumar Roy, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner.
Sharifuddin Chaklader, Assistant Attorney-General ------ For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Jinnatunessa ------ Petitioner 
VS 
Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh  ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30.10.89 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. 1st Court, Mymensingh in OC Appeal No. 125 of 1986 affirming the ex parte judgment and decree dated 11.2.86 passed by the Assistant Judge, 2nd Court Sadar, Mymensingh in OC Suit No. 492 of 1981 decreeing the suit.

2. The short facts for disposal of the Rule are that the opposite party government as plaintiff, instituted a suit for declaration against the petitioner as defendant for a declaration that the ex parte decree passed in Misc. Case No. 142 of 1970 by the learned Munsif, Sadar Mymensingh is fraudulent, illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff, alleging inter alia that the suit land measuring 0.200 Sahasrangsha recorded in Plot Nos. 7025 and 7026 under new Khatian No. (SA) No. 2383 and old Plot No. 702 under old Khatian No. 95 of Mouza Mymensingh town is Government Khas land; that the present petitioner filed Misc. Case No. 141 of 1970 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Sadar Mymensingh for correction of the record of rights in her name and obtained an ex parte decree therein on 9.1.71 beyond the knowledge of the opposite party-government; that thereafter AGP Mymensingh filed an application for setting aside the aforesaid decree under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure but the same was eventually dismissed for default on 28.2.72; that thereafter, the government filed Misc. Case No. 72 of 1972 and the same was dismissed on contest on 13.2.73; that on the basis of the aforesaid ex parte order the defendant (present petitioner) sought for the correction of the record of rights in her name before the CO (Rev), Sadar Mymensingh on 22.12.79 when the plaintiff came to know about the said ex parte order and hence the suit, being Suit No. 492 of 1981, for a declaration for cancellation of the ex parte order dated 9.1.71 passed in Misc. Case No. 142 of 1970.

3. The petitioner contested Suit No. 492 of 1981 by way of filing written statement denying all material allegations as contained in the plaint contending inter alia, that the suit is hopelessly barred by limitation, that the landlord Moharaja Shashi Kanta Acharjya Bahadur of Mymensingh being 16 annas owner settled the suit land in favour of the petitioner in 1347 BS on proper Nazar Salami and since then she has been owning and possessing the same in her own right and adversely against all others on payment of rent with the appropriate authority; the suit land being wrongly recorded in the Collector's Khas Khatian she filed the said Misc. Case No. 142 of 1970 in the 1st Court of Munsif Mymensingh under section 143(a) of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act for correction of the ROR and the present plaintiff Government i.e. opposite party, contested the case by filing written objection; that on 09.01.71 when the Misc. Case was fixed for peremptory hearing, the opposite party government filed hazira but was found absent on repeated calls and the suit was taken up for hearing and after recording deposition of the petitioner and marking the relevant documents as exhibits the court was pleased to allow the said Misc. Case; that the opposite party Government had full knowledge of the said ex parte order dated 09.01.71; that the opposite party Government filed Misc. Case No. 23 of 1971 under Order 9 rule 13 CPC for setting aside the said ex parte order but the said Misc. Case No. 23 of 1971 was dismissed for default on 28.02.72 and thereafter the present plaintiff Government filed another Misc. Case No 72 of 1972 which was also dismissed on contest on 13.2.1973.

4. That on 11.2.86 when Suit No. 492 of 1981 was taken up for hearing the petitioner, as has been stated, being ill could not appear before the Court. The plaintiff-government examined only one witness Tahshilder Abdul Majid. It appears from the deposition of the said Tahshilder (Annexure 'A') that he says nothing about obtaining the ex parte order in Misc. Case No. 142 of 1970 fraudulently or by suppression of summons or by any other fraudulent means.

5. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree passed in OC Suit No. 492 of 1981 the petitioner preferred an appeal being Appeal No. 125 of 1986 before the learned District Judge. The said appeal was heard by the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh and the same was dismissed. Thereafter the defendant-petitioner filed this revisional application.

6. Mr. Gour Gopal Shaha, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the suit was for declaration and cancellation of the ex parte order passed in Misc. Case No. 142 of 1970 and the suit is hopelessly time-barred inasmuch as the opposite party-government had full knowledge of the ex parte order dated 9.1.71. While making his submission he has referred to me the plaint of the OC Suit No. 492 of 1981 (paragraph 5) wherein it has been stated:

"That the plaintiff. after coming to know of the said ex parte decree dated 9.1.71 filed Misc. Case No. 23 of 1971 for setting aside the ex parte decree under Order 9 rule 13 CPC and unfortunately, the Misc. Case was dismissed for default on 28.2.72 as the then Associate GP could not get any opportunity to appear when the case was called on for hearing. Thereafter Misc. Case No 72/72 was filed on behalf of the Government and the same was dismissed on contest on 13.2.73."

From the statement made by the opposite party Government in their plaint it is absolutely clear that the opposite party Government had full knowledge of the ex parte order of Misc. Case No. 142 of 1970 when it was so passed. Article 95 of the Limitation Act 1908 (Act No. IX of 1908) provides that:

"To set aside a decree obtained by fraud, or for other relief on the ground of fraud, the period of limitation is three years when the fraud becomes known to the party wronged"

7. Taking into account the assertions made by the plaintiff-government in their plaint itself and reading of the aforesaid Article of the Limitation Act I have no hesitation to hold that the suit namely, Suit No. 492 of 1981, for cancellation of the ex parte order dated 9.1.71 passed in Misc. Case No. 142 of 1970 is hopelessly time barred.

8. Mr. Gour Gopal Shaba further submits that for setting aside or cancelling a decree passed by a competent Court the plaintiff has to prove that the decree was obtained fraudulently or by any other fraudulent means but in the aforesaid OC Suit No. 142 of 1970 the plaintiff has led no evidence whatsoever to that effect.

<u>9. It appears from the evidence of the lone witness who deposed in the said OC suit that he said nothing about obtaining the ex parte order in the Misc. Case No. 142 of 1970 by practising any fraud upon the Court or by any other fraudulent means. As such, I find substance in the above submission of the learned Advocate. Mr. Gour Gopal Shaha submits that in passing the ex parte order in Suit No. 492 of 1981 the learned Munsif did not apply its judicial mind; the suit being a suit for cancellation of a decree it was incumbent upon the plaintiff to show that the decree was obtained by practising fraud upon the Court. No evidence to that effect being adduced by the plaintiff, the learned Assistant Judge committed an error of law in decreeing the suit ex parte. He also submits that it is the plaintiff who has to prove his case through his witness and papers. In support of his above contentions he has rightly placed reliance upon the case of Md. Naimuddin Sarder vs. Md. Abdul Kalam Biswas and another, reported in 39 DLR (AD) 237 and Bangladesh vs. Israil Ali and others reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 371. In the aforesaid two cases their Lordships of the Appellate Division observed that the plaintiff in order to succeed must establish his own case and the weakness of the defendant's case is no ground for passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff.</u>

10. On behalf of the opposite party-government no counter affidavit has been filed. Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the government, has submitted that the ground for limitation was not duly agitated before the trial Court or before the appellate Court, and also submits that in the interest of justice the case should be remanded to the trial Court for hearing on the point of limitation.

11. I have already observed that the courts below committed errors of law and I find no justification for remanding the case to the trial Court.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court Sadar, Mymensingh in OC Suit No. 492 of 1981 and the Judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Mymensingh in OC Appeal No. 125 of 1986 are hereby set aside and the OC Suit No. 492 of 1981 is dismissed.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 771 of 1991 with FAT No. 369 of 1991 and Cross-objection Case No. 735 of 1991.
lawyer:
Ashrarul Hossain with Mvi. Md. Wahidullah, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner Cross-objection.
M Zahir with M Hasan, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Party Appellants.
Ozair Faroaq, Advocate ----- For the Defendant-Appellant.
parties:
National Bank Limited   ----- Appellant.
Vs.
New Sonali Garments (Private) Ltd. & Ors ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
ARM Amirul Islam Chowdhury, J.: This appeal being FA No. 771 of 1991 at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant National Bank Ltd. is directed against the judgment and decree respectively dated 31.3.91 and 2.4.91 passed by Mr. Md. Shahidul Hoque. Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 3, Dhaka in Money Suit No. 528 of 1991. The Memo of appeal was presented in this Court on 7.8.91 and the appeal was registered.

2. The ordering portion of the judgment dated 31.3.91 reads as under:—

অত্র মানি মোকদ্দমাটি দোতরফা সূত্রে ২, ৪, ৫ ও ৯ নং বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে এবং একতরফা সূত্রে ১ ও ৭ নং বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে খরচাসহ আংশিক ডিক্রী দেওয়া হইল এবং দোতরফা সুত্রে ১১ নং বিবাদী ও একতরফা সুত্রে ৩, ৬, ৮ ও ১০ নং বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে বিনা খরচায় ডিসমিস করা হইল।

৫ নং বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে এককভাবে ২৯,১৮,৭৫২.০০ টাকায় ডিক্রী দেওয়া হইল। এই বিবাদী এবং ১, ২, ৪ ও ৯ নং বিবাদী ডিক্রী বাকী ১,৬৭,৭৭,১৪৪.৩১ টাকার জন্য দায়ী থাকিবেন।

বিবাদীগন ডিক্রির ১ (এক) বৎসরের মধ্যে সমান ৬ (ছয়) কিস্তিতে সম্পূর্ন ডিক্রিকৃত অর্থ মামলার খরচাদি বাদী ব্যাংক বরাবরে পরিশোধ করিবে।

The relevant portion of the decree dated 2.4.91 reads as under:

অত্র মানি মোকদ্দমাটি দোতরফা সূত্রে ২, ৪, ৫ ও ৯ নং বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে এবং একতরফা সূত্রে ১ ও ৭ নং বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে খরচাসহ আংশিক ডিক্রী দেওয়া হইল এবং দোতরফা সুত্রে ১১ নং বিবাদী ও একতরফা সুত্রে ৩, ৬, ৮ ও ১০ নং বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে বিনা খরচায় ডিসমিস করা হইল। ৫ নং বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে এককভাবে ২৯,১৮,৭৫২.০০ টাকায় ডিক্রী দেওয়া হইল। এই বিবাদী এবং ১, ২, ৪ ও ৯ নং বিবাদী ডিক্রী বাকী ১,৬৭,৭৭,১৪৪.৩১ টাকার জন্য দায়ী থাকিবেন। বিবাদীগন ডিক্রির ১ (এক) বৎসরের মধ্যে সমান ৬ (ছয়) কিস্তিতে সম্পূর্ন ডিক্রিকৃত অর্থ মামলার খরচাদি বাদী ব্যাংক বরাবরে পরিশোধ করিবেন। এবং এই মোকদ্দমার খরচার বলপে ২০০২০.০০ টাকা বাদীকে আদায় দেন।

3. It appears that defendant No. 5 Abul Kalam Azad presented a Memo of appeal before this Court on 27.6.91 against the judgment and decree passed in the aforesaid Money Suit No. 528 of 1991. The Stamp Reporter gave a note dated 20.7.91 and returned the Memo of appeal to Mr. Md. Ozair Farooq, the learned Advocate for the appellant Abul Kalam Azad (defendant No. 5).

4. The Stamp Reporter's note dated 20.7.91 reads as under:

অত্র মেমো অব আপীলটি বিবাদী আপীলকারী কর্তৃক সংশোধিত অর্থ ঋণ আদালতের আইন অনুযায়ী ডিক্রি প্রদত্ত অর্থেও অর্ধেক টাকা জমা দেওয়ার সংক্রান্ত কোন চালানের কপি অত্র সংগে সংযুক্তি করা হয় নাই বিধায় ইহা বিজ্ঞ আইনজীবীকে ফেরৎ দেওয়া হইল।

5. It further appears that Md. Zahurul Islam, defendant No. 9 presented a Memo. of Cross-Objection being Cross-Objection Tender No. 735 of 1991 under Order 41, rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure in FA No. 771 of 1991 on 11.12.91. Thereafter an application under Order, 1, rule 10 CPC was filed by Abul Kalam Azad, defendant No. 5 for adding him as respondent No. 8 in FA No. 771 of 1991 and his prayer was allowed by an order of this Court dated 17.12.91. Thereafter on the same day i.e. 17.12.91 Abul Kalam Azad defendant No. 5 filed an application for treating the Memo of appeal returned by the Stamp Reporter with his note dated 20.7.91 as cross-objection under Order 41, rule 22 CPC. Thereafter on 25.2.92 Abul Kalam Azad defendant No. 5 filed a Memorandum of Cross-objection under Order 41, rule 22 CPC an application for accepting the same. Plaintiff-appellant National Bank Ltd. filed an affidavit-in-opposition on 1.3.92 against the prayer for condonation of delay in filing the Cross-objection by Abul Kalam Azad Defendant No. 5

6. It appears that plaintiff-appellant National Bank Ltd. has filed no affidavit-in-opposition for rejecting the Memorandum of Cross-objection filed by Md. Zahirul Islam defendant No. 9.

7. Since all these matters have arisen out of the same judgment and decree passed by the trial Court they are taken up together for disposal. The questions involved are (1) whether a Cross-objection is maintainable in respect of an appeal preferred in this Court under the Artha Rin Adalat Act: (2) whether a Cross-objection preferred in respect of an appeal in this Court under the Artha Rin Adalat Act must satisfy all the requirements necessary for preferring an appeal in this Court; (3) Whether the Cross-objection has been preferred within the period of limitation as provided under Order 41, rule 22 CPC; (4) whether the memorandum of appeal presented by the defendant No. 5 Abul Kalam Azad returned to Mr. Md. Ozair Farooq, the learned Advocate could be treated and accepted as a Cross- objection; (5) whether regular Cross-objection filed by a defendant No. 5 Abul Kalam Azad could be entertained and registered; (6) whether the Cross-objection filed by defendant No. 9 Md. Zahirul Islam could be entertained arid registered.

8. All the points are taken up together for convenience and for disposal.

9. First of all we are to see whether the Artha Rin Adalat is an ordinary civil Court or a special civil Court.

10. There is no doubt that Artha Rin Adalat is a civil Court The question is how far the Code of Civil Procedure would be applicable in respect of a proceeding in an Artha Rin Adalat. In this connection we may refer to section 5 of the Artha Rin Adalat Act (hereafter referred to as the Adalat Act) which reads as under:

অর্থ ঋণ আদালতের ক্ষমতা ও এখতিয়ার (১) অন্য কোন আইনে যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানের ঋণ আদায় সংক্রান্ত যাবতীয় মামলার অর্থ ঋণ আদালতে দায়ের করিতে হইবে এবং উক্ত আদালতেই উহা নিষ্পত্তি করা হইবে :

তবে শর্ত থাকে যে কোন আইন দ্বারা কোন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান প্রতিষ্ঠা করাইয়া থাকিলে এবং উক্ত আইনে উহা ঋণ আদায়ের জন্য কোন বিশেষ বিধান বা পদ্ধতি থাকিলে সেই বিধান বা পদ্ধতি এই ধারায় বিধান দ্বারা ক্ষুন্ন হইবে না।

আরও শর্ত থাকে যে ধারা ২ এর দফা (ক) এর উপ-দফা (৯, ১০), (১১) ও (১২) এ উল্লেখিত আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক সরকারকে প্রদত্ত ঋণ আদায় সংক্রান্ত কোন মামলার ক্ষেত্রে এই ধারার কোন কিছুই প্রযোজ্য হইবে না।

(২) কোন জেলায় এক বা একাধিক অর্থ ঋণ আদালত থাকিলে, মামলা দায়েরের জন্য উহাদের এখতিয়ার জেলা জজ কর্তৃক নির্ধারণ করা হইবে।

(৩) জেলা জজ স্বেচ্ছায় বা মামলার কোন পক্ষের আবেদনের পরিপ্রেক্ষিতে প্রয়োজন বোধ করিলে কোন অর্থ ঋণ আদালতে বিচারাধীন মামলা তাহার নিজ এখতিয়ারাধীন এলাকায় অবস্থিত অন্য কোন অর্থ ঋণ আদালতে স্থানান্তর করিতে পারিবেন এবং এই প্রকার স্থানান্তরিত মামলা জেলা জজ পূনরায় স্থানান্তরিত করিতে পারিবেন।

(৪) অর্থ ঋণ আদালত একটি দেওয়ানী আদালত (civil Court) বলিয়া গন্য হইবে এবং (Code of Civil Procedure, 1908(Act V of 1908) এ দেওয়ানী আদালতের যে সমস্ত ক্ষমতা ও এখতিয়ার এই আইনের বিধান সাপেক্ষে অর্থ ঋণ আদালতেরও থাকিবে।

(৫) এই আইনে নিম্নরূপ কিছু না থাকিলে র্অথ ঋণ আদালত উহার র্কাযক্রম পরচিালনার ব্যাপারে (civil court) (Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908) এ দেওয়ানী আদালতের কার্যক্রম পরিচালনা সম্পর্কে যে বিধান করা হইয়াছে উহা অনুসরন করিবে।

(6) অর্থ ঋণ আদালতের কার্যধারা Penal Code (Act XLV of 1860) এর Section 193 এবং 228 এ উল্লিখিত বিচার সম্পর্কীয় কার্যধারা (Judicial Proceedings) বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে।

Artha Rin Adalat is competent to take cognizance only in respect of suits instituted by a financial institution for recovery of debt dues i.e. in respect of matter enumerated in section 2(খ) of the Adalat Act. The Artha Rin Adalat is only competent to take cognizance of suits for recovery of debt dues (instituted only by a financial institution as plaintiff) as enumerated in section 2(ক). In other words, in such a suit (i) the plaintiff must be a financial institution and (2) the suit must be for recovery of debt dues. Artha Rin Adalat has no jurisdiction to take cognizance of any cause of action other than debt dues in a suit instituted by a financial institution (as plaintiff).

11. The question is whether the Artha Rin Adalat is an ordinary civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure (hereinafter referred to as the Code) read with the Civil Court Act (hereinafter referred to as the Act) or a special civil Court. Section 15 of the Code reads as under:

"15. Every suit shall be instituted in the Court of the lowest grade competent to try it"

Sections 18 and 19 of the Act read as under:-

18. Save as otherwise provided by any enactment for the time being in force, the jurisdiction of a District Judge or Subordinate Judge extends, subject to the provisions of section 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure to all original suits for the time being cognizable by civil Courts.

19. (i) Save as aforesaid, and subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), the jurisdiction of a (Assistant Judge) extends to all like suits of which the value does not exceed fifty thousand taka.

(2) The (Government) may, on the recommendation of the High Court Division, direct, by notification in the Official Gazette, with respect to any (Assistant Judge) named therein (that his jurisdiction shall extend to all like suits of such value not exceeding (one lac taka) as may be specified in the notification).

(provided that the (Government) may, by notification in the Official Gazette, delegate to High Court Division its powers under this section)."

12. Under section 19 of the Act an Assistant Judge has pecuniary jurisdiction upto Taka 50,000.00 only. Under section 18 of the Act subject to section 15 of the Code the District Judge or a Subordinate Judge has unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction. In the case of the Artha Rin Adalat sections l8 and 19 of the Act and section 15 of the Code have no manner of application.

Section 21 of the Act reads as under:

"21.-(1) Save as aforesaid, an appeal from a decree or order of a' Subordinate Judge shall lie-

(a) to the District Judge where the value of the Original Suit in which or in any proceeding arising out of which the decree or order was made did not exceed (one lac and thirty thousand taka)

(b) to the (High Court Division) in any other case.

(2) Save as aforesaid, an appeal from a decree or order of a (Assistant Judge) shall lie to the District Judge.

(3) Where the function of receiving any appeals which lie to the District Judge under sub-section (i) or sub-section (2) has been assigned to an Additional Judge, the appeals may be preferred to the Additional Judge.

(4) The (High Court Division) may, with the previous sanction of the (Government), direct, by notification in the official Gazette, that appeals lying to the District Judge under sub-section (2) from all or any of the decrees or orders of any (Assistant Judge) shall be preferred to the Court of such Subordinate Judge as may be mentioned in the notification, and the appeals shall thereupon be preferred accordingly.

<u>13. There is no dispute that the Artha Rin Adalats are presided over by Subordinate Judges, Section 21 of the Act provides that against a decree or order of a Subordinate Judge where the value of the suit or any other proceedings does not exceed taka one lac thirty thousand, an appeal shall lie to the District Judge and in any other case to the High Court Division. In the case of Artha Rin Adalat section 21 of the Act has no manner of application as much as against the decree passed by an Artha Rin Adalat (irrespective of value of the suit) an appeal shall lie only to the High Court Division. Under section 9 of the Adalat Act read with section 24 of the Code (section 24 of the Code not being in conflict with Adalat Act and administrative in nature) the District Judge may transfer a suit from one Artha Rin Adalat to another Artha Rin Adalat within his territorial jurisdiction. Except the power of transfer of a suit from one Artha Rin Adalat to another Artha Rin Adalat the District Judge, has not been given any jurisdiction over the suits cognizable by an Artha Rin Adalat. The Adalat Act has made the Artha Rin Adalat subordinate to the High Court Division. In respect of exercise of the jurisdiction by the High Court Division over the Artha Rin Adalat and the suits cognizable by the Artha Rin Adalat we may refer to sections 6 and 7 of the Adalat Act. They read as under:</u>

<u>৬। অর্থ ঋণ আদালতের সিদ্ধান্ত চূড়ান্ত (১) ধারা ৭ এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, অর্থ ঋণ আদালতের কার্য ধারা, আদেশ রায় ও ডিক্রী সম্পর্কে কোন আদালত বা অন্য কোন কর্তৃপক্ষের নিকট প্রশ্ন উত্থাপন করা যাইবে না।</u>

<u>(২) উপধারা (১) এ যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, কোন অর্থ ঋণ আদালত কর্তৃক বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে প্রদত্ত কোন এক তরফা ডিক্রি রদ করার জন্য বিবাদী (Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908) এর Order IX এর rule 13 এর বিধান মোতাবেক আদালতে দরখাস্ত করিতে চাহিলে তাহাকে তাহার বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রিকৃত অর্থের অন্তত অর্ধেক অর্থ বা উহার সমপরিমান অর্থেও ব্যাংক জামানত দরখাস্তের সহিত আদালতে জমা করিতে হইবে এবং উক্তরুপ দরখাস্ত জমা করা না হইলে তাহার দরখাস্ত গ্রহণযোগ্য হইবে না।</u>

<u>৭। আপীল-(১) কোন ব্যক্তি অর্থ ঋণ আদালতে কোন রায় বা ডিক্রি দ্বারা ক্ষুব্ধ হইলে তিনি উক্ত রায় বা ডিক্রি প্রদানের তারিখ হইতে ৩০ দিনের মধ্যে হাইকোর্ট করিতে পারিবেন।</u>

<u>তবে শর্ত থাকে যে অর্থ ঋণ আদালতে কোন অনুবর্তী আদেশের বিরুদ্ধে কোন আপীল দায়ের করা যাইবে না।</u>

<u>(২) ধারা ৬ (২) এর অধীন দায়েরকৃত দরখাস্তের উপর অর্থঋণ আদালত কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত চূড়ান্ত আদেশের বিরুদ্ধে কোন বিবাদী</u>

<u>(অ) আপিল দায়ের করিতে ইচ্ছুক হইলে বা</u>

<u>(আ) আপীল দায়ের না করিয়া মূল মামলার রায় বা ডিক্রির বিরুদ্ধে আপীল দায়ের করিতে ইচ্ছুক হইলে-</u>

<u>তিনি উক্ত ধারার অধীন জমাকৃত অর্থ বাদ দিয়া মূল মামলায় ডিক্রিকৃত অবশিষ্ট অর্থের অন্ততঃ অর্ধেক অর্থ ডিক্রি প্রদানকারী আদালতের নিকট জমা করিয়া, উক্ত চূড়ান্ত আদেশ প্রদানের তারিখ হইতে ৩০ দিনের মধ্যে হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে আপীল করিতে পারিবেন।</u>

<u>(৩) অর্থঋণ আদালতের কোন রায় বা ডিক্রির বিরুদ্ধে কোন বিবাদী আপীল দায়ের করিতে ইচ্ছুক হইলে এবং তিনি উক্ত রায় বা ডিক্রির বিরুদ্ধে</u>

<u>(অ)	ধারা ৬(২) এর অধীনে দরখাস্ত না করিয়া থাকিলে, তাহার বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রিকৃত অর্থের অন্ততঃ অর্ধেক অর্থ</u>

<u>(আ) ধারা ৬ (২) এর অধীন দরখাস্ত এবং উপধারা (২) (ক) এর অধীন আপীল করিয়া থাকিলে, উক্ত ধারা ৬ (২) এবং উপধারা (২) (ক) এর অধীন জমাকৃত অর্থ বাদ দিয়া মূল মামলার ডিক্রিকৃত অবশিষ্ট অর্থের অন্ততঃ অর্ধেক অর্থ-</u>

<u>ডিক্রি প্রদানকারী আদালতে জমা করিয়া উপ-ধারা (১) এ নির্ধারিত সময়ের মধ্যে হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে আপীল দায়ের করিতে পারিবেন।</u>

<u>(৪) কোন বিবাদী উপ-ধারা (২) এবং (৩) এ নির্ধারিত অর্থ ডিক্রি প্রদানকারী আদালতে জমা না করিলে উক্ত বিবাদীর আপীল গ্রহণযোগ্য হইবে না।</u>

<u>Section 6 provides that except in accordance with section 7 no order, judgment, decree and the procedure followed by the Artha Rin Adalat can be challenged in any Court. Under section 7 of the Adalat Act an appeal is provided for to the High Court Division against the decree of an Artha Rin Adalat within 30 days by the aggrieved party. And where the aggrieved party is the defendant he can prefer an appeal only on depositing 50% of the decretal amount in the trial Court. Further, it is provided in section 7 that no appeal shall lie against an ad-interim order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat.</u>

<u>14. The Adalat Act as amended upto date provides for filing an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code at the instance of the defendant in respect of an ex parse decree on condition of the defendant depositing 50% of the decretal amount (or like amount by bank guarantee) in the trial Court. An appeal is provided for against the rejection of an application under Order 9, rule 13 to the High Court Division only on depositing half of the balance of the decretal amount i.e. 1/4 of the total decretal amount. Section 8 of the Adalat Act provides as under.</u>

<u>৮। ঋণের কিস্তি । - অর্থ ঋণ আদালত ডিক্রিকৃত টাকা কিস্তিতে পরিশোধ করা যথাযথ বলিয়া বিবেচনা করিলে উহা পরিশোধের জন্য ডিক্রীদারের বিনা সম্মতিতে এক বৎসরের অধিক সময় দিতে পারিবে না।</u>

<u>তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, কোন কিস্তি মঞ্জুরকালে আদালত ডিক্রী দেনাদারকে কিস্তির সময়ের জন্য আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানের সহিত সম্পাদিত চুক্তিতে নির্ধারিত সুদের হাওে সুদ প্রদানের নির্দেশ দিবে।</u>

<u>Under section 8 of the Adalat Act the trial Court is precluded from giving instalments to the judgment debtor not exceeding one year to satisfy the decree without the consent of the decree-holder. Section 8 of the Adalat Act clearly shows that once a decree is passed the trial Court has very limited power to give instalments to the judgment-debtor to satisfy the decree. If we read sections 6, 7 (as amended upto date Act No. 25 of 1992) and section 8 of the Adalat Act it would be clear that a decree passed by an Artha Rin Adalat could not be interfered with except in accordance with the provisions of the Adalat Act.</u>

<u>15. An appeal may be preferred before the High Court Division within 30 days against the decree or the order of rejection of application under Order 9, rule 13 passed by an Artha Rin Adalat. Under section 7 of the Adalat Act High Court Division is the appellate forum both against the decree or the order of rejection of an application under Order 9, rule 13 passed by an Artha Rin Adalat. The period of limitation is the same for the Appeal and the Miscellaneous Appeal. The normal period for preferring a regular or miscellaneous appeal in his court is 90 days. The period of limitation under section 7 of the Adalat Act for preferring a regular or miscellaneous appeal is 30 days. From the above discussion it is quite clear that the Artha Rin Adalat is not an ordinary Civil Court but a Special Civil Court.</u>

<u>16. The question is whether under the special law i.e. (Artha Rin) Adalat Act a Cross-objection is maintainable. In this connection it appears that section 5 of the Artha Rin Adalat is relevant We have already considered sections 5, 6, 7 and 8 of the (Artha Rin) Adalat Act. Order 41, rule 22 CPC has been enacted in the procedural law. Order 41 rule 22 has given the respondent in the appeal the right to prefer a cross-objection. We are dealing with a special law creating a special forum for adjudication of suits which only can be filed by a financial institution and only for recovery of debt dues. In the circumstances, the general provision of Order 41, rule 22 CPC how far could be applicable in the case of an appeal pending against the judgment and decree passed by an Artha Rin Adalat which is a Special Civil Court. (Artha Rin) Adalat Act has specifically provided for an appeal against the judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat in a suit it has also provided for a remedy under Order 9, rule 13 CPC against an ex parte decree. The special law has made a distinction between the plaintiff and the defendant in respect of their respective rights, against the judgment and decree passed by an Artha Rin Adalat. In the case of a defendant the appeal against the decree must be filed accompanying evidence of the payment of 50% of the decretal amount in the trial Court. In the case of an ex parte decree the defendant must produce the evidence along with the application under Order 9, rule 13 CPC of the payment of 50% of the decretal amount (or evidence of like amount of bank guarantee has been filed in the trial Court) in the trial Court. We have already held that a decree passed by an Artha Rin Adalat can be impugned or assailed only in accordance with the provisions laid down in the (Artha Rin) Adalat Act and not otherwise. The legislature intended that the appeal must be filed by the aggrieved defendant against the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court within 30 days by presenting a memorandum of appeal along with the evidence of payment of 50% of the decretal amount. If cross-objection under Order 41, rule 22 CPC at the instance of the defendant is allowed to be filed that will frustrate the very intention of the legislature. In other words, by giving the right to the defendant-respondent in the appeal to file a cross-objection would indirectly amount to extending the period of limitation as prescribed by the (Artha Rin) Adalat Act which cannot be done, in view of the fact that section 5 of the Limitation Act has no manner of application in respect of a period of special limitation. To allow the defendant-respondent to file a cross-objection in respect of a decree passed by an Artha Rin Adalat would amount to frustrate the very purpose for which the Artha Rin Adalat Act had been passed. In this connection we may refer to the case of Government of Bangladesh Vs. Aziz Mollah being dead his heirs of the Appellate Division given in Civil Appeal No.4 of 1986 (dispossd of on 7th August. 1991). What cannot be done directly cannot equally be done indirectly. For the reasons stated above we are of the opinion that in respect of a decree passed under Artha Rin Adalat no cross-objection is maintainable by the defendant- respondent inasmuch, as the cross-objection is in substance an appeal.</u>

<u>Even assuming that a cross-objection is maintainable the question is whether it must satisfy all the requirements necessary to prefer an appeal.</u>

17 . Order 41, rule 22(1) reads as under:

"22(1) Any respondent, though he may not have appealed from any part of the decree, may not only support the decree on any of the grounds decided against him in the Court below but take any cross-objection to the decree which he could have taken by way of appeal, provided he has filed such objection in the appellate Court within one month from the date of service on him or his pleader of notice of the day fixed for hearing the appeal or within such further time as the appellate Court may see fit to allow."

18. Under rule 22(2) of Order 41 the cross- objection shall be in the form of a memorandum, and the provisions of rule 1 (of Order 41) so far as they relate to the form and contents of the memorandum of appeal, shall apply thereto. In other words the memorandum of cross-objection must conform to the form and contents of a memorandum of appeal. Under rule 22(3) unless the respondent files with the cross-objection a written acknowledgment from the party who will be affected by such objection or his pleader of having received a copy thereof. the Appellate Court shall cause a copy to be served as soon as may be after the filing of the objection on such party or his pleader at the expense of the respondent In other words service of notice of the cross-objection must be effected on the person to be affected by 'the cross-objection. Under rule 22(4) even where that original appeal (in respect of which a cross-objection has been filed) is withdrawn or is dismissed for default the objections filed may nevertheless be heard and determined after such notice of the other parties as the Court thinks fit. In other words the cross-objection shall proceed in accordance with law relating to the disposal of appeal even if the original appeal had been withdrawn or dismissed for default. It clearly shows that a proceeding initiated by filing a cross-objection under Order 41. rule 22(1) is a proceeding independent of the original appeal inasmuch as the cross-objection shall proceed in accordance with the provisions of law relating to an appeal and the Appellate Court shall exercise all the powers as such in disposing of the cross-objection. In substance cross-objection is an appeal. On the memorandum of cross-objection the respondent is liable to pay necessary court fee and observe other formalities which are necessary for preferring an appeal in respect of the reliefs claimed for in the cross-objection. Order 41, rule 22(1) gives the respondent in the original appeal the right to prefer a cross-objection against the concerned judgment and decree within one month of the receipt of the notice of filing of the appeal or the date fixed for hearing of the appeal. This in fact is a right given to the respondent to prefer 'an appeal in substance in the form of a cross-objection. In substance a cross-objection is nothing but an appeal. Therefore it must confirm to all the requirements that are necessary for preferring an appeal. If it does not, then the cross-objection cannot be registered and is liable to be returned. In other words we are of the opinion that no cross-objection can be entertained in respect of an appeal which has been preferred against the judgment and decree of an Artha Rin Adalat which requires that the appeal must be filed by the defendant respondent within 30 days accompanied by evidence of payment of 50% of the decretal amount. Unless the memorandum of cross-objection satisfies all the requirements necessary to prefer an appeal under section 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Act the same cannot be entertained by this court and memorandum of' cross-objection is liable to be returned to, the concerned respondent In this connection we may refer to the decision reported in 1960 AIR (SC) 1349.

19. Section 7 of the (Artha Rin) Adalat Act provides for an appeal by the aggrieved party within 30 days of the decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat. The normal period of preferring regular appeal or Misc. appeal in this Court is 90 days. Therefore it appears that Artha Rin Adalat Act has provided for a special period of limitation of 30 days for preferring an appeal against the judgment and decree passed by an Artha Rin Adalat. The period of limitation prescribed for preferring an, appeal against the judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat is different from the ordinary period of limitation for preferring an appeal in this Court. This being the position, this Court has no power to condone the delay in respect of an appeal preferred beyond 30 gays against the judgment and decree of an Artha Rin Adalat The question now before us is whether the period of limitation for preferring the cross-objection in this Court under Order 41rule 22(1) CPC would be 30 days or could be extended by the leave of the Court. In section 7 of the (Artha Rin) Adalat Act the period of limitation is 30 days. Under Order 41, rule 22(1) CPC the period of limitation for preferring a cross-objection is one month. Superficially. there is hardly any distinction between 30 days and one month. By judicial interpretation it had been held that the two are not identical. The mode of calculation on the basis of 30 days and on the basis of one month are different and this view had already been approved by the Appellate Division of our Supreme Court relying on certain English decisions. In the circumstances it cannot be said that the period of limitation prescribed for preferring an appeal in section 7 of the (Artha Rin) Adalat is identical or the same with the period of limitation prescribed for preferring a cross-objection under Order 41 rule 22 (1) CPC. In the instant case the memorandum of appeal preferred by defendant No. 5 Abul Kalam Azad had according to the note of Stamp Reporter been returned. In the circumstances there is no memorandum of appeal pending before us and as such the question of converting the memorandum of appeal into a cross-objection does not arise at all. Furthermore  memorandum of appeal presented by defendant No. 5 Abul Kalam Azad even if accepted as cross-objection, being not accompanied by the evidence of the payment of 50% of the decretal amount in the trial Court cannot be entertained by this Court. In any view of the matter the prayer of defendant No.5 to treat the memorandum of appeal (which had been returned to him) as memorandum of cross-objection is hereby rejected. The cross- objection which has been filed by defendant No. 5 Abul Kalam Azad has been filed beyond one month. In the circumstances the formal memorandum of cross-objection appears to have been presented beyond the period of limitation. We have discussed this point already. In case of a special period of limitation we have no power to condone the delay. Accordingly the regular cross-objection filed by defendant No. 5 Abul Kalam Azad appears to be barred by limitation and is liable to be rejected on that ground. Furthermore, regular memorandum of cross-objection has not been accompanied by evidence of payment of 50% of the decretal amount in the trial Court. The regular memorandum of cross-objection is also liable to be rejected for noncompliance of the requirement of the payment of 50% of the decretal amount in the trial Court. What cannot be done directly cannot equally be done indirectly. Accordingly the prayer for accepting the regular memorandum of cross-objection filed by defendant No. 5 Abul Kalam Azad is also rejected.

20. The memorandum of cross-objection filed by defendant No. 9 Zahirul Islam cannot be entertained on the ground that the provision of Order 41 rule 22 CPC can hardly be made applicable in respect of an appeal preferred in this Court against the judgment and decree passed by an Artha Rin Adalat. It appears that the memorandum of cross- objection preferred by defendant No. 9 Zahirul Islam is not accompanied by any evidence of the payment of 50% of the decretal amount in the trial Court and, as such, the same is to be returned.

21. For the reasons stated above the application filed by defendant No. 5 is rejected. The office is directed to return the memorandum of cross-objections to defendant Nos. 5 and 9.

The office is directed to make the appeal ready expeditiously.

End.
