full_judgment:
Bijan Kumar Das J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Chandpur in Title Suit No. 63 of 1985. By the impugned judgment dated 30-6-1986 the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit.

2. The short fact leading to this appeal is, that the appellant as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 63 of 1985 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Chandpur impleading the respondents as defendants praying for declaration of title by adverse possession in respect of the suit land described in schedule to the plaint and for declaration that the judgment and decree passed on 19-2-1985 and 25-2-1985 respectively by the learned Subordinate Judge, Chandpur in Title Appeal No. 34 of 1984 which arose out of Title Suit No. 20 of 1983 of the Court of the Munsif, Upazila, Hajigonj (Original Title Suit No. 156 of 1983 of the Second Court of Munsif, Chandpur) instituted by defendant No. 3 are fraudulent, collusive, void and not binding upon the plaintiff. The plaintiff asserted in the plaint that the suit land originally belonged to one Madhab Chandra Paul, who died leaving behind 4 sons, namely, Horo Kumar Paul, Chandra Kumar Paul, Kali Kumar Paul and Raj Mohan Paul and each son inherited 4 annas share out of the suit jote. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are the sons of Chandra Kumar Paul and they left for India before partition. The plaintiff also asserted that Chandra Kumar Paul gifted his 1/4/- annas share to his wife Marani Paul who being owner thereof sold the same to the plaintiff on payment of Taka 2,000.00 by executing a bainapatra on 4-2-1959 in favour of the plaintiff. According to the plaintiff Dag No. 830 has been wrongly endorsed as Dag No. 833 in the bainapatra. The plaintiff has been possessing the suit land since his purchase. It has been further asserted that there was a rent suit bearing No. 292 of 1973 in the Court of the Munsif, Chandpur in which there was a compromise by the plaintiff with one Prasanna. Since purchase the plaintiff has been in possession of the suit land for more then 12 years. The plaintiff further asserted that after the liberation the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 came to Bangladesh and joined with the plaintiff’s enemy and when the plaintiff asked the defendant No. 2 on 31-10-1981 to execute and register a kabala deed in his favour, the defendant No. 2 flatly refused. The defendant Nos. 3-6 filed a petition under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 20-5-1982 in Title Suit No. 564 of 1981, which was filed by the plaintiff when the plaintiff learned about the alleged sale deed of the defendants and about the decree in Title Suit No. 267 of 1977 and hence filed the present suit.

3. Before the trial Court the defendant No. 3 entered appearance and contested the-suit by filing a written statement. Having denied all the averments made in the plaint the contesting defendant contended that the suit land originally belonged to Madhab Chandra, who died leaving behind 4 sons, namely, Hore Kumar Paul, Chandra Kumar Paul, Kali Kumar Paul and Raj Kumar Paul. According to this defendant, Chandra Kumar Paul sold 0.80½ decimals of land for Taka 3,000.00 to this defendant No. 3 on the basis of bainapatra and delivered possession to this defendant. This defendant further alleged that as Chandra Mohan did not execute and register the sale deed on the basis of the bainapatra and accordingly, after the death of Chandra Mohan, this defendant No. 3 filed Title Suit No. 156 of 1983 against the sons of Chandra Mohan and others in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Chandpur which on transfer was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 20 of 1983. The said suit was dismissed by the trial Court against which the present defendant No.3 as appellant filed Title Appeal No. 34 of 1984 and the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the appeal. The defendant also asserted that the present plaintiff filed an application under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for adding him as a party in the said Title Suit No. 156 of 1983 which was rejected by the trial Court against which the plaintiff did not move any higher forum. This contesting defendant clearly asserted that the plaintiff has obtained a false and forged bainapatra in the name of Maroni Paul, who was not the wife of Chandra Kumar Paul and the alleged bainapatra dated 4-2-1959 is false and forged. The plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 564 of 1981 in the 2nd Court of the Munsif, Chandpur which on transfer to the Court of Munsif, Hajigonj was renumbered as Title Suit No. 298 of 1983 and subsequently on the prayer of the plaintiff this suit was withdrawn. The defendant asserted that the plaintiff has filed this suit on the same cause of action which is bad in law. This defendant further asserted that one Prasanna Kumar Paul and the present plaintiff in collusion with one another filed Title Execution Case No. 32 of 1972 which was beyond the knowledge of this defendant. It has been further asserted that in Title Suit No. 292 of 1973 no summons was served upon Gopal Chandra Paul and Chinta Haran Paul, who are the sons of Chandra Kumar Paul and solenama filed in that suit is collusive and void. Accordingly, this defendant prayed for dismissal of the suit.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the pleadings of the parties and the evidence on record dismissed the suit on contest against the defendant No. 3 with cost and ex parte against the rest without costs. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree the plaintiff as appellant has preferred this appeal.

5. Mr. Md Nurul Mostafa, the learned Advocate for the appellant, submits that the trial Court misconstrued the bainapatra Ext. 1 and committed an error in holding that the bainapatra has not been written at the instance of the executants Marani Paul. The learned Advocate submits that the learned Subordinate Judge mis-read the evidence of PW 4 and omitted to consider the admission of PW 1 made in his evidence that there is a homestead on the suit land which fits in with the plaintiff’s case. The learned Advocate also contends that since defendant Nos. 1-2, who are sons of Chandra Kumar Paul and Maroni Paul did not contest the suit to deny the fact of acquisition of title by their mother Marani Paul, on the basis of gift from Chandra Kumar Paul and also the execution of the bainapatra by her in favour of the plaintiff, the suit should have been decreed. The learned Advocate for the appellant further submits that acquisition of title by Marani Paul on the basis of oral gift from her husband Chandra Kumar Paul is valid in law. The learned Advocate submits that since donor and the donee both belong to Hindu community, provision of Hindu Law being their personal law shall prevail over the provision of the Transfer of Property Act and the oral gift is therefore valid to confer title on Marani Paul.

6. Mr. Mokbul Ahmed Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff- respondent, on the other hand, supports the decision of the trial Court and submits that Marani did not acquire any title on the basis of oral gift from her husband Chandra Kumar Paul and therefore she had no authority to transfer the property on the basis of the agreement in favour of the plaintiff. The learned Advocate submits that for effecting a gift for immovable property by a Hindu the same may only be made by an instrument which must be a registered one and no oral gift is permissible. The learned Advocate referred to section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act and submits that for the purpose of making a gift of immovable property, the transfer must be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor, and attested by at least two witnesses. The learned Advocate also submits that the bainapatra Ext. 1 is a forged and collusive document. The learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiff filed the suit claiming declaration of title on the basis of adverse possession but in his evidence the plaintiff did not utter a single word about possession and he was not also supported by PW 2. On the other hand, the learned Advocate contends that PW 3 and 4 supports the possession of defendant No. 3 in the suit land.

7. We have perused the pleadings of the parties, the impugned judgment and heard at length the learned Advocate for both the parties.

8. Admittedly the suit land belonged to Madhab Chandra Paul. It is also admitted that Madhab Chandra Paul died leaving behind 4 sons, namely, Horo Kumar Paul, Chandra Kumar Paul, Kali Kumar Paul and Raj Mohan Paul. It is also admitted that Chandra Kumar Paul inherited 14/- annas share. It has been proved that the defendant Nos.1-2 is the sons of Chandra Mohan Paul and they left the country for India before partition. The plaintiff asserted that Chandra Kumar Paul gifted the property in favour of his wife Marani Paul while the contesting defendant denied such gift. In the plaint no disclosure has been made as to when the oral gift took place. In evidence also the plaintiff as PW I could not state the date of the alleged oral gift. The plaintiff was examined as PW 1. He deposed in his evidence that he could not say in which year oral gift was made. He also stated in his evidence that he was not present at the time of the gift nor he could say who else were present PW 2 Nagendra Chandra Paul in his evidence deposed that Chandra Kumar Paul gifted his property to his wife in his present. This PW 2 also could not say as to when this oral gift took place. He admitted that names of the wives of Pauls are not known to him. PW 3 Abdul Latif Talukder in his evidence stated that Chandra Kumar Paul orally gifted the suit land to his wife Marani Paul. He also could not state the date of the alleged oral gift. He could not say the names of the wives of the sons of Madhab. From the above evidence, it appears that the plaintiff failed to prove his case of oral gift by Chandra Kumar Paul in favour of his wife Marani Paul.

<u>9. We have also considered the submission of the learned Advocate for the respondent that under section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, for the purpose of making a gift of immovable property, the transfer must be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor, and attested by at least two witnesses. In the absence of a registered instrument a gift of immovable property by a person belonging to Hindu community and governed by Dayabhaga school of Hindu Law is not valid in view of the provision of section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act. In a decision in the case of Hari Kison Pandy vs Nageswari Debi and others reported in 8 DLR 65, it has been held:</u>

<u>"As regards Hindu gifts to which the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, applies the rule of pure Hindu Law that delivery of possessions essential to the validity of gift is abrogated by section 123 of that Act. Under that Act delivery of possession is no longer necessary to complete a gift, nor is mere delivery sufficient to constitute a gift except in the case of movable property. A gift under that Act can only be effected in the manner provided by section 123".</u>

10. In the said decision his Lordship referred to a decision of their Lordships of the Privy Council reported in 53 Indian Appeals 89 (Kelyana Sundaram vs Korurps (1927),50 (Mad) In the said decision their Lordships of the Privy Council held that "On delivery of the deed of the donee there was an acceptance of the transfer within the meaning of section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 and thereupon the gift became effectual subject to registration as required by section 123."

11. The learned Advocate for the appellant submits that under the Hindu Law oral gift is permissible and relied on a decision reported in AIR 1930 Patna 610 (Harihar Prasad vs Sifi Gurugranth Saheb). The said decision relates to an oral endowment according to Hindu law and it has been found that: "A Hindu can therefore create an oral dedication of immovable property in favour of an idol." This proposition of law decided in the said decision is not applicable in the facts of the present case. The learned advocate for the appellant also relied on the case of Karam Ilahi vs Share-ud-Din reported in 35 Indian Cases 14 and AIR 1927 Calcutta 197. In both the decisions the essentials of a gift under the Muhammadan Law were considered, thus the said decisions are not applicable in the facts of the present case.

<u>12. Having considered the submissions of both the learned Advocates we hold that in the absence of a registered instrument a gift by a person belonging to Hindu community and governed under the Dayabhaga School of Hindu law is not valid in view of the provision of section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act. In view of this legal position Marani Paul did not acquire any title in the suit land on the basis of alleged oral gift and she was not competent to make any transfer of the same in any manner whatsoever including by a bainapatra as in the case before us.</u>

13. The plaintiff asserted that Marani Paul executed a bainapatra on 4-2-1959 in his favour on receipt of Taka 2,000.00. To prove his case as regards execution of the bainapatra which has been marked Ext. 1, the plaintiff as PW deposed that one Jogendra Chandra Paul wrote the bainapatra. Bainaparra Ext. 1 shows that one Nagendra Chandra Paul was the scribe of the bainapatra. This Nagendra Chandra Paul was examined as PW 2 who while proving the bainapatra Ext. 1 stated that he wrote the bainapatra. He also stated that he is a deed writer by profession but this Ext. 1 was not written as a professional man. He admitted that he has no licence. He does not know the name of the wife of Madhab Chandra Paul. He also does not know the names of the wives of the Pauls. This PW 2 clearly stated in his evidence that Marani Paul was not the wife of Chandra Kumar Paul. He further stated that bainapatra was written at the instruction of the daughter-in-law and wife of Chandra Kumar Paul. We find that there is a vital contradiction in the evidence of PW 1 and PW 2 as regards the scribe of the bainapatra Ext. 1. PW 1 stated that the bainapatra was written by one Jogendra Chandra Paul while PW 2 Nagendra Kumar Paul claimed that he had written the bainapatra. This vital contradiction in the evidence of PW 1 and 2 clearly indicates that the bainapatra Ext. 1 is not genuine. We shall find support in this view from the evidence of PW 3 Abdul Latif Talukder who stated that he signed the bainapatra as attesting witness. PW 4 Rustom Ali Kabiraj also stated that he signed the bainapatra as attesting witness. This was not the case of the plaintiff either in the plaint or in his evidence. PW 4 also stated that the bainapatra was written as instructed by Nitta Nanda Paul. He also stated that the plaintiff purchased the stamp. It appears from the bainapatra Ext. 1 that it was written on a plain paper and not on any stamp though PW 4 stated stamp was purchased by the plaintiff for writing of the bainapatra. From all these evidence, we are of the view that the plaintiff has failed to prove the genuineness of the bainapatra Ext. 1. We shall now consider the plaintiffs case of possession as asserted in the plaint. To prove his case of possession the plaintiff as PW 1 has not uttered a single word that he was ever in possession of the suit property. It is strange that when the plaintiff based his title on adverse possession, he did not claim possession in his evidence. We have gone between the lines of his evidence and we find that the plaintiff has not uttered a single word as regards his possession in the suit land, far less on the basis of the bainapatra Ext. 1. Since the plaintiff has not stated anything in his evidence as regards his possession of the suit property, there was no occasion of his witnesses to corroborate him on this vital issue. As a matter of fact PW 2 Nagendra Chandra Paul also did not utter a single word about plaintiff’s possession in the suit land. On the other hand, PW 3 and PW 4 clearly deposed in their cross- examination that defendant No. 3 possesses the lands of Pauls by purchase. Since the plaintiff filed the suit claiming acquisition of title by adverse possession, the onus in entirely on him to show by clear and definite evidence that his possession is continuous, open, undisturbed uninterrupted and hostile to the real owner. Here in the present case the plaintiff has not uttered a single word as regards his possession in his evidence. We therefore, find that the plaintiff has failed to prove his possession in the suit land.

14. On the otherhand, the contesting defendant No. 3 asserted that the suit land belonged to Chandra Kumar Paul and he purchased the same from him by a bainapatra but as Chandra Kumar Paul died before the execution of a sale deed, the defendant No. 3 continued in possession and subsequently filed a suit against the heirs of Chandra Kumar Paul and obtained a decree from the appellate Court in Title Appeal No. 34 of 1984 .which arose out of Title Suit No. 20 of 1983. The said judgment has been marked as Ext. 6 in the suit. It appears from Ext. 5 that in Title Suit No. 20 of 1983 filed by the contesting defendant No.3 against Gopal Chandra Paul son of Chandra Kumar Paul, the present plaintiff filed an application for impleading him as a party in the said Title Suit No. 20 of 1983 which was rejected. The contesting defendant No. 3 proves his possession in the suit land in evidence and he was supported by PW 3 and PW4.

<u>15. The plaintiff has claimed his title in the suit land by .adverse possession on the basis of the bainapatra Ext. 1 from Marani Paul. We have held that Marani Paul did not acquire any title from her husband Chandra Kumar Paul on the basis of the alleged oral gift and, as such, she has no transferable right to execute the bainapatra Ext. 1. We have also found that the plaintiff has failed to prove the genuineness of the bainaparta Ext. 1 and his possession in the suit land on the basis thereof. Since the plaintiff has no possession in the suit land, the suit for declaration of title on the basis of adverse possession cannot succeed. The learned Subordinate Judge, it appears to us, has not committed any error or illegality in dismissing the plaintiffs suit.</u>

16. The learned Subordinate Judge, of course, did not consider the prayer made by the plaintiff as regards declaration that the decree passed in Title Appeal No. 34 of 1984 which arose out of Title Suit No. 20 of 1983 is collusive, void and not binding on the plaintiff. Since we have found that the plaintiff has failed to prove his title to the suit land, the plaintiff cannot challenge the decree obtained by defendant No. 3. Further, it appears that this plaintiff unsuccessfully tried to be impleaded in the said suit which was decreed in appellate stage.

17. We have found that the plaintiff could not prove his case of acquisition of title by adverse possession and, as such, the plaintiff has no locus-standi to challenge the decree obtained by defendant No.3. Court fees paid are correct.

18. In the result, this appeal is dismissed with costs. The judgment and decree passed by the trial Court are hereby affirmed. The order dated 17-8-1987 passed by this Court earlier' staying further proceedings of Money Execution Case No. 15 of 1987 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Chandpur stands vacated.

Send down the Lower Court records at once.

End.

Vs.
Brajendra Lal Dhar and others ------- Respondents.
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 14.1.1985 passed by the High Court Division, Chittagong Bench in the Civil Revision No. 11 of 1984).
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J. : This appeal following leave by the plaintiff-appellants is from the revisional judgment of a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, Chittagong Bench, discharging the Rule in affirmation of the order dated 11.9.83 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong allowing Miscellaneous Case No. 56 of 1979 under Order 41 rule 19, CPC.

2. The plaintiff-appellants' Other Suit No. 95 of 1973 for declaration of title and recovery of possession was decreed against the defendant-respondents ex parte on 11.8.75. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 instituted Miscellaneous Case Nos. 300 and 325 of 1975 respectively under Order 9, rule 13 CPC for restoration of Other Suit No. 95 of 1973 before the trial Court. At the same time respondent No. 1 preferred Other Appeal No. 142 of 1976 against the said ex parte decree before the District Judge, Chittagong. Miscellaneous Case No. 323 of 1975 was dismissed for default on 24.1.76, but Miscellaneous Case No. 300 of 1975 is still pending. Other Appeal No. 142 of 1976 was also dismissed for default by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong to whom the appeal was transferred for hearing and disposal. The said appeal was restored on 28.7.77 upon filing of a miscellaneous case by respondent No. 1 under Order 41, rule 19 CPC and the appeal was fixed for hearing on 12.11.79. On 12.11.79 the appeal was again dismissed for default. Respondent No. 1 preferred Miscellaneous Case No. 56 of 1979 under Order 41, rule 19 CPC on 27.11.79 for restoration of Other Appeal No. 142 of 1976 and after a contested hearing the learned Subordinate Judge set aside the order of dismissal for default dated 12.11.79 and restored the appeal to its file and number, subject to payment of a cost of Tk. 400.00 by respondent No. 1 to the plaintiff-appellants.

3. The High Court Division in revision affirmed the order of the learned Subordinate Judge with the further condition that respondent No. 1 shall pay an increased sum of Tk. 1,000.00 including Tk. 400.00 as compensatory costs to the plaintiff-appellants within one month. Leave was granted to consider whether in view of the conduct of the defendants, which is negligent at all stages, and in view of an absence of a clear finding that the defendant was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the appeal was called on for hearing, the order of restoration of the appeal was bad in law and would promote harassment of the plaintiff-appellants.

4. Mr. Azizur Rahman Chowdhury, learned Counsel for the plaintiff-appellants, submits that the conduct of the respondents, as revealed from the facts above, is self-explanatory. The suit was decreed ex parte on 11.8.75 and the series of laches and negligent conduct on the part of the defendants have only added to the harassment and misery of the appellants.

5. It is the finding, of the learned Subordinate Judge, affirmed in revision, that respondent No. 1 was present in Court on the date of hearing of the appeal on 12.11.79, but the lawyer engaged by him was busy otherwise and was not present in Court. It is also the concurrent finding that a petition was filed on behalf of respondent No. 1 on 12.11.79 stating that the respondents' lawyer was otherwise engaged and praying for one month's adjournment and admittedly that petition was rejected. In that view of the matter both the learned Subordinate Judge and the High Court Division held that for ends of justice respondent No. 1 should be given an opportunity for placing his case before the Court on payment of compensatory costs to the appellants.

<u>6. The previous conduct of the respondents may be reprehensible but the matter cannot be decided on the ground of mere previous conduct. Whether the defendant was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the appeal was called on for hearing will determine the outcome of the proceeding under Order 41 rule 19 CPC. On this count both the Courts have given cogent reasons for non-appearance of the defendants and found them to be sufficient if not by express words, but by necessary implication. Since the order has been passed upon proper assessment of evidence we find no ground to interfere with the same.</u>

The appeal is, therefore, dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

parties:
Modern Shipping Agencies ----- Plaintiff-Appellant
Vs. 
Central Inland Water Trans port Corporation Limited and another ----- Defendant–Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, Chittagong, Bench, dated 4.11.1985 in Civil Revision No. 241 of 1984).
full_judgment:
MH Rahman J: The appellant, M/s. Modem Shipping Agencies, instituted Money Suit No. 94 of 1980 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Third Court, Chittagong against the respondents. Respondent No. 1, Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Limited, defendant No. 2 in the suit, entered appearance on 28th November, 1980 and filed as many as eight applications for time for filing written statement. The last application for time, filed on 8th April, 1982, was rejected, there being no one to move that application. Thereafter the defendants did not take any step nor did they file any written statement. The suit was decreed ex parte on 18th November, 1982. On 30th March, 1983 respondent No. 1 filed an application under Order 9 rule 13 for setting aside the ex parte decree.

2. Respondent No. 1's case for setting aside the ex parte decree is that they entered appearance in the suit through Mr. AM Rashiduzzaman, Advocate, who once informed them that time had been granted by the court for filing the written statement, but the company did not receive any other or further information from him and was under an honest belief that their learned Advocate would inform them about the date of filing of the written statement. Subsequently on a query they came to learn that 8th April, 1982 was fixed for filing written statement and an application for further time for filing written statement was rejected as there was no one to move that application. The suit was fixed on 22nd June, 1982 for service return on defendant No. 1. The plaintiff filed an application in this regard and on 23rd June, 1982, and it was ordered that the matter be put up on 26th June, 1982 and both the parties be informed, but the learned Advocate of respondent No. 1 was not informed. By a further order dated 24th August? 1982 the plaintiffs application with regard to service of summons on defendant No. 1 was ordered to be put up on 28th August, 1982 with intimation to both the parties, but no such information was given to the respondent's learned Advocate. On 28th August, 1982 the plaintiffs prayer in respect of service of summons on defendant No. 1 was allowed. Subsequently on 19th September, 1982 the suit was filed for ex parte disposal on 18th November 1982. Respondent No.I's learned Advocate Mr. Rashiduzzaman went to the United Kingdom in April, 1982. As the directions of the Court for informing the parties with regard to two different dates 26th June, 1982 and 28 August, 1982 were not complied with the developments in the suit could not be known to respondent No. l's Advocate. After inspection of the record the respondent came to know on 2nd March, 1983 about the ex parte decree and filed the Miscellaneous case No. 14 of 1983 on 30th March, 1983.

3  The trial Court allowed the Miscellaneous Case. On the plaintiffs revisional application, Civil Revision No. 241 of 1984, the High Court Division remanded the case to the trial Court for considering the question of limitation after giving the parties reasonable opportunity of being heard and examining witnesses if they so liked. Respondent No. 1 was allowed to file an application for condonation of delay if so advised.

<u>4. The appellant contends that the respondent had duly appeared before the Court after receiving the summons and the decree was passed ex parte against them long thereafter and their application for setting aside the decree after the expiry of 30 days from the date of the ex parte decree was time-barred under Article 164 of the Limitation Act, 1908. In support of their contention the appellant relied on Mian Kamal Din Vs. Malik Muhammad Bashir, PLD 1952 Lahore 456 wherein it was held that once a party receives intimation of an action it is for him to pursue it and to keep himself in touch with the proceedings, either personally or through his counsel.</u>

5. It is contended that the High Court Division was wrong in remanding the case to the trial Court since respondent No. 1 did not apply for condonation of delay as provided in amended provisions of Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is further contended that as there was no application by respondent No. 1 for condonation of delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act the trial Court was not called upon thereof to consider the question of delay and it did not in fact address itself to that question but the High Court Division even after noticing this aspect of the matter illegally remanded the matter for giving an opportunity to respondent No. 1, particularly when they failed to keep watch over the proceedings in the suit for more than seven months after rejection of their ninth application for time to file a written statement.

<u>6. The appellant has drawn our attention to the following observation made in Ahsan Ali & ors. Vs. District Judge and Settlement Commissioner Sukkur and others 21 DLR (SC) 139=PLD 1969 SC 167.</u>

<u>"It has also been held by this Court in several cases that mere disposal of the appeal on merits is not sufficient to lead to the inference that the delay must have been condoned. There must be something in the order or judgment itself to show that the Court concerned was conscious of the fact that the proceeding was out of time and had applied its mind to the question of limitation before dealing with the proceeding on merits."</u>

7. The respondents, on the other hand, contend that section 5 of the Limitation Act itself docs not postulate making of a separate and independent application for condonation of delay. In support of this contention they have cited Chowdhury Saifuddin Ahmed Vs. Shamsuddin & ors 40 DLR (1988) 10 wherein it was held that "The section lays stress on satisfying the court that the appellant or applicant had sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal or making the application within the statutory period. It does not say that the only medium through which the Court can be satisfied is by way of a separate application".

<u>8. In that decision a reference was made to Mt. Kulsoomun Nissa and another Vs. Noor Mohammad alias Sultan Haider and another, AIR. 1936 (Allahabad) 666, where Sulaiman, CJ did not approve or a dismissal of appeal as time-barred merely on the ground that the appellant had not made a formal application for extension of time under section 5 of the Limitation Act, and also to Firm Kaura Mal Vs. Firm Mathra Dass, AIR 1959 (Punjab) 646 wherein it was held that "Merely because there was no written application filed by the appellant is hardly a sufficient ground for refusing him the relief, if he is otherwise entitled to it."</u>

9. The respondents contend that in the application for setting aside the ex parte decree the reasons for delay in filing the Miscellaneous Case were explained and as such there were sufficient materials on record, and that the High Court Division did not committee any illegality in remanding the case to consider the question of limitation.

<u>10. The respondents have also placed reliance on Mohammad Yousaf Vs. Member, Board of Revenue, West Pakistan, Lahore & 6 others, 1970 SCMR 170. In that case the Pakistan Supreme Court after considering the aforementioned case of Ahsan Ali and others Vs. District Judge and others upheld the High Court's view that the appellate Court impliedly condoned the delay when the question of limitation was specifically brought to the notice of the appellate authority and in spite of that he allowed that appeal by deciding it on merits.</u>

<u>11. In the case of Ahsan Ali and others Vs. District Judge and others on which the appellant has placed much reliance the Supreme Court remanded the matter to the Additional Settlement Commissioner for the disposal of the appeal in accordance with law after giving the parties adequate opportunity of representing their respective cases and adducing evidence both on the question of limitation as well as the question of fraud. The ratio in that case, as brought in focus in Mohammad Yusuf's Case 1970 SCMR 170, is that the authority concerned should be conscious of the question of limitation before deciding the proceeding pending before it. Though section 5 of the Limitation Act does not provide for filing of a separate and independent application for condonation of delay it is desirable for the convenience of the Court and the contending parties that such an application should be filed explaining each day of delay otherwise the question of limitation or condonation of delay can not effectively be mooted and determined, and it will be difficult for the contending parties to join issues and adduce evidence in the matter. Where such an, application is not filed the court may, however, condone the delay if it is satisfied on other materials on record that there was sufficient cause for not preferring the application or the appeal within the prescribed period of limitation. In the instant case no question of limitation was mooted or discussed by the trial Court and hence it could not be said that by restoring the case the delay was impliedly condoned.</u>

In that view of the matter, the question of delay must be enquired into and, in fitness of things, it is to be done by the trial Court. When a matter is sent back and the superior Court in its discretion directs that the parties be given an even opportunity to place their respective cases such discretionary order should not ordinarily be interfered with unless it causes a serious prejudice to one of the contending parties. In the facts of the case the High Court Division's order docs not suffer from any infirmity. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed. No costs.

End.

parties:
Santi Gopal Dey and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Maliza Rani Saha and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule calls in question the order dated 19- 2-96 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Narshingdi, in Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 1994 setting aside the ex-parte judgment and decree dated 14-11-94 passed in Title Suit No. 108 of 1988. By this impugned order the learned Senior Assistant Judge allowed the case of the opposite party under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. Short facts relevant for disposal of the case are that, the petitioners as plaintiffs instituted a Suit in the Court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Narshingdi being Title Suit No. 108 of 1988, for declaration of easement right in the suit land.

3. The defendant opposite parties contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations of the plaint, contending, inter alia, that the suit as framed is not maintainable in law and it is barred by limitation. It was further alleged that the plaintiffs filed the suit with false and frivolous allegations and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. At the trial, the plaintiff examined 3 witnesses and the contesting defendants also examined 3 witnesses in support of their respective cases. The learned Senior Assistant Judge by his impugned judgment dismissed the suit. Against the order of dismissal, the plaintiffs preferred an appeal before District Judge, Narshiugdi being Title Appeal No. 29 of 1990.

5. The learned appellate Court after hearing the appeal set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court and sent the case back on remand to the trial Court for fresh hearing in accordance with law. Thereafter the plaintiffs examined witnesses on 9-11-94 in the absence of the defendants, and obtained an ex-parte decree on 14-11-94, following which the plaintiffs started Title Execution Case No. 5 of 1995 and obtained delivery of possession through Court.

6. Thereafter the defendant opposite parties filed an application under Order 9 rule XIII of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree whereupon miscellaneous case No. 24 of 1995 was started. It has been contended in the application under Order 9 rule XIII of the Code of Civil Procedure that the defendants had no occasion to know about the peremptory date of hearing of the suit on 9-11-94 and the subsequent ex-parte decree on 14-11-94 after the case came back on remand and, as such, they were prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was taken up for ex-parte disposal.

7. At the trial of Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 1995 petitioners examined 3 witnesses and the plaintiffs examined 5 witnesses in support of their respective cases. The learned Assistant Judge by his impugned order dated 19-2-96 allowed Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 1995 with a cost of Taka 2,000.00 payable to the plaintiffs. Being aggrieved by the said order, the plaintiff-petitioners moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr. Abdul Hamid, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners, submits that the learned Assistant Judge as well as the learned District Judge erred in law in allowing Miscellaneous Case No. 14 of 1995 under Order 9 rule XIII of the Code of Civil Procedure in a most casual manner and the same has occasioned failure of justice.

9. Mr. Nikhilesh Dutta, the learned Counsel appearing for the opposite parties, on the other hand, submits that the learned Assistant Judge was perfectly justified in allowing the application under Order 9 rule XIII of the Code of Civil Procedure applying the correct principle of law dominating the field and the same has caused no failure of justice.

10. Mr. Abdul Hamid placed before me the impugned order dated 19-2-96. The learned Counsel also placed before me the application under Order 9 rule XIII of the Code of the Civil Procedure. It appears that the learned Assistant Judge, in the impugned order itself, found that the defendant opposite parties had some laches in pursuing the progress of the suit for quite a long time and on such consideration saddled them with a cost of Taka 2,000.00. It also appears that the learned Assistant Judge found that no notice was served upon the defendants after the suit came back on remand to the trial Court, although they ought to have been notified. The learned Assistant Judge held the Court officials responsible for such faults.

11. From the scrutiny of the order sheet of Title Suit No. 108 of 1988 it is found that after the suit came back on remand to the trial Court, the plaintiffs amended the plaint twice arid obtained an order for local investigation beyond the knowledge of the defendant-opposite parties. Such important measures affecting the merit of the suit cannot, be allowed keeping the contesting defendant in the dark. The learned Assistant Judge evidently erred in law in allowing amendment of the plaint and the holding of the local investigation beyond the knowledge of the defendants. The impugned decree is thus found to have been obtained by resorting to illegal manoeuvres and on that ground also it cannot be allowed to stand.

<u>12. In support of his submission Mr. Dutta has cited the case of Mozaffer Ahmed and others vs Moulvi Saleh Ahmed and others reported in 40 DLR 239 =1988 BCR 125. In this case, the suit was transferred from the Court of the Munsif, Satkania to the Court of the Assistant Judge Bashkhali but no notice was served upon the defendants after the case was transferred to the Court of the Assistant Judge,</u>

<u>Bashkhali.</u>

<u>13. In the cited case it has been held that such an important order as the transfer of the case from one Court to another should invariably be communicated to the parties concerned and in making of such communication the signature of the parties or their advocates should be obtained and when signatures are not obtained, the order sheets should show that the information has been communicated.</u>

14. The cited decision lends support to the defendant and it is found that the defendants were prevented by sufficient cause from appearing before the Court when the suit was taken up for ex-parte disposal. The learned Senior Assistant judge committed no error of law in allowing the case under Order 9 rule 13 CPC.

15. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned order dated 19-2-96 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Narshingdi in Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 1995 is hereby affirmed. The order of stay earlier granted by this Court stands vacated.

16. This is a suit of the year of 1988 and, as such, it is expedient in the interest of justice that it be disposed of with utmost expediency. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Narshingdi is directed to dispose of the case as expeditiously as possible, preferably within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of the order, without granting adjournments to the parties except on most convincing grounds.

Communicate the order to the learned Assistant Judge, Narshingdi at once.

End.

Abul Kalam and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Kafiluddin and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Sirajul Islam J: Thus Rule under section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 was directed against the judgment and order dated 5-10-95 passed by Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 22 of 1995 staying the further proceeding of Title Execution Case Nos.6 and 7 of 1994 of that court till disposal of First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 244 of 1994 pending in the High Court Division.

2. The facts necessary for the disposal of this Rule are that the opposite party No. 1, Kafiluddin Ahmed as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 22 of 1995 against the defendant-petitioner and others in the Court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Sadar, Chittagong for a declaration of his title to the suit property described in the plaint and for a declaration that the title Execution Case Nos. 6 and and 7 of 1994 arising from the decrees of the petitioner's Title Suit No. 50 and 54 of 1984 are not binding upon the plaintiff. The plaintiffs case is that the opposite party No. 2 (defendant No. 3) Mahmuda Begum Chowdhury being owner of the suit property made a contract to seIl the suit property to the plaintiff by executing a bainapatra and thereafter the plaintiff by filing Title Suit No. 89 of 1993 for Specific Performance of Contract obtained an ex parte decree on 9-4-1994 against the said Mahmuda Begum Chowdhury and started Execution Case No. 4 of 1994, got the kabala from her on 2-8-1994 and thus the Execution Case No. 4 of 1994 was disposed of on satisfaction. That the defendant-petitioners earlier filed two separate suits being Title Suit Nos. 50 and 54 of 1984 against the same vendor opposite party No. 2, Mahmuda Begum Chowdhury on the basis of their two separate bainapatras and obtained decrees in both the suits on analogous trial. The judgment debtor opposite party No. 2 preferred First Appeal Nos. 24 and 25 of 1989 in the High Court Division and the appeals were dismissed on contest on 18-7-1993. The opposite party No.2 then filed Civil Petition for Leave LO Appeal Nos. 480 and 481 of 1993 and these petitions were dismissed by the Appellate Division on 29-6-1994 and thereafter the petitioners started Execution Case Nos. 6 and 7 of 1994 for execution of their above decrees. Thereafter the plaintiff, Kafiluddin filed his Title suit No. 21 of 1995 for declaration as aforesaid and filed an application in the suit praying for a temporary injunction for restraining the petitioners 1 and 2 from proceeding with their Title Execution Case No.6 and 7 of 1994 and obtained an ad-interim order of status quo on 19-2-1995 which after hearing was made absolute vide order dated 15-7-1995.

3. Against this order dated 15-7-1995, the defendant-petitioners, AbulKalam and Hosneara Begum filed First Miscellaneous Appeal Tender No. 512 of 1995 corresponding to First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 244 of 1995 in this court. This court while admitting this appeal stayed the operation of the impugned order dated 15-7-1995 for a period of 3 months which was extended from time to time in the Rule. Thereafter the plaintiff-opposite party No.1 again filed an application in the Court of learned Subordinate Judge under section 151 with a prayer for staying the Title Execution Case Nos. 6 and 7 of 1994. At the same time this defendant- petitioners also filed an application under section 10 CPC for staying the further proceeding of Title Suit Nos. 22 of 1995 till disposal of First Appeal No. 13 of 1995 filed by the defendant-petitioners in this court against the ex parte decree of plaintiffs' Title Suit No. 89 of 1993. After hearing both parties, the learned Subordinate Judge stayed further proceedings of Title Suit No.22 of 1995 and also stayed the proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 6 and 7 of 1994 till disposal of FMAT No. 512 of 1995 (FMA No. 244 of 1995) pending before this High Court Division vide order dated 5-10-1995.

4. Being aggrieved by this order dated 5-10-1995 staying the further proceeding of Title Execution Nos. 6 of 7 of 1994 the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 as petitioners have filed this revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in this court and obtained the present Rule.

5. Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioners has submitted that opposite party No. 2 Mahmuda Begum Chowdhury had entered in two separate contracts dated 25-12-83 with these petitioners to sell the suit property to the petitioners and for non-fulfillment of terms of contract, these petitioners filed Title Suit Nos. 50 and 54 of 1984 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong and obtained two separate contested decrees by analogous judgment dated 31-1-1989 for specific performance of contract against which Mahmuda Begum Chowdhury filed First Appeal Nos. 24 and 25 of 1989 (Chittagong) renumbered as First Appeal Nos. 218 of 1991, 225 of 1991 (Dhaka) and both the appeals were dismissed in the High Court Division on 18-7-1993 against which Mahmuda Begum Chowdhury went upto Appellate Division with the two leave petitions which were dismissed summarily on 29-6-1994. The learned Advocate submits that after obtaining decree for Specific Performance of Contract having been confirmed upto the Appellate Division, the petitioners filed Title Execution Case Nos. 6 and 7 of 1994 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, but in the meantime, this plaintiff opposite party No. 1 Kafiluddin Ahmed filed Title Suit No. 89 of 1993 and obtained ex parte decree without the knowledge of the petitioners on 9-4-1994, and after knowing about that decree this petitioners filed First Appeal No. 131 of 1995 in this court but thereafter the opposite party No. 1 again filed another. Title Suit No. 22 of 1995 and obtained the impugned order staying the Title Execution Case Nos. 6 and 7 of 1994 with the sole purpose to frustrate the petitioners' both the decrees obtained by a lapse of 11 years upto the Appellate Division and, as such, the impugned order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is an erroneous order superseding this court's order dated 14-1-1996 staying operation of the earlier stiu us quo order and thus the impugned order has occasioned a failure of justice to the petitioners and, as such, the impugned order is liable to be set aside.

6. Mr. SR Pal, the learned Senior Counsel along with Mr Subrata Chowdhury appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 has on the other hand, submitted that when a suit is pending against a decree, it is incumbent upon the court to stay the execution arising out of that decree as per provision contained in Order 21 rule 29 CPC and, as such, the order of stay of two execution cases passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is quite a correct order and there is nothing wrong in it. The learned counsel further submits that there was necessity for staying the execution cases pending disposal of Title Suit No. 22 of 1995 and in that view of the matter also, the learned Subordinate Judge has correctly passed the impugned order for avoiding multiplicity of cases.

The Order 21 rule 29 CPC reads as under-

"where a suit is pending in any court against the holder of a decree of such court, on the part of the person against whom the decree was passed, the court may on such terms as to security or otherwise, as it thinks fit, stay execution of the decree until the pending suit has been decided"

<u>7. By a reading of the provision contained in Order 21 rule 29 CPC as quoted above, itappears that this provision contemplates the pendency of a suit between the decree-holder and the judgment debtor in respect of the decree in question. But in the instant case before us, the pending Other Suit No. 22 of 1995 is not between the decree-holder and the judgment-debtor of the two decree (Execution Case No.6 and 7 of 1994) sought to be executed. So, it appears that at that time no suit was pending before the court against the decree-holder on the part of the judgment-debtor. The Other Suit No. 22 of 1995 although pending against the decree-holder but it is not filed by the judgment-debtor Mahmuda Begum Chowdhury against him but it is filed by a 3rd party Kafiluddin Ahmed and more so, the two decrees sought to be executed have not been challenged in Other Suit No. 22 of 1995, rather it has been admitted in the affidavit-in-opposition by the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 that the petitioners obtained two separate decrees for Specific Performance of Contract in Other Suit No. 50 and 54 of 1984 which were upheld upto the Appellate Division and then the petitioners started Title Execution Case No. 6 and 7 of 1994. This judgment debtor Mahmuda Begum Chowdhury has not filed any other suit for setting aside that decree against the decree holders. Therefore, the question of staying that decree by a 3rd party does not arise.</u>

8. In the facts and circumstances of the case as discussed above, the provision of Order 21 rule 29 CPC, in our opinion, will not be applicable in this case.

9. In this connection Mr. Khan Saifur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, referred to a decision in the case of Ashraful Huq and others vs. Anwar Ahmed and others reported in 1981 BCR (HC) 301 wherein it has been held held by a Division Bench of this court that" A decree-holder cannot be allowed to be deprived of the fruits of a lawful decree obtained after 15 years of litigation". It appears that the similar view has been expressed by their Lordships of the Appellate Division of this court in the case of Asia Khatun being dead her legal heirs and representatives Bulbul Ahmed and others vs. Rahatun Nessa and another reported in 15 BLD (AD) 47 wherein it has been held as under:

"If it appears to the Court that the petitioner filed successive suits to frustrate the decree obtained in an earlier suit, the prayer for staying the further proceedings of the execution case is liable to be rejected as being not bonafide."

10. In the instant case, the defendant-petitioners 1 and 2 obtained the decree on contest against Mahmuda Begum Chowdhury in Title Suit Nos. 50 and 54 of 1984 which was confirmed on contest upto the Appellate Division and the moment they started execution case No. 6 and 7 of 1994 after a period of about 10 years, then this 3rd party-plaintiff opposite party No.1 Kafiluddin entered into the scene and started filing suits, one after another, firstly, he filed Title Suit No. 89 of 1993 and then again Other Suit No. 22 of 1995.

11.Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, the learned Advocate, said that at any stage of the suit Nos. 50 and 54 of 1984 upto the Appellate Division, this Mahmuda Begum never disclosed about any contract with the present plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 and, as such, it will appear that all subsequent suits filed by the 3rd Party Kafiluddin are nothing but adoption of some means and methods to frustrate the fruits of the decree obtained by the petitioners upto the Appellate Division. In the facts and circumstances as stated above, it will clearly appear that the approach of the 3rd party-opposite party No. 1 is not bonafide approach but it appears to be an approach made in collusion with that Mahmuda Begum Chowdhury with the sole purpose of frustrating the hard-earned decrees of the decree-holder-petitioners obtained during a period of about 10 years. Under such a position of the matter, there cannot be an stay order of the Execution Case Nos.6 and 7 of 1994.

12. By a perusal of the impugned order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in Other Suit No. 22 of 1995, it appears that the impugned order contained two parts. She has written the one part of the order in English staying the further proceedings of Title Suit No. 22 of 1995 till disposal of the appeal No. 131 of 1995 pending in the High Court Division against the ex parte decree of plaintiff- opposite party's Other Suit No. 89 of 1993 filed by these petitioners. The learned Subordinate Judge has written the other part of the same order in Bengali language staying the Execution Case No. 6 and 7 of 1994. Mr Khan Saifur Rahman submits that when the proceeding of other suit No. 22 of 1993 has been stayed by the learned Subordinate Judge by the first part of her order the question of further proceeding in the same suit for the purpose of staying the execution case Nos. 6 and 7 of 1994 does not arise. We are also of the opinion that when the further proceeding of Title Suit was stayed, that means it cannot proceed further. But from the impugned order it appears that on one hand, the learned Subordinate Judge stayed the further proceeding of Title Suit No. 22 of 1995 but, on the other hand, she again herself stayed the proceeding of Execution Case Nos.6 and 7 of 1994. These apparently appears to be a self-contradictory order.

13.It again appears that admittedly the learned Subordinate Judge earlier passed a status quo order in this same suit No. 22 of 1995 amounting to restraining the defendant-petitioners from proceeding with their Execution case Nos.6 and 7 of 1994 against which the petitioners filed Miscellaneous Appeal Tender No. 512 of 1995 (FMA No.244 of 1995) in this court and obtained an order staying operation of status quo order. Stay operation of that status quo order is still there. In such circumstances, we fail to understand that in spite of there being a stay operation of her status quo order from this court how could the learned Subordinate Judge pass a further order staying the whole proceeding of Execution Case No. 6 and 7 of 1994. This order of the learned Judge totally negates the above order of this High Court Division. The learned Subordinate Judge has passed the impugned order dated 5-10-1995 in English and in Bengali language combined together. We have never seen before such a single order passed both in English and in Bengali language. In the facts and circumstances of the case we are of the opinion that the learned Subordinate Judge has passed the impugned order in an over-enthusiastic manner.

14.Considering all the above facts and circumstances of the matter, we find that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law and facts resulting in error in her decision by passing the order which has occasioned a failure of justice to the petitioners who are entitled to proceed with the execution of their decrees against the judgment- debtor. The impugned order, therefore, calls for interference by this court.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute with costs. The impugned order dated 5-10-1995 so far as it relates to the staying of Execution Case Nos. 6 and 7 of 1994 is hereby set aside.

End.

Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Additional Attorney-General (Mr. AY Salehuzzaman, Deputy Attorney-General with him) instructed by Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record -----For the Appellants in all the appeals
