case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 12.3.90 & 14.3.90 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in  FA Nos. 31 and 32 of 1989 & Civil Revision No. 328 of 1989 respectively).
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal J : Civil Appeal Nos. 53 and 54 of 1990 arose by leave from the judgment and order dated 12.3.90 passed by the High Court Division in FA Nos. 31 and 32 of 1989 dismissing the appeals and thereby affirming the decree dated 5.12.88 and order dated 28.1.89 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 350 of 1988 arising out of Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 63 of 1988. Civil Appeal No. 55 of 1990 arose by leave from the judgment and order dated 14.3.90 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Case No. 328 of 1989 reversing the order dated 2.3.89 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 378 of 1988 rejecting the application filed by the defendant-appellant under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint. 2. These three appeals have been heard together and will be disposed of by this common judgment. 3. By Memo No. 1809/4(4) dated 2.8.78 the Government of Bangladesh in the Ministry of Communications, Roads and Highways entered into an agreement with Contractor KM Shafi Limited, a Private Limited Company (respondent in all the three appeals) for providing average 2-1/2 thick compacted premixed bituminous concrete work on the Airport Road, Dhaka. A dispute arose between the parties over payment of bill of the Contractor-respondent after completion of the work which was referred to the sole Arbitrator, namely, the Superintending Engineer, Roads and Highways. On 30.10.78 the Arbitrator gave his award. The respondent filed Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1979 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka under section 33 read with section 30 of the Arbitration Act for setting aside the award. It was disallowed by order dated 19.9.79. The respondent then preferred First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 494 of 1980 in the High Court Division. By judgment and order dated 24.11.81 the High Court Division allowed the appeal in part and upheld the award in part. The High Court Division found that the Arbitrator left another dispute undecided, namely, whether the supplementary tender items claimed by the Contractor were admissible or not. The High Court Division remitted the Award to the Arbitrator to determine the unresolved dispute directing him to call for statements from both the parties, take evidence if tendered, give hearing to the parties and proceed to decide the dispute in accordance with law." 4. Mr. Monirul Islam succeeded Mr. Matiur Rahman as Superintending Engineer, Roads and Highways, Dhaka Roads Circle and Mr. Monirul Islam thus became the succeeding Sole Arbitrator. Seven years passed by, but the Arbitrator did not act. The respondent filed a petition of contempt of Court and the High Court Division issued a Rule which was served upon the Superintending Engineer. Then he took up the matter and passed an award for Tk. 5,59,680.02 in favour of the Contractor-respondent by Memo No. 1652 dated 27.4.88. The Contractor-respondent thereupon filed Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 63 of 1988 on 13.7.88 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka under section 14/17 of the Arbitration Act for making the award a Rule of the Court. The notice was served on the appellants on 17.7.88. The appellants prayed for time thrice to file written objection on the ground, first, that papers could not be collected and secondly, that there was flood, which were allowed. On 15.9.88 the appellants prayed for time for the fourth time but the prayer was rejected on the ground that they failed to file their written objection within 30 days from service of notice on 17.7.88. The Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 63 of 1988 was decided ex parte in favour of the respondent on 29.9.88 and the award was made a Rule of the Court. Another ex parte order was passed by the Court on 10.11.88 directing the appellants to pay the awarded amount to the Contractor by 30.11.88. By order dated 19.11.88 the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka converted the said Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 63 of 1988 into Title Suit No. 350 of 1988 and accordingly a decree was drawn up making the aforesaid Award a part of the decree on 5.12.88. The appellants filed an application under section 151 CPC which was dismissed by , the learned Subordinate Judge by order dated 28.1.89. 5. The appellants filed Title Suit No. 378 of 1988 in the same Court for a declaration that the aforesaid orders dated 29.9.88 making the "so-called" award a Rule of the Court and the subsequent order dated 10.11.88 are illegal, fraudulent, null and void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff-appellants. 6. In the said Title Suit No. 378 of 1988 the defendant-Contractor filed an application under Order VII, rule 11(d) CPC for rejection of the plaint which was dismissed by the learned Subordinate Judge by order dated 2.3.89, holding that section 32 of the Arbitration Act was no bar to the filing of the suit. The defendant-Contractor preferred Civil Revision No. 328 of 1989 against the said order dated 2.3.89. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute by the impugned judgment and order dated 14.3.90 out of which arises Civil Appeal No. 55 of 1990. The High Court Division held the suit to be barred by section 32 of the Arbitration Act. 7. The appellants also filed FA No. 31 of 1989 against the decree dated 5.12.88 passed in Title Suit No. 350 of 1988 converted from Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 63 of 1988 and FA No. 32 of 1989 against the order dated 28.1.89 rejecting the appellants' application under section 151 CPC. Both the appeals have been dismissed by the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order dated 12.3.90 out of which arise Civil Appeal Nos. 53 and 54 of 1990. 8. Leave was granted to consider the appellants' submission that the letter addressed by Mr. Monirul Islam, the Superintending Engineer to the Additional Chief Engineer by Memo No. 1652 dated 27.4.88, which has been made a Rule of the Court, was not an award at all within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Arbitration Act. The appellants' plaint was rejected by the High Court Division in consideration of section 32 of the Arbitration Act but as the Memo. in question was not an award at all, section 32 has no application and the plaint of Title Suit No. 378 of 1988 ought not to have been rejected. 9. As the leave granted revolves round the interpretation of the said Memo No. 1652 dated 27.4.88, it will be profitable to set out in a nutshell the contents thereof. 10. In the Memo in question addressed to the Additional Chief Engineer, Roads and Highways, Dhaka Zone, the Superintending Engineer stated that "in the context of the judgment of the highest Court" the Contractor was asked to submit bills in connection with his claim and necessary papers in connection with supplementary tender items. He did so on 15.3.88. The Executive Engineer, Roads & Highways, Dhaka Roads Circle was asked to examine those bills and papers. By Memo Nos. 605 dated 4.4.88 and 781 dated 19.4.88, the Executive Engineer "as per direction of the highest Court", examining the Contractor's bills and verifying the quantum of work done and the rates, submitted reports. Considering the Contractor's bills and papers and those reports, the Contractor's dues come to Tk. 5,59,680.02. It is necessary to sanction the said amount to be able to pay the Contractor. There is no sanction for road development in the current financial year. The Airport Road has been transferred to the control of Municipal Corporation. The Contractor is pressing hard for payment and for "duly obeying the order of the highest Court". Hence to "settle the matter on an urgent basis" the Additional Chief Engineer was requested to sanction the said amount. A copy of this Memo.was also sent for information to the Executive Engineer and the Contractor. 11. Mr. AW Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for the appellants, advances several arguments in support of his submission that the Memo. in question is not an award. He submits that the Memo. was not written by Mr. Monirul Islam is his capacity as an Arbitrator. He wrote the same in his capacity as the Superintending Engineer. There is no determination of any sum payable to the Contractor and there is no direction either to pay any sum to the Contractor. The Memo.does not reveal that any arbitration proceeding was held, any witness was examined, any cross-examination took place, any documents were exhibited or any hearing took place. He submits that the Memo. was purely an inter-departmental communication addressed by the Superintending Engineer to his higher authority, namely, the Additional Chief Engineer, with a view to obtaining advance sanction for the Contractor's claimed amount in case the department has to pay the claimed amount after a regular arbitration proceeding. In fact no arbitration took place either on 27.4.88 or before or after the said date. The High Court Division, he submits, committed an illegality in dismissing the First Appeal Nos. 31 and 32 of 1989 after construing an inter-departmental letter to be an award. 12. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel for the Contractor-respondent, submits that Mr. Monirul Islam had applied his mind to the dispute and gave a decision in the dispute. There is no gainsaying the fact that the Superintending Engineer was the Arbitrator as per agreement dated 2.8.78 and therefore failure to use the word Arbitrator will not render the decision invalid. He also submits that there is no particular form for passing an award. An award need not contain a judgment, no reasoning need be given. According to Mr. Ahmed, the Memo.in question contains two parts. The first part is the award proper and the second part contains the ways and means of implementing the award. Unless the amount staled in the Memo is payable to the Contractor, no sanction, far less advance sanction, will be made by the higher authority. Mr. Ahmed next submits that the officer to whom the Memo was addressed, namely, the Additional Chief Engineer, treated the Memo. in question as an award which, he submits, is evidenced from the note given by the Additional Chief Engineer on the body of the Memo in question as follows : কোর্টের সিদ্ধান্তের উপর জরুরীভাবে প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা নিন। ঠিকাদারের পাওনা পরিশোধ করা দরকার। মেরামত খাত হইতে উহা পরিশোধ করুন। আপনার অফিসে এত দেরী হ’ল কেন প্রতিবেদন দিন।

স্বাক্ষর/-অস্পষ্ট

৩-৫-৮৮

অতিরিক্ত প্রধান প্রকৌশলী

13. The note shows that the Additional Chief Engineer directed the Superintending Engineer not to wait for any sanction. He directed immediate payment for the maintenance account and also asked the Superintending Engineer to explain why there was so much delay in the payment of award to the Contractor. This is dated 3.5.88. Mr. Ahmed then submits that a copy of the Memo. in question was forwarded to the Executive Engineer, Roads and Highways and to the Contractor-respondent who understood the Memo. in question to be an award. On the day of delivery of this judgment Mr. Ahmed has filed a copy of legal notice dated 12.6.88 served by the contractor,respondent upon the Super-intending Engineer calling upon him to pay the awarded amount of Tk. 5,59,680.02 within 7 days. A copy of the acknowledgement due receipt has also been filed showing that the legal notice was received by registered post on 15.5.88. Mr. Ahmed also submits that after filing of the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 63 of 1988 on 13.7.88 the appellants prayed for time to file written objection on three occasions but never did they raise an objection that the award was not an award within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Arbitration Act. To raise this objection no papers were necessary and the plea of flood, etc. was also untenable. He submits that the appellants raised this question for the first time in the First Appeals in the High Court Division as an after thought. 14. It is quite apparent from a bare reading of the Memo. in question that the Superintending Engineer was anxious to implement the High Court Division's judgment and order dated 24.11.81 passed in FMA No. 494 of 1990. All the exercises he made, namely, asking the Contractor to submit the bills and necessary papers in support of his claim in regard to supplementary tender items, asking the Executive Engineer to check up the Contractor's bills and papers and then considering both the Contractor's bills and papers and the reports of the Executive Engineer, giving a finding as to the Contractor's claim and arriving at a figure of Tk. 5,59,630.02 have been done in compliance with the order of the High Court Division. True, no formal statements were asked for from the parties, no evidence was taken and the parties were not formally heard, but the nature of exercise leaves no room for doubt that the High Court Division's order was substantially complied with. After having applied his mind to the facts of the case the Superintending Engineer came to a clear decision that the amount determined by him has to be paid to the Contractor. He was aware that there was no money sanctioned for road development in the current financial year. The Airport Road has since been transferred to Dhaka Municipal Corporation. The Contractor was pressing hard for payment of his dues and for implementing the order of the High Court Division. As such the Superintending Engineer requested the Chief Engineer to sanction the aforesaid amount to settle the matter on an urgent basis. 15. The learned Additional Attorney-General argues that when the Superintending Engineer wrote “বিষয়টি জরুরী ভিত্তিতে মীমাংসা করার নিমিন্ত” (to settle the matter on an urgent basis) he clearly implied that the matter was not yet arbitrated upon. He submits in support of his contention that Memo dated 27.4.88 is not an Award, that the appellants stated in paragraph 6 of Title Suit No. 378 of 1988 that the Arbitrator served a notice upon the Contractor to come for arbitration on 4.7.88, but the Contractor or his representative did not present himself on that date. The arbitration was adjourned till 9 AM of 18.7.88. A notice to that effect was not accepted by the Contractor on 6.7.88 and so the notice was sent on 7.7.88 to the Contractor by registered post. Additionally a copy of the notice was received by the learned Advocate for the Contractor. The Contractor or his representative did not attend the arbitration proceeding on 18.7.88. As the District Anti-Corruption Officer seized all the papers in this connection the appellants also could not proceed with the arbitration on 18.7.88. The Contractor filed Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 63 of 1988 on 13.7.88 after receipt of the notice of arbitration dated 6.7.88. The learned Additional Attorney-General submits that all these notices were annexed in the paper book of First Appeal No. 31 of 1989, but the High Court Division failed to consider the same. 16. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that the appellants in haste manufactured a fictitious arbitration proceeding starting from 4.7.88 after the receipt of die respondent's legal notice dated 12.6.88. 17. We refrain from deciding whether the Arbitrator proceeded afresh with an arbitration on and from 4.7.88 suo motu or on receipt of the respondent's legal notice dated 12.6.88 because this issue was not tried and decided in any Court. The High Court Division did not rightly consider the appellants' papers, because those were neither produced before the trial Court nor proved. For the same reason we shall not consider the respondent's alleged legal notice dated 12.6.88. 18. If the Memo. in question was not an award at all and if Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 63 of 1988 was filed during the subsistence of the arbitration proceeding, then the appellants should not have taken any time to file a written objection in the matter. The proceeding of Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 63 of 1988 could have been nipped in the bud had such a plea been taken at the earliest available opportunity. 19. We do not find any indication in the Memo. in question that the Superintending Engineer wrote to the Chief Engineer for "advance sanction" of the awarded amount. It is also unusual to pray for advance sanction without determining whether any money is payable to the Contractor or not. It is also not understandable why copies of the Memo. were sent to the Executive Engineer and to the Con-tractor. A purely departmental communication ought to be confined within the relevant departments. Outsiders are not to be given copies of the same, but forwarding copies thereof to the two parties involved in the arbitration is also indicative of the Memo being an award. There is indeed no particular form for expression of an Arbitrator's decision. It is not a judgment and it need not contain the reasonings of the Arbitrator. It is enough if the award contains the decision of the Arbitrator, which the Memo. in question does. 20. It does not appear, therefore, that the High Court Division erred in law in construing the Memo in question as an award. 21. The High Court Division, however, held that one of the appellants two appeals, namely, FA No. 31 of 1989 filed against the decree dated 5.12.88 was not maintainable. Section 17 of the Arbitration Act provides that no appeal shall lie from a decree making an award the Rule of the Court except on the ground that it is in excess of or not otherwise in accordance with, the award. The High Court Division held that the decree dated 5.12.88 is not in excess of the award and it is in accordance with the award. 22. Though no leave was granted on this part of the finding of the High Court Division the learned Additional Attorney-General argued that the appeal was maintainable under section 39(1)(vi) of the Arbitration Act which is as follows : "39. Appealable orders-(1) An appeal shall lie from the following orders passed under this Act (and from no others) to the Court authorised by law to hear appeals from original decrees of the Court passing the order : An order — (i) ----------------------- (ii) ----------------------- (iii) ----------------------- (iv) ----------------------- (v) ----------------------- (vi) setting aside or refusing to set aside an award." 23. He submits that by refusing to set aside the award the decree dated 5.12.88 became amenable to appeal under section 39(1)(vi) of the Arbitration Act. 24. The argument has no legs to stand. The appellants have not filed any application to set aside the award under section 17 of the Arbitration Act. Nor have they filed any application under section 33 to challenge the existence or validity of the award. It is absurd to say that by making the award a Rule of the Court, the Court has refused to set aside the award. The act of refusal must be in pursuance of a positive move by the party affected either under section 17 or under section 33. An ex parte order, as in the present case, making an award the Rule of the Court is not amenable to appeal under section 39(1) (vi) of the Arbitration Act. 25. The High Court Division was, therefore, correct in holding that FA No. 31 of 1989 was not maintainable. 26. With regard to Civil Appeal No. 55 of 1990 the High Court Division held, relying upon section 32 of the Arbitration Act, that the appellants' Title Suit No. 378 of 1988 was barred. Section 32 of the Arbitration Act is as follows: "32. Bar to suit contesting arbitration agreement or award—Notwithstanding any law for the time being in force, no suit shall lie on any ground whatsoever for a decision upon the existence, effect or validity of an arbitration agreement or award, nor shall any arbitration agreement or award be set aside, amended, modified or in any way affected otherwise than as provided in this Act." 27. The learned Additional Attorney-General submits that the suit in question was not filed for a decision upon the existence, effect or validity of the award. It was filed for a decision that the award was not an award at all in the eye of law. Hence section 32 could not be a bar to the suit. 28. This argument has also no basis, because though the appellants pleaded in the plaint that the Memo.in question was not an award within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Arbitration Act, yet there was no prayer for a declaration to that effect. On the other hand the appellants challenged the decree dated 29.9.88 and the order dated 10.11.88 as illegal, fraudulent, etc., which is in effect an invocation to decide upon the validity of the award. 29. Secondly, in view of our decision that the Memo. in question is an award the appellants' suit will for all practical purposes be a fruitless pursuit even if the suit is allowed to proceed. Conversely, even if we set aside the award on the ground that it is not an award at all, still it will be useless for the appellants to proceed with Title Suit No. 378 of 1988. In any view of the matter the appellants' suit is infructuous. 30. The learned Additional Attorney-General has further argued that the photocopy of the award in question was filed in Court on 15.9.88 in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 63 of 1988. The award was made a Rule of the Court on 29.9.88. Under Article 158 of the Limitation Act the appellants were entitled to 30 days time from 15.9.88 to file their written objection. The award was made a Rule of the Court before the expiry of 30 days. 31. This submission based on facts was not made at any time previously. Hence we are not inclined to consider the same. For all the above reasons, all the three appeals are dismissed with costs. End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 157 of 1990.
lawyer:
Sultan Ahmad, Advocate, instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioner. 
Not represented ----- Respondent.
parties:
Abdul Kader Chowdhury ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Nurul Islam and Others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 15-5-90 passed by the High Court Division, Comilla Sessions, Comilla, in Civil Revision No 161 of 1986.)
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J: This leave to appeal by the defendant petitioner is from the revisional judgment of a learned single Judge of the High Court Division, Dhaka making the Rule absolute and setting aside an order of the trial Court cancelling its earlier order dismissing a miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13, CPC and restoring the miscellaneous case to its file and number.

2. The plaintiff-respondent's suit for declaration of title was decreed ex parte and the defendant-petitioner filed a miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13, CPC for setting aside the ex parte decree. The said miscellaneous case was also dismissed for default of the defendant-petitioner on 14.5.86 at 12-30 PM. The defendant-petitioner filed hajira soon thereafter and submitted that he could not file hajira in time owing to hartal and prayed for an adjournment of the case. The prayer for adjournment was refused on the ground that the miscellaneous case was already dismissed for default. 7 days thereafter the defendant-petitioner filed an application under section 151 CPC for vacating the order dismissing the miscellaneous case for default and for restoration of the same. The trial Court having allowed the same the plaintiff-respondents moved in revision before the High Court Division which set aside the impugned order on the ground that an appeal lies against an order under Order IX, rule 13 CPC rejecting an application for an order to set aside the decree passed ex parte. Hence an application under section 151 is not maintainable.

<u>3. Mr. Sultan Ahmed, learned Counsel for the defendant-petitioner, submits that the order of the trial Court dismissing the miscellaneous case for default is not an order "under Order IX, rule 13, CPC rejecting an application form order to set aside a decree passed ex parte" and hence Order 43, rule 1 (d) had no application.</u>

<u>4. The argument is not tenable. The effect of an order of dismissal of the miscellaneous case for default is one of rejecting an application to set aside a decree passed ex parte. It is not an order passed on merit, but ex parte. Appeal lies in both cases under Order 43, rule 1(d), CPC. The view taken by the High Court Division is correct.</u>

<u>5. The defendant-petitioner, therefore, had a remedy by way of appeal under Order 43, rule 1 (d), CPC which he did not avail of. This is not to say that the application under section 151, CPC is barred under all circumstances, but since the defendant-petitioner filed the application under section 151 CPC 7 days after the dismissal of miscellaneous case for default without any explanation for delay, we do not think that in this particular case application of section 151 CPC would have been justified.</u>

6. The petitioner may avail of the remedy of appeal if he is so advised and if it is still open to him.

7. The petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
TH Khan, Senior Advocate instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Appellants. 
M Nowab Ali, Advocate-on-Record  ------- For the Respondent.
parties:
Manik Chand Bibi alias Rezian Nahar and another ------- Appellants 
Vs. 
Abdul Mutakabbir Chowdhury alias Sufi Mia Chowdhury ------- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 15th March, 1990 passed by the High Court Division,  Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 104 of 1989 (Sylhet)
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman, J.: This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment of the High Court Division passed in Civil Revision No. 104 of 1989 making the Rule absolute and directing to proceed with the execution case in accordance with law.

2. The material facts relevant for disposal of this appeal are that appellants and the respondent are the heirs of one Shamsu Mia Chowdhury who brought a partition suit being Title Suit No. 192 of 1964 in the 4th Court of Munsif, Habiganj and who obtained a preliminary decree therein. This decree was upheld upto the High Court Division. In the meanwhile Shamsu Mia Chowdhury died leaving the appellants and the respondent as heirs along with others. The appellants' case was that, the heirs of Shamsu Mia Chowdhury decided to partition the properties left by him amicably in terms of which a Swaranlipi dated 30th March, 1980 was executed by the respondent and his mother Noor Chand Banu (son and 1st. wife of Shamsu Mia Chowdhury) in favour of the appellants (second wife and daughters of Shamsu Mia Chowdhury) and Abdul Muktadir Chowdhury (another son of Shamsu Mia Chowdhury by appellant No.1 who died subsequently) by which they assigned the land under the decree to the appellants retaining other portion to themselves. After the disposal of the Second Appeal in the aforesaid suit, the case record was transmitted to the Court of Assistant Judge, Chaunarughat and it was renumbered as Title Suit No. 49 of 1988. Thereafter the appellants on the basis of the aforesaid Swaranlipi filed an application before the Assistant Judge under Order 22 rule 10 read with section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure for assignment of the decree in their favour and the same was rejected by the trial Judge and the final decree was ordered to be drawn up in terms of the preliminary decree. The respondent thereafter put the decree into execution in Title Execution Case No.6 of 1989 in the name of deceased Shamsu Miah Chowdhury allegedly without bringing the other heirs including appellants on record.

3. The appellants being aggrieved by the order of the rejection of their prayer for assignment of the decree moved the High Court Division in revision first, and thereafter realizing that appeal lies before the District Judge filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 22 of 1989 with a prayer for condonation of delay. The appeal was provisionally admitted by the District Judge Habiganj and all further proceedings of the execution case was stayed. The respondent moved the High Court Division in revision against the order of the District Judge and obtained a Rule being Civil Revision No. 104 of 1989. All further proceeding of the appeal was stayed. The respondent thereafter moved the Assistant Judge for proceeding with the execution case and the same having been rejected the respondent obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 951 of 1989 against the stay order. In revision the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division heard the revision cases together and made the Rules absolute. Leave was granted to consider whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division was correct in holding that Order 22 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not attracted in the facts of the case inasmuch as this application was filed before the drawing up of the final decree and whether the learned Single Judge erred in holding that in such a case Order 21 rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure was attracted and also whether the Revision cases at the instance of the respondent were misconceived or not as an appeal was pending before the District Judge and also whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division misdirected himself in failing to appreciate correctly the legal and factual aspects of the matter and thereby fell into an error of law occasioning a failure of justice.

4. It appears from the order dated 27.12.88 passed by the Assistant Judge, Chaunarughat that the application under Order 22 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the appellants for assignment of the decree in favour of them was rejected by him as the respondent objected to the same. The trial Judge further directed for drawing up of the final decree. The appellants first filed a revision before the High Court Division, withdrew the same and then filed an appeal before the District Judge, Habiganj who provisionally admitted the appeal subject to condonation of delay. The appeal was pending. Hence, a pertinent question comes up as to whether the High Court Division was justified in entertaining the revision when the appeal was pending and the legality of the order of the trial Court was challenged before it. It may be pointed out here that the appellate judge was within its competence to consider and decide the question as to whether the appeal as filed before him was maintainable in law and fact. The appellate forum was competent to dispose of the appeal finally, including the matter of condonation of delay. In such circumstances, the learned Single Judge has not acted correctly in holding that the appeal is not maintainable when the same was provisionally admitted and pending before the appellate court.

5. The learned Single Judge has committed another mistake in holding that the application does not lie under Order 22 rule 10 of the Code and consequently he illegally held that appeal does not lie.

<u>6. Order 22 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as follows:</u>

<u>"Procedure in case of assignment before order in suit (1) in other cases of an assignment, creation or devolution of any interest during the pendency of a suit, the suit may, by leave of the court, be continued by or against the person to or upon whom such interest has come or devolved."</u>

<u>It is clear that in a pending suit the provision of the aforesaid Order is applicable. The words" during the pendency of the suit" clearly mean before a final decree or order has been passed or made in the suit. The provision of this rule apply before the final decree. Thus, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division failed to consider that in partition suit only preliminary decree was passed and the final decree was not drawn up, which was apparent from the order of the Assistant Judge, Chaunarughat dated 27.12.88. Since the Swaranlipi was executed between the decree-holders, the appellants filed the application under Order 22 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for assignment of their respective shares in their favour as per the Swaranlipi. As the decree was not finally drawn up there could not be any lawful objection in filing the application under Order 22 rule 10 of the Code. It appears that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division failed to consider this material aspect that in the suit preliminary decree was drawn and the suit was not completely disposed of and before that stage the appellants filed the Swaranlipi in court for assignment of their shares as per the Swaranlipi. Thus, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division wrongly held that Order 22 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not applicable in the instant case as to him it appeared that execution had already been started and on that wrong view of law he misdirected himself in holding that the application of the appellants was one under Order 21 rule 16 of the Code and not one under Order 22 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It may be mentioned that the only question to be decided on an application under Order 21 rule 16 of the Code is whether the applicant is the person entitled to execute the decree and that stage did not reach till then.</u>

Hence, the impugned order is set aside and the appeal is allowed with costs.

End.

lawyer:
Abdul Hamid, Advocate ------ For the Petitioner. 
Md. Abdul Haque, Advocate ------ For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Abdul Hamid Mollah ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Md. Abdul Hye and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner calls in question the judgment and decree dated 30-10-91 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Kushtia in Title Appeal No. 229 of 1988 reversing the judgment and decree dated 29-8-88 passed by the Assistant Judge, Kumarkhali, Kushtia in Title Suit No. 84 of 1986 decreeing the suit.

2. The fact involved in this case, in brief, is that the plaintiff-petitioner filed Title Suit No. 84 of 1986 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Kumarkhali Upazila, Kushtia for a declaration that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are his Benamders and he has title in the suitland. The plaintiff-petitioner alleged in his plaint, inter alia, that he by registered kabala dated 23-4-59 purchased the suitland in the names of his minor sons namely, defendant Nos.l and 2, who were 8 and 1½ years of age at that time to avoid his creditor and has been possessing the same since then by constructing dwelling huts and garden therein. Since defendant Nos. 1 and 2 became disobedient and wanted to sell the suitland to others by taking advantage of the fact that the said kabala stands in their names he asked them to reconvey the kabala deed in his favour. But the defendant Nos.l and 2 lastly refused to do so on 4-7-86. Hence, the plaintiff-petitioner filed the present suit on 2-9-86.

3. The plaintiff petitioner also filed an application for temporary injunction on 8-9-86 in order to restrain the defendant Nos.l and 2 from dispossessing the suitland including huts and trees standing thereon. The trial Court, thereupon, issued show cause notice on the said defendants and passed an ad-interim order of injunction to the above effect. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 thereafter appeared and filed written objection on 17-9-86 denying the material allegations contending that they purchased the suitland measuring .29 decimal in equal shares by a registered kabala dated 23-4-59 with their own funds and since the purchase they were residing on the suitland by erecting dwelling huts. It is further contended that while in possession defendant No. 2 by two registered kabala deeds dated 5-4-86 sold the southern half of the suitland measuring 14½ decimal to defendant Nos. 4 to 6 ie, defendant-opposite parties No. 3-5 and left for village Panti where he has been living with his family including mother. Defendant-opposite parties Nos. 3 to 5 were given possession of 14½ decimals from southern portion of the suitland and since then they have been enjoying the possession thereof by erecting dwelling huts and demarcating the area with boundary walls on payment of government and municipal rents.

4. In this background of the case the plaintiff-petitioner filed an application on 1-12-87 for addition of defendant-opposite parties Nos. 3 to 5 by way of amendment of the plaint, which was allowed vide order dated 1-12-87. The plaintiff- petitioner thereafter filed an application for appointment of an Advocate Commissioner for local inspection and report as to whether, among others, the defendant-opposite party Nos. 3 to 5 were in possession of the said 14½ decimal of the suitland in the southern portion by erecting huts stating that it was necessary in view of the claim by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in their written objection. The trial Court vide order dated 1-3-87 allowed the local inspection and the Advocate Commissioner Mr. Md Moksed Ali submitted his report dated 27-4-87 in court on 24-5-87 and this was not objected to by any party.

5. The report of the Advocate Commissioner reveals that there is a tin shed kutcha hut constructed by the defendant Nos. 3 to 5 on the southern portion of the suitland. In this background of the matter, the trial Court by order dated 3-12-87 passed an order of status quo on an application for temporary injunction filed by the plaintiff petitioner on 1-12-87 restraining the defendant-opposite party Nos.3 and 5 from erecting any boundary wall and dwelling huts on the southern portion of the suitland and also issued a show cause notice on the above-mentioned defendants.

6. Thereafter, defendant-opposite party Nos.3 to 5 appeared and contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaintiff-petitioner contending, inter-alia, that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 purchased the suitland by registered sale deed dated 23-4-59 by their own earning as well as by the sale proceeds of some ornaments of their mother, when their father left them behind uncared for and lived with his second wife in Baradi village in the district of Kushtia. It was contended by defendant-opposite party Nos.3 to 5 that they took over possession of 14½ decimals of land from southern part of the suitland and had been possessing the same by demarcating the area with boundary wall and constructing dwelling hut on payment of rents by mutating their names.

7. The plaintiff-petitioner examined 3 PWs and defendant-opposite party Nos. 3 to 5 examined 4 DWs in support of their respective case. No document was proved and exhibited on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioner. But defendant-opposite party Nos. 3 to 5 proved and exhibited the kabala dated 23-4-59 as well as kabalas dated 5-4-86 including the rent receipts as Exhibits-A to C(3). The trial Court on consideration of evidence on record decreed the suit on finding that the plaintiff-petitioner purchased the suitland by registered kabala dated 23-4-59 with his own money when defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were minors being 8 and 1½ years old respectively and was in possession.

8. Defendant-opposite party Nos. 3-5 being aggrieved filed Title Appeal No. 229 of 1988 in the Court of District Judge, Kushtia. The Subordinate Judge, Kushtia heard and disposed of the appeal on transfer allowing the same by the impugned judgment and decree reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court on coming to the finding that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 bought the suitland with their earnings as well as out of the usufruct of their mother's property when they were about 18 and 12 years of age mainly relying on the evidence of DW 2. The appellate Court below also found that defendants including defendant opposite parties 3-5 were in possession of the suitland and not the plaintiff-petitioner. The appellate Court below also held that the suit was barred by limitation, as according to it, the cause of action arose since the date of original purchase of the suitland on 23-4-59 and the suit was liable to be filed within six years from that date in terms of Article 120 of the Limitation Act. This apart, the appellate Court below also found that the suit was not maintainable being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, as defendant-opposite party Nos. 3-5 were in possession of 14½ decimals of land from southern portion of the suitland.

9. Mr Abdul Hamid, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner submits that the trial Court on due consideration of evidence on record, decreed the suit. But the appellate Court below reversed the trial Court's judgment without proper discussion and consideration of the evidence except the evidence of DW 2. Mr. Hamid next argues that even if the plaintiff is not found in possession in respect of a part of the suitland, having been dispossessed after the filing of the suit, the present suit for declaration will not be hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act in the absence of the prayer for recovery of khas possession by amending the plaint. It is urged by the learned Advocate that the appellate Court below having held that the suit is barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act has committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice.

10. It is noticed that the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner, in course of hearing of the Rule, considered it advisable to include a prayer for recovery of khas possession of the suitland by amending the plaint and accordingly, obtained a week's adjournment. But when the hearing resumed the learned Advocate filed an application for amendment of the plaint, not for recovery of khas possession of the suitland from the defendants but for yet another declaration that the aforesaid two kabalas dated 5-4-86 executed by defendant-opposite party Nos. 3-5 in respect of the southern half of the suitland were inoperative and not binding on the plaintiff-petitioner submitting that such amendment can be made at any stage as this would not alter the character of the suit.

11.Mr Md Abdul Haque, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant opposite parties Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 5 contends that the preponderance of evidence on record go to show that the suit land was, in fact, purchased by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 out of their own earnings and also with the money made available by their mother by selling her ornaments and at the time of purchase defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were 18 and 12 years of age respectively and were employed in weaving factory. It is also contended by the learned Advocate that inability to file title documents including rent receipts by the plaintiff-petitioner also proves the claim of the defendant-opposite parties that the suitland was not purchased by the plaintiff-petitioner but by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. Learned Advocate further contends that the oral evidence read with the report of the Advocate Commissioner prove that the defendant opposite parties are in possession of the suit land and the plaintiff petitioner having failed to pray for recovery of khas possession of the suitland by amending the plaint the suit is not maintainable being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

12.Learned Advocate for the opposite parties next contends that even if it is accepted that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are the ostensible owners of the suit land since they are in possession of the suit land along with title documents, defendant-opposite parties Nos. 3 to 5 have acquired a good title in terms of section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act by purchasing the southern half of the suit land by two kabalas dated 5-4-86 from defendant No.2 as they are bonafide purchasers for value.

13. The important question that has arisen for consideration in this Rule is whether the purchase of the suitland in 1959 in the name of the defendant Nos.l and 2 is a benami transaction. In other words, whether defendant Nos.l and 2 are Benamders of the plaintiff-petitioner in relation to the purchase of the suitland by kabala dated 23-4-59. In a Benami transaction the onus is on the plaintiff to prove that he is the real owner and the purchasers are merely name-lenders. It appears from the evidence of PW 2 who was admittedly the landlord of the plaintiff as well as the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 at the time of purchase of the suit land and PW 3 that the suit land was purchased by the plaintiff-petitioner when the defendant No.1 was 8 and defendant No. 2 was 1½ years of age and they were not capable of earning. It is also clear from the evidence of PW 3 that soon after purchase of the suitland the plaintiff-petitioner bought bricks from him and built a dwelling house and the existence of such brick-built house in the suit land has not been denied by the defendants. The appellate Court below without considering material evidence of PWs 2 and 3 came to a wrong finding that the suitland was purchased by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 with their own fund and not by the plaintiff- petitioner and thus committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice. This non-consideration of material evidence is also evident from the judgment of the appellate Court below. With regard to the possession of the suit land there is preponderance of evidence on record showing that defendant No. 2 sold out his southern half of the suit land measuring 14½ decimal to defendant-opposite party Nos. 3 to 5 by kabalas dated 5-4-86 and delivered possession thereof and started residing in a different village named Panti and before selling his portion of the suitland both the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 used to live on the northern portion of the suitland where defendant No. 2 is still residing with his family. The available evidence on record including the report of the advocate commissioner show that the defendant-opposite party Nos. 3 to 5 are in possession of the southern half of the suitland from before the filing of the suit by demarcating the land, constructing boundary wall and have been paying rents after mutating their names on the record of the government and the municipality. It is also found from the evidence on record that the plaintiff-petitioner mostly lives with his third wife in a different village and occasionally comes and resides alone in his brick-built house standing on a portion of the northern side of the suitland. In this background of the matter, I agree with the finding of the appellate Court below that defendant No.1 is in possession of the northern half and defendant opposite party Nos.3 to 5 are in possession of the southern half of the suitland from before the filing of the suit.

<u>14. Since on preponderance of evidence it is found that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were in possession of the suit land along with the title documents including rent receipts although they were not real owners the defendant-opposite party Nos. 3 to 5 acquired good title to the southern half of the suit land in terms of section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act. Because, there is no evidence on record showing that the defendant-opposite party Nos. 3 to 5 had any notice that the suitland in fact belonged to the plaintiff-petitioner and the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were merely his benamdars. Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act provides as under:</u>

<u>"Section 41. Transfer by Ostensible Owner: Where, with the consent express or implied, of the persons interested in immovable property, a person is the ostensible owner of such property and transfers the same for consideration, the transfer shall not be voidable on the ground that the transferor was not authorised to make it provided that the transferee, after taking reasonable care to ascertain that the transferor had power to make the transfer, has acted in good faith."</u>

<u>15. The above view is supported by the decision in the case of H amidullah Talukdar & others vs. Muslim Khan and others reported in 8 DLR 606. The relevant portion of the said judgment regarding the scope of section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act reads as under:</u>

<u>"It is a principle of natural equity which must be universally applicable that, where one man allows another to hold himself out as the owner of an estate and a third person purchases it, for value, from the apparent owner in the belief that he is the real owner, the man who so allows the other to hold himself out shall not be permitted to recover upon his secret title, unless he can overthrow that of the purchaser by showing either that he had direct notice, or something which amounts to constructive notice, of the real title; or that there existed circumstances which ought to have put him upon an inquiry, that, if prosecuted, would have led to a discovery of it. This is the foundation of section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act."</u>

<u>16. Since it is found on evidence including the report of Advocate Commissioner that the defendants were in possession of the suitland from before the filing of the suit, the plaintiff-petitioner was required to include the prayer for recovery of khas possession of the suit hind by amending the plaint by way of consequential relief. So, mere suit for declaration that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are Benamders of the plaintiff-petitioner and that the plaintiff-petitioner has title in the suit land without praying for a consequential relief for recovery of khas possession from defendant Nos. 1, 4-6 the suit is liable to be dismissed being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. If any authority is necessary in this connection cases reported in 13 DLR (SC) 228 and 39 DLR (AD) 46 may be referred to.</u>

17. In this context the application for amendment of the plaint by the plaintiff-petitioner for another declaration at this belated stage merits no consideration and is rejected. Because allowing of another declaratory relief will not cure the legal defect in the suit.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without cost and the judgment and decree dated 29-8-88 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Kumarkhali, Kushtia is set aside without any order as to cost.

End.

lawyer:
Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Senior Advocate (Mahbubey Alam, Advocate with him) instructed by Sajjadul Huq, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Appellant.
TH Khan, Senior Advocate, Wahhab Miah & Ml Faruqui, Advocates with him), instructed by Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record  ------- For the Respondent No.1. 
Ex-parte  ------- Respondent Nos. 2 & 3.
parties:
Abdul Mannan ------- Appellant.
Vs.
Jobeda Khatun and others ------- Respondents.
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 19th November, 1985 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Revision No.773 of 1984).
full_judgment:
MH Rahman, J: On 7th December, 1991, appellant instituted Title Suit No. 874 of 1979 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for specific performance of a contract for exchange of property. The suit was decreed ex parte on 15th February, 1980. For setting aside that decree respondent No.1 instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 205 of 1980 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He also filed an appeal, being Title Appeal No. 32 of 1981, in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka. While the Miscellaneous Case was pending before the trial Court, his appeal was heard and dismissed on 25th August, 1984.

2. Respondent No.1 filed a revisional application, Civil Revision No. 773 of 1984, before the High Court Division. On 30th July, 1985 on his prayer Md. Altaf Hossain, J. of the High Court Division allowed the revisional application to go out of the list with a direction to send down the records to the trial Court for disposing of the Order 9, rule 13 matter expeditiously, preferably within three months, and also gave liberty to the learned Advocate to mention the case again after the disposal of that matter by trial Court.

3. The plaintiff-appellant who was not represented before the Court when that order was passed appeared on 6th November, 1985. He filed an application under section 151 of the Code before Sultan Hossain Khan, J, in seisin of the matter, for vacating that order on the ground that after the disposal of Title Appeal No. 32 of 1981, affirming the ex parte decree passed by the trial Court, the miscellaneous case under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code had become infructuous.

4. The learned Single Judge noted the following observation made in Md. Wasiq Khan Vs. Md. Sabiq Khan 31 DLR (AD) 51:

"The petitioner can legitimately pursue his remedy under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure notwithstanding his filing of appeal which is pending subject to the limitation that the appeal itself is not disposed of in the meantime on merit whereupon he loses his right to pursue the Miscellaneous Case because on the principle of merger the decree of the trial court merges into that of the appellate court."

5. After holding that the appeal in the instant case was dismissed not on merit but on the ground of limitation the learned Single Judge by the impugned order dated 19th November, 1985 refused to recall the order dated 30th July, 1985.

6. Leave was granted to consider whether in the facts of the case the disposal of the appeal on the point of limitation amounts to disposal on merit, and whether the decision in Md. Wasiq Khan Vs. Md. Sabiq Khan 31 DLR (AD) 51 has been correctly interpreted by the High Court Division.

7. Drawing our attention to the order of the appellate Court the plaintiff-appellant contends that the appellate Court not only dismissed the appeal on the ground of limitation, but it also "confirmed" the trial court's order passing the ex parte decree. As the matter was disposed of finally, it is urged, the order of the trial Court got merged in that of the appellate Court and the Order 9 rule 13 matter lost all its relevance.

<u>8. In support of his contentions, the learned Counsel for the appellant has cited MIs. Meta Ram &Sons Vs. Commissioner of Income Tax Punjab, AIR 1956 (SC) 367, Banwarilal Bhoid VP Neelkantham AIR 1965 Orissa 102, Jagat Jamani Dibi Vs. Jyotsna Basu AIR 1978 Calcutta 392 and Surinder Kaur Vs. Mohinder Bahadur Singh AIR 1978 HP 27.</u>

9. Respondent No.1 contends that she challenged the appellate Court's order refusing to condone the delay in filing the memorandum of appeal and as the latter was disposed of on the ground of limitation, before its being formally admitted, it cannot be said that the matter was disposed of on merit and the order of the trial Court did merge with that of the appellate Court.

10. The learned Counsel for the respondent has persistently drawn our attention to the merit of the respondent's case. He has pointed out that the appellant had earlier instituted a suit, Title Suit No. 263 of 1976, for the same cause of action and in that the plaint suit was rejected on 9th June, 1978 for not depositing the deficit court fees. An application under section 151 of the code for review of that order being rejected, the appellant filed a revisional application before the High Court Division and during pendency of that application he filed the instant suit, being title suit no. 874 of 1979 in respect of the same subject matter suppressing the fact that a civil revision was pending in the High Court Division. The subsequent suit was valued at Tk. 15,000.00 suppressing the fact that in the earlier suit the valuation had already been determined at Tk. 55,000.00. It is further contended that by suppressing the summons in the subsequent suit the appellant obtained the ex parte decree, put it to execution and got the respondent evicted on 3rd October, 1980 when the Court was closed for autumn vacation. After obtaining certified copies of the judgment and decree the respondent filed the appeal along with an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act to condone the delay for 169 days.

11. As the matter is pending in revision before the High Court Division we do not like to make any comment on the merit of respondent No. 1 's case.

<u>12. A person aggrieved by ex parte decree may pursue three remedies in the Court, namely, (1) by filing an application under Order 9, rule 13 for setting aside the ex parte decree, (2) by filing an application for review under Order 47, rule 1 or (3) by filing an appeal under section 96. Of the three remedies, the remedy by way of an appeal is the widest, and when an appeal is dismissed he will have no other remedy available to him.</u>

<u>13. We need not discuss the decisions cited by the appellant in detail. The upshot of all these decisions, in brief, is that the term 'appeal' has not been defined in the Code; that it is meant to be an application by an aggrieved party to an appellate court asking it to set aside, modify or revise a decision of a subordinate court; that an appeal even if irregular, incompetent or time-barred is nonetheless an appeal; and that the order of dismissal of a memorandum of appeal as time-barred comes within the deeming provision of sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, because by such an order the rights of parties with regard to matters in dispute are finally determined.</u>

<u>14. In this case the High Court Division by its order dated 30th July, 1985 gave a patently wrong direction to the trial court for the disposal of the order 9 rule 13 matter when the ex parte order stood merged in the appellate order and the latter was merely pending yet to be revised by itself. This court’s decision in 31 DLR (AD) 51 was not properly construed by the High Court Division when by the impugned order dated 19th November, 1985 it refused to set aside its earlier direction to the trial Court for the disposal of the Order 9, rule 13 matter.</u>

In view of the above the appeal is allowed. No costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 15.5.1983 passed by the High Court Division, Comilla Bench, in SA No. 471 of 1973).
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal J: This is the plaintiffs appeal from the second appellate judgment and decree of a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, Comilla Bench dated 15-5-83 in SA No. 471 of 1973 allowing the appeal and dismissing the suit, thereby setting aside the concurrent judgments and decrees of the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Additional Court, Sylhet in Title Appeal No. 141 of 1970 dated 1-6-72 and of the leaned Munsif, 3rd Court, Habiganj in Title Suit No. 207 of 1969 dated 26-12-69, decreeing the suit.

2. The plaintiffs TS No. 207 of 1969 of the 3rd Court of Munsif, Habiganj (originally TS No. 432 of 1968 of the 4th Court) was for a declaration of his jote right in 20 decimals of suit land by gift of 6 pies share, confirmation of possession or recovery of possession if dispossessed during the pendency of the suit and for permanent injunction.

3. There are some admitted aspects of the case. The suit land, along with other lands, belonged to two brothers Abdul Hashim and Abdul Jabbar, predecessor of present defendant Nos. 4-9 in equal shares. Abdul Hashim and defendant Nos. 4-9 instituted TS No. 1 of 1962 against the plaintiff and his brother as defendant Nos. 1 and 2 for declaration of title to the present suit land and other lands and recovery of possession and mesne profit. The suit was decreed and the said defendants' appeal was dismissed. Upon the death of Abdul Hashim his heirs, the present defendant Nos. 1-3, were made parties in Title Execution Case No. 5 of 1967. The present defendant No. 10, one of the two wives of Abdul Hashim, was not made a party to the execution proceedings. She instituted Misc. Case No. 16 of 1968 under the then existing section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and it was resisted by the decree-holders on the ground that defendant No. 10 was a divorced wife of Abdul Hashim, and so she inherited nothing. It was held in the Miscellaneous case that defendant No. 10 was not formally divorced by Abdul Hashim, but then she was not a necessary party to the execution proceeding as she along with the decree-holders represent the same decree-holder. Section 47 did not apply. Consequently defendant Nos. 1-9 of the present suit got delivery of possession from the judgment-debtors of that suit not only of the suit land but also of other lands covered by TS No. 1 of 1962 on 4-8-68 which was confirmed on 19-8-68.

4. It is the plaintiffs case that he is a distant grandson of present defendant No. 10. During the pendency of the said execution case defendant No. 10 had gifted to him on the 2nd Sravan, 1375 BS, corresponding to 18-7-68 her undivided share of 6 pie i.e, the suit 20 decimals of land by a registered hiba-bil-ewaz. His donor was in exclusive possession thereof and she inducted him into possession of the suit land and the plaintiff is in possession thereof on that account. Defendants made an attempt to dispossess him. Hence the suit.

5. Defendant No. 4, the contesting defendant, contended that defendant No. 10 was the divorced wife of Abdul Hashim, so she did not inherit anything from Abdul Hashim. The hiba-bil-ewaz was collusively entered into between defendant No. 10 and the plaintiff during the pendency of the execution proceedings with a view to creating difficulties in the way of the decree-holders' getting possession in TS No. 1 of 1962.

6. Both the Courts below concurrently held that the suit was not barred by res judicata, that it was maintainable, that defendant No. 10 was not formally divorced by Abdul Hashim, that she was entitled to 6 pies share as an heir of Abdul Hashim and that the hiba-bil-ewaz was genuine and acted upon. The two Courts below concurrently decreed the suit, except the prayer for confirmation of possession and permanent injunction.

7. The High Court Division reversed the concurrent judgments on the finding that the first appellate Court totally misconceived the pleadings and misread the evidence on record. In view of the admitted facts of the case it is inconceivable that defendant No. 10 had any exclusive possession of the suit land, whether before or after the decree passed in TS No. 1 of 1962. The plaintiff obtained an unspecified share of 6 pie said to be that of defendant No. 10 in the property left by Abdul Hashim. In the absence of a suit for partition, the alleged share of defendant No. 10 or the plaintiff cannot be determined.

8. Leave was granted to consider the plaintiff-appellant's submission that the suit was instituted specifying 20 decimals of land of the plaintiffs share in the Schedule of the plaint butted and bounded by definite demarcation and therefore the plaintiff was entitled to a relief without praying for partition.

9. Mr. NH Khandker, learned Advocate on-Record for the appellant, submits that the suit land was not only well-demarcated and well-delineated in the plaint, but was exclusively possessed by defendant No. 10 who delivered possession thereof to the plaintiff. He submits that the High Court Division acted erroneously in holding that a partition suit was necessary.

10. Unfortunately, these submissions do not carry Mr. Khandker very far. Admittedly, the plaintiffs case is that defendant No. 10 inherited 6 pies share in her husband Abdul Hashim's property after his death, not during his lifetime. The trial Court finds that in TS No. 1 of 1962 it was held that the defendants of that suit dispossessed the plaintiff of that suit from the present suit land and other lands in 1367 BS, vide Ext. A, the judgment There is absolutely no evidence that defendant No. 10 exclusively possessed her specific share of 6 pies from before the decree in TS No. 1 of 1962. Abdul Hashim and others originally filed TS No. 1 of 1962 for confirmation of possession. During the pendency of the suit they were dispossessed. The plaint was amended and a prayer for recovery of possession and mesne profit was incorporated. Abdul Hashim died, it appears, after the decree and the appeal. His heirs, defendant Nos. 1-3, were made parties in the execution proceedings. So Abdul Hashim died when he was already dispossessed of the suit land and other lands. There can be no question of inheritance of Abdul Hashim's properties by his heirs and successors, including defendant No. 10, during his lifetime. Question of inheritance arises only after Abdul Hashim's death, which took place after the decree in TS No. 1 of 1962. And there can be no question of partitioning Abdul Hashim's properties amicably or by metes and bounds between his heirs and successors before the decree-holders took possession of the suit land and other lands on 4-8-68 in Title Execution Case No. 5 of 1967. As already stated, there is no averment and no evidence either that defendant No. 10 possessed any specific portion of Abdul Hashim's properties before his death, i.e; before the decree in TS No. 1 of 1962 or before he' was dispossessed by the present plaintiff and his; brother in 1367 BS. There is no escape from the conclusion of the High Court Division that it is inconceivable in the admitted facts of the case that defendant No. 10 had any exclusive possession of the suit land, either before or after the decree passed in TS No. 1 of 1962. The High Court Division was right also in holding that the lower appellate Court misread the evidence on record in that defendant No. 10 was not at all a party to Title Execution Case No. 5 of 1967 and therefore she could not have taken possession of the suit land on 4-8-68 along with the decree-holders of TS No. 1 of 1962. There is also misconception of pleadings on the part of the lower appellate Court in that the plaintiff never claimed defendant No. 10 to be in possession of the suit land in pursuance of the execution case. It was his case that defendant No. 10 was in exclusive possession of the suit land independent of the decree of that suit, a claim not supported by evidence.

11. It is therefore not enough that the plaintiff had delineated and demarcated the suit land in the plaint. It was also necessary for him to prove that defendant No. 10 was in exclusive possession thereof. The trial Court held that on the date of execution of the hiba-bil-ewaz, 18-7-68, the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land as a dispossessor or trespasser, but on and from 18-7-68, his possession was that of a donee. This finding is contradictory to the plaint case. The plaintiff averred that his donor was in exclusive possession of the suit land at the time of hiba. She inducted him into possession and the plaintiff is in possession on that account. That case has been demolished by the trial Court itself. The lower appellate Court has not dwelt on his aspect of the case.

<u>12. We find nothing wrong in the High Court Division's finding that the suit being one for declaration of title to an unspecified 6 pies share of an undivided plot of land and there being no evidence that the donor thereof was in exclusive possession at any time the present suit is not maintainable without a prayer for partition.</u>

Hence the appeal is dismissed without costs.

End.

lawyer:
