Vs
Arif Ahmed ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the defendant-petitioner under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act was issued calling upon the plaintiff-opposite party to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 19-5-92 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Camilla in SCC Suit No.10 of 1985 rejecting an application under section 23 of the said Act should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The short facts giving rise to this Rule may be stated as follows:

The opposite party, Mr. Arif Ahmed as a plaintiff filed SCC Suit No. 10 of 1985 in the 3rd Court of Assistant Judge and SCC Judge, Camilla for eviction of the defendant Mr. Faiz Ahmed Chowdhury from the suit premises. The case of the plaintiff is that the suit land originally belonged to Maharaja of Tripura who subsequently made a settlement of the same to Nibaran Chandra Ganguli by a registered patta dated 23-9-1938 and that Nibaran Chandra Ganguli constructed a building in the suit property after taking settlement from the Maharaja of Tripura. Thereafter, Nibaran Chandradied leaving behind 4 sons, namely, Mukunda Chandra Ganguli, Nirrnal Chandra Ganguli, Nipendra Chandra Ganguli and Nirode Ganguli and on amicable arrangement Mukunda Chandra became the owner of the other property and the other three brothers became owners of the suit property. The 3 brothers subsequently exchanged their property with one Abdus Sattar and others by way of general power of attorney executed on 17-4-64 which was regularised by way of a registered deed of exchange dated 1-8-67. Abdus Sattar and others again made an exchange of the same property with the plaintiff by a registered deed dated 29-12-80. The defendant who was a tenant under Abdus Sattar in the suit premises became tenat under the plaintiff firstly at a monthly rent of Taka 10.00, then at the rate of Taka 30.00 and finally at the rate of Taka 40.00 per month. But the defendant defaulted in payment of rent and that the plaintiff also required the suit premises for his own bonafide use and occupation and as such, the plaintiff terminated the tenancy of the defendant by serving a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and then filed the SCC Suit as aforesaid.

3. The defendant contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the claim of the plaintiff staing, inter alia, that the suit is barred under section 23 of the Small Cause Courts Act and that there is no relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiff and the defendant, that the plaintiff has no right, title or interest in the suit property. The further case of the defendant is that Nibaron Chandra and Harendra Chandra, the two full brothers, were in joint mess and property who jointly took settlement of the suit property from Moharaja of Tripura but for some difficulty of Horendra, the settlement was taken only in the name of Nibaran Chandra Ganguli but both the brother /8/-anna share each in the suit property. Then Nibaran Chandra died leaving behind 4 sons as above and Harendra Chandra Ganguii being owner of 8 anna share also died leaving behind sons, Kanu Deb Ganguli, Benodeb Ganguli and Ranjit Kumar Ganguli who became owners in that 8 anna share. The defendant was a tenant in the suit premises under the sons of Harendra Chandra Ganguli having a tailoring business therein. The defendant did not take any lease of the suit premises from Nibaran Chandra or from his sons and did not pay any rent to them. No title was conferred in favour of Abdus Sattar and others nor in favour of the present plaintiff on the basis of their deed of exchange.

4. During the proceeding of the SCC suit, the defendant filed an application under section 23 of the SCC. Act on 2-5-92 praying for return of the plaint to the filing lawyer for presentation to the proper Court of Civil jurisdiction stating therein that a complicated question of title is involved in respect of the suit property. After hearing both the parties, the learned Senior Assistant Judge and SCC Judge rejected the defendan's prayer vide his order dated 19-5-1992.

5. Being aggrieved by this order of the learned Assistant Judge and SCC Court, the defendant as a petitioner has filed this application under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act before this Court and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr. Amir Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioner submits that the relief as sought for by the plaintiff in the suit depends upon the proof of his title to the suit land in view of the fact that the defendant has raised a serious question in respect of plaintiffs title to the suit land and as such, it was proper for the learned SCC. Judge to return the plaint for presentation to a civil Court for deciding title of the suit land but instead of doing that, the learned SCC Judge has rejected the defendant's prayer and thereby he has committed an error of law occasioning a failure of justice to the defendant-petitioner.

7. AKM Mozibur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party, has submitted that no question of title is involved in the suit property of this case in view of the fact that the plaintiff has got his registered exchange deed and that his vendor acquired title to the property by registered deed from the sons of the admitted owner Nibaron Chandra Ganguli and that nobody else is coming to deny the plaintiffs title and that the defendant-petitioner being admittedly a tenant in the suit premises is also not setting up his own claim of title therein.

<u>8. In the facts and circumstances of the case, it appears that admittedly Moharaja of Tripura was the original owner of the suit property with other properties. The plaintiffs case is that Nibaron Chandra Ganguli took settlement of the suit property from Maharaja of Tripura by a registered pasta dated 23-9-38. This settlement dated 23-9-38 is not denied by the defendant-petitioner. The only case of the defendant-petitioner is that this settlement was taken jointly by Nibaron Chandra and his brother Harendra Chandra but for some difficulty, the-document was registered in favour of Nibaron Chandra alone. This is a registered pasta deed of 1938 standing in the name of Nibaron Chandra Ganguli and that nobody is coming to challenge his title. Neither Harendra nor his sons nor anybody through them is coming to claim any share in the suit property. Therefore, it appears that there is dispute in respect of the title of Nibaron. The plaintiffs case is that one Abdus Sattar got the suit property by a registered deed from the sons of Nibaron and thereafter the plaintiff got it by a registered deed from this Abdus Sattar.</u>

<u>The plaintiffs title has not been challenged by anybody except the defendant who is admittedly a tenant in respect of the suit premises. A tenant has no right to challenge the title of the landlord in the name of a 3rd person who is absent and not coming to claim the suit property and that the document is also not in his name.</u>

9. Under the above facts and circumstances of the case, it appears that only question for decision by the SCC court in this case is whether a relationship of landlord and tenant exists between the plaintiff and the defendant in respect of the suit premises. The defendant-petitioner is not setting up any claim of his own title in respect of the suit property and that he could not also produce any paper to show his tenancy under the sons of Harendra.

10. Mr. Mozibur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party submits that the SCC suit was filed on 1-2-85 and that when the suit was about to be disposed of, then only the defendant-petitioner filed this application on 2-5-92 after 7 years of the filing of the suit raising a question of title in the name of a 3rd person with the sole purpose to delay the disposal of the SCC suit. The learned Advocate referred to a decision in the case of Mohammad Salim vs. Md. Siddick Jamal and others reported in 22 DLR 841 wherein it has been held by his Lordship in the following:

"In a suit for eviction of tenant the SCC Judge can go into the question of title incidentally only when such step was absolutely necessary to decide the points at issue."

11. In this connection the learned Advocate referred to another decision in the case of Ahmed Shah Khan vs. Abdul Barkat reported in 11 DLR 427 where in his Lordship has held as under: "A tenant inducted by the plaintiff landlord cannot deny the title of the landlord during the continuance of the tenancy."

12. In the facts and circumstances of the instant case, it appears that no complicated question of title is involved in this case in view of the fact that nobody is challenging the plaintiffs title. The defendant being a tenant cannot deny the plaintiffs title in the name of somebody else who himself is not coming to challenge the plaintiffs title.

13. Mr. Amir Hossain referred to a decision in the case of Abdul Khalek Mia vs. Maya Debi and others reported in 35 DLR (AD) 310. It has been observed by their Lordships in that case in the following:

"The Court of Small Causes is entitled to consider the question of title incidentally but not when the question of title becomes an issue on law."

14. In the above referred case, the question involved was whether Monoranjan Singha, pre-deceased his father, Rajani Kama, the owner of the suit property and whether the vesting of 1/5th of the property to Enemy Custodian and the grant of lease of that share to the petitioner were legal or not. Furthermore, that matter arose out of an order passed by the learned District Judge under section 28A of the Small Cause Courts Act and not by the SCC. Judge under section 23. Therefore, that matter has no relevancy with the facts and position of the instant case which is a quite different matter under section 2 of the SCC Act and not under section 28 A of the SCC Act. Moreover, I have already found above that nobody is challenging the plaintiffs title in the instant case and that the defendant-petitioner is also not claiming any title of his own therein. Section 23 of the SCC. Act runs thus:

"Return of plaints in suit involving question of title-(1) Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing portion of this Act, when the right of a plaintiff and the relief claimed by him in a Court of Small Causes depend upon the proof or disproof of a title to immoveable property or other title which such a court cannot finally determine, the Court may at any stage of the proceedings return the plaint to be presented to a Court having jurisdiction to determine the title."

15. The word 'may' has been used in the provisions of section 23 which makes it clear that it is a matter of discretion of the court to return or not to return the plaint according to the circumstances of each individual case. The Court is therefore to see whether the question raised by the defendant is a bonafide question or not and whether the question of title involved is a complicated question or not. Here in the instant case we have already seen that the registered documents are in the name of the plaintiff and that the defendant-petitioner is a tenant in respect of the suit premises. So the simple question involved in this case is a question of relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiff and the defendant. The question of title as raised by the defendant-petitioner in the name of a 3rd person who himself is not coming to claim it, apparently appears to be not a bonafide question.

16. By a perusal of the impugned order 19-5-92 passed by the SCC. Judge, it appears that the learned SCC, Judge found that the question of title and ownership in respect of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff and his vendor is a settled question. Thus it appears that the learned SCC. Judge also found that no complicated question at all is involved in the case. Still then the learned SCC. Judge observed that if any question of title appears to be there that incidental question can be decided by the see court.

17. Under all the above facts and circumstances, I find that the impugned order passed by the learned SCC Judge has been passed with valid reason and therefore, I find that the learned SCC Judge has not committed any error of law resulting in any error in the decision. It has not caused any failure of justice to the petitioner. The impugned order does not call for any interference by this court.

18. For the reasons stated above, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

The stay granted earlier by this court is hereby vacated.

Communicate this order to the court concerned at once.

End.

with Writ Petition Nos. 759 of 1993, and 760 of 1993 with Writ Petition Nos. 762 of 1993, 763 of 1993 and Writ Petition No. 764 of 1993.
lawyer:
MA Wahab Miah with Obaidul Hasan and M Enayetur Rahim, Advocates ------ For the Petitioners.

parties:

full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque J: Since identical questions of facts as well as law are involved in these seven writ petitions, namely, Writ Petition Nos. 757/1993, 758/1993, 759/1993, 760/1993, 762/1993, 763/1993 and 764/1993 these were heard together and are being disposed of by one judgment.

2. In Writ Petition No. 757 of 1993, Rule was issued calling upon respondents to show cause as to why they should not be directed to absorb the petitioner as a Lecturer of the Department of Management of Cheora Government College, Cheora Police Station Chaddyagram, District Comilla

3. Annexures-A and B to this application show that by a notice dated 30-9-86 and by another notice dated 8-9-87 the Governing Body of the Cheora College Authority published advertisement for appointment of Lecturers and Demonstrators in the aforesaid college. In pursuance of those advertisements the petitioner applied for the post of Lecturer of Management. He appeared before the Interview Board and after the interview he was selected and appointed as Lecturer of Management by a letter dated 2-6-87 and he joined in that post on 4-6-87. In the meetings of the Governing Body held on 21-4-87 and 20-6-87 the appointments made by the Governing Body were approved. After being appointed as such, the petitioner was performing his function as Lecturer of Management of that college.

4. In Writ Petition No. 758 of 1993 Mr. Md. Jashimuddin Patwari is the petitioner. In this petition, a Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why they should not be directed to absorb the petitioner as Demonstrator in the Department of Physics of Cheora Government College at village Cheora, Police Station Chaddyagram, District Comilla.

5. In pursuance of the advertisements mentioned above he appeared before the Interview Board and after his interview he was selected as Demonstrator of the Department of Physics of the aforesaid college and his appointment was made on 12-4-87 and he joined that post on 13-4-87 and since then he had been performing his function as Demonstrator of the aforesaid college.

6. In Writ Petition No. 759 of 1993 Halima Akhter is the petitioner. In this case, Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why, they should not be directed to absorb the petitioner as Lecturer in the Department of Bengali of Cheora Government College at village Cheora, Police Station Chaddyagram, District Comilia.

7. In pursuance of the aforesaid advertisements, she appeared before the Interview Board and she was duly selected as Lecturer on 2-6-87 and she joined that post of Lecturer in the Department of Bengali on 4-6-87 and since then she had been preforming her duties as Lecturer in the aforesaid college.

8. In Writ Petition No. 760 of 1993 Yasmin Ara Begum is the petitioner. In this case, Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why she should not be directed to absorb the petitioner as a Lecturer in the Department of Economics of Cheora Government College.

9. In pursuance of the aforesaid advertisements she appeared before the Interview Board and she was duly selected as Lecturer. On 2-6-87 her appointment letter was issued and she joined that post on 4-6-87 and since then she had been performing her duties as Lecturer of Economics in the aforesaid college.

10. In Writ Petition No. 762 of 1993 Ratna Rani Das is the petitioner. In this case, Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why they should not be directed to absorb the petitioner as Demonstrator in the Department of Biology of Cheora Government College.

11. In pursuance of the aforesaid advertisements she appeared before the Interview Board and she was duly selected as Demonstrator in the Department of Biology. On 12-4-87 her appointment letter was issued and she joined that post on 13-4-87 as Demonstrator in the Department of Biology and since then she had been performing her duties in the aforesaid College.

12. In Writ Petition No. 763 of 1993 Salina Akhter is the petitioner. In this case, Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why they should not be directed to absorb the petitioner as a Lecturer in the Department of Political Science of Cheora Government College.

13. In pursuance of the aforesaid advertisements she appeared before the Interview Board and she was duly selected as Lecturer and thereafter her appointment letter was issued on 12.4.87 and she joined that post on 13-4-87 as Lecturer and since then she had been performing her duties in the aforesaid college, as Lecturer in the Department of Political Science.

14. In Writ Petition No. 764 of 1993 Md. Faizullah is the petitioner. In this case, Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why they should not be directed to absorb the petitioner as Lecturer in the Department of Economics of Cheora Government College.

15.  In pursuance of the aforesaid advertisements he appeared before the Interview Board and he was duly selected as Lecturer in the Department of Economics by appointment letter dated 12-4-87 and he joined that post on 13-4-87 and since then he had been performing his function as Lecturer in Economics in the aforesaid college.

16. It may be stated that on 28-3-87 the then President of Bangladesh made a declaration in the public meeting at Cheora that the Cheora Degree College would be taken as Government College. On 10-3-88 the Gazette notification was published vide notification dated 18-2-88 declaring the Cheora Degree College as Cheora Government College with effect from 19-9-87 and by that notification the Cheora Government College was nationalised. On 15-9-87 a deed of agreement was entered into in between the College Authority and the Government settling the terms and conditions of nationalisation including the retention of the teachers and other staff of the college as well as the assets and properties of the said college. In this deed of agreement vide Annexure-11 it is stipulated that:

“অত্র কলেজের নাম চিওরা সরকারী ডিগ্রী কলেজ হিসাবে স্থায়ীভাবে অপরিবর্তীত থাকেবে। কলেজের বর্তমান কর্মরত শিক্ষক ও অন্যান্য কর্মচারীবৃন্দকে সর্বদা সরকারী-কর্মচারী হিসাবে বাংলাদেশ সরকার গ্রহণ করিবে।”

17. Thereafter the Director General of Higher Secretary Education, Bangladesh, Dhaka, wrote a letter to the Principal of Cheora Government College on 17-6-87 stating that restriction was given for appointment of teachers and other staff of the aforesaid college from the date of declaration by the President, that is, 28,3,87. By this letter dated 17-6-87 the Director General, in fact, indicated that before the declaration of the President on 28-3-87 all the teachers and staff would be absorbed and the teachers and staff appointed after declaration dated 28-3-87 would not be absorbed. Annexure-K is the letter dated 15-10-87 written by the Director General Respondent No. 3 to the Secretary Respondent No. 1 requesting the Ministry to create 14 posts of teachers and staff including the posts of the present seven writ petitioners and thereby to absorb them. It is further stated that they all got the Govt. benefits. The petitioners got the salaries and remunerations as approved by the Government to a Government College teacher. Annexure-L contains the Rules which are called 'The Teachers and Non-Teaching Staff on Nationalised Colleges (Directorate of Public Instruction) Absorption Rules, 1981. In that Rules the definition of 'Teaching' is given under Rule 2(1) which runs as follows:

"Teacher" means a teacher of a nationalised college and includes a Principal and Vice-Principal of the said college, appointed before the imposition of embargo on appointment by the Director of Public Instruction, or appointed, after such embargo, with his approval.

18. Annexure-M to the petition is dated 27-10-90 which shows that the petitioners were given the Government salaries and remunerations. Annexure-N to the petition is dated 6.5.91. The Principal of the college wrote to the Director General to absorb the petitioners in their respective posts inasmuch as it appears from Annexure-Q that the Government salaries and remunerations were given to the petitioners upto May, 1989 on Government teachers scale, but thereafter the respondent stopped paying the salaries and remunerations to the petitioners. For that reasons the Principal wrote to the Authority for regular absorption.

19. The petitioners tried their best for getting appropriate relief from the respondents, but the respondents did not give any reply to their representations. In such a situation they were compelled to institute a suit, namely, Title Suit No. 32 of 1992 for their absorption in the services of the aforesaid college. Annexure-(1) is the judgment of the Court which passed an order stating that the suit was not maintainable and the petitioners ought to have sought relief before the Administrative Tribunal. It is stated that since they had not been absorbed or accepted as Government teachers, they would not get any justice in the Administrative Tribunal or that their application would not be entertained by the Administrative Tribunal.

20. Annexure-P to the petition is the Gazette notification dated 3-3-88 showing that Chaddyagram College was nationalised by the Government with effect from 16-7-87. Annexure-P(1) dated 8-6-87 is the appointment letter of one Abdul Momin Majumder, a teacher of Chaddyagram Government College and Annexure-P(2) dated 9-5-92 shows that this Abdul Momin Majumder's appointment as Govt. College teacher was accepted and given effect from 16-7-87 when the College was nationalised by Gazette notification. Annexure-Q shows that the present petitioners got remunerations and salaries from the Government upto May, 1989 on Government teachers scale.

21. Now, the legal question arises in the instant cases in respect of all the petitioners that whether they are entitled to be absorbed in their respective posts in the aforesaid Cheora Government College with effect from the date of nationalisation of the College. Mr. MA Wahab Miah, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that under law the respondents are bound to absorb the petitioners in their respecting posts in Cheora Government College which they held on 19-9-87, the date from which the nationalisation notification was given effect to. It is not disputed that in the notification dated 18-2-88 declaring the Cheora Degree College as Cheora Government Degree College was published in the Gazette notification on 10-3-88 and by that Gazette notification dated 10-3-88 Cheora Degree College was nationalised with effect from 19-9-87. Mr. Wahab submits that all the petitioners got their job in the aforesaid college much before 19-9-87 and since then they had been discharging their functions in their respective posts in that college. Mr. Wahab further submits that this Gazette notification of nationalisation of the Cheora Degree College as Cheora Government College, with effect from 19-9-87 should be read along with Annexure-D, the deed of agreement, executed in between the President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Upazila Nirbahi Officer and the College Authority, represented by the Principal of the Cheora Degree College. As we have quoted above the stipulation in this agreement is that the teachers and other staff working there in the college would always be treated and absorbed as Government teacher and staff by the Government.

<u>22. In this connection we may consider this Annexure-I dated 17-6-87 which is the letter of the Director General of Secondary and Higher Secondary Education, Dhaka, which shows that the teachers and staff, in fact, would be absorbed who were there before the declaration by the President for taking up the college as Government college, that is, before 28-3-87. Mr. Wahab has challenged this order stating that this letter is dated 17-6-87 and the Director General was not authorised to give it a retrospective effect. He further submits that this letter of the Director General cannot override the Gazette notification vide Annexure-G published on 10-3-88 and the agreement executed in between the President of Bangladesh and the college authority on 15-9-87 for nationalisation of the college. It may be further mentioned that the self-same DG Respondent No. 3 issued a letter dated 10-10-87 requesting the respondent No. 1 for creating posts for absorption of the present petitioners and other staff in the said Cheora Government College. Mr. Wahab further submits that the petitioners were appointed in the services of the aforesaid Cheora Degree College before 15-9-87 and since they acquired vested right in their services before 15-9-87 and 19-9-87 on which date the college was nationalised, their vested rights cannot be taken away by the letter dated 17-6-87 which was, in fact, given a retrospective effect and this Director General had no authority to pass an order giving retrospective effect to the prejudice of the present petitioners who by that time acquired a vested right in their respective posts of the said college. Further, it appears that the present petitioners got their salaries and remunerations from the Government upto May, 1989 and it shows that the Gazette notification dated 10-3-88 giving effect from 19-9-87 and the agreement dated 15-9-87 had already been given effect to and in the eye of law the present petitioners were absorbed in their respective posts of the college by the Government upto May, 1989. Mr. Wahab submits that for giving salaries and remunerations to the petitioners by the Government upto May, 1989, in the eye of law, they had been absorbed to their respective posts and, as such, this letter of the Director General dated 17-6-87 cannot be given retrospective effect from 28-3-87.</u>

23. We find substance in the above contentions of Mr. Wahab. By this letter dated 17 -6-87 the vested right of the petitioners cannot be taken away retrospectively in view of the fact that on and from 15-9-87 and 19-9-87 they had been absorbed as Government teachers in their respective posts of the aforesaid Govt college and such a vested right cannot be taken away by this letter dated 17-6-87 retrospectively. Mr. Wahab submits that even if this letter of the Director General is accepted, it may be accepted on and from 17-6-87, but not before that. He submits that a declaration may be given by any Governmental authority for nationalisation of a college, but it will be, in the eye of law, actually nationalised with effect from the date which is fixed by the Gazette notification in order to nationalise it. In the instant cases we find that although Gazette notification was published on 10-3-88, yet it was given effect from 19-9-87 and on that date, in the eye of law, the Cheora Degree College stood nationalised as Cheora Government Degree College and the teachers and staff who were serving there on the date, that is, 19-9-87, should be deemed to be Government teachers and staff of the said Govt. College.

24. In this case no affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the respondents. Mr. Kaiseruddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, appeared on behalf of the respondents and opposed these Rules stating that the Director General respondent No. 3 was competent to put embargo on the appointment of teachers and staff and since the Director General put embargo from the date of declaration by the President on 28-3-87, the teachers and staff appointed thereafter will not be absorbed. We have already discussed this point above and we find that there is no substance in the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney-General.

25. Mr. Wahab further submits that by Annexure-H dated 15-9-87, that is, the agreement between the Government and the College Authority, the Government promised to absorb the existing teachers and staff of the college when it will be nationalised and now the Government is not entitled to back out from its own promise which is written down in a registered document executed by the Government and the College Authority. In support of his contention Mr. Wahab has referred to the cases of Gujrat State Financial Corporation vs. M/s Lotus Hotels Pvt. Ltd. AIR 1983 (SC) 848; MP Sugar Mills vs. State of UP AIR 1979 (SC) 621 and 1981 BLD (AD) 91. In the aforesaid cases their Lordships have settled the principle of promissory estoppel. Once the Government authority makes a promise and in pursuance of such promise something is done, subsequently it cannot back out from its own promise and that is why they are debarred by the promissory estoppel. Mr. Wahab submits that since the Government made a promise in their registered deed Annexure-H to the writ petition and since the petitioners worked and got pay upto May, 1989, now the Government cannot back out from its own promise and they are bound to absorb the present petitioners in their respective posts of the college. We find substance in the above contentions of Mr. Wahab. The present cases are covered by the principle of promissory estoppel as settled by their Lordships in the above cases.

<u>26. Mr. Wahab further submits that there is discrimination in the instant cases in view of the fact that teachers of Chaddyagram Government College which was also nationalised by the Government were absorbed in their respective posts and, as such, it offends Articles 27, 31 and 40 of the Constitution. He has drawn our attention to Annexure-P(1) to the petition which shows that one Mr. Abdul Momin Majumder was appointed as teacher of Chaddyagram College on 25-3-87, From a Gazette notification dated 3-3-88 it shows that this Chaddyagram College was nationalised by a notification dated 17-2-88 which was published in the Gazette dated 3-3-88 and this notification was given effect from 16-7-87, that means, though the Gazette notification was published on 3-3-88, yet the effect was given from 16-7-87 and as a result the Chaddyagram College was taken over as a nationalised Government College on 16-7-87. Mr. Md. Abdul Momin Majumder was appointed as teacher on 8-6-87 in that college. Annexure-P(2) shows that the Government absorbed him in his own post of the aforesaid Chaddyagram Government College with effect from 16th July, 1987, that is, from the date when it was nationalised by official Gazette notification. This Annexure-P(2) is dated 9-5-92. Mr. Wahab submits that similar question arose for absorption of the teachers of the aforesaid Chaddyagram College when it was nationalised. Ultimately this Annexure-P(2) shows that the Government absorbed Mr, Md. Abdul Momin Majumder in Chaddyagram Government College as a teacher with effect from 16th July, 1987. Mr. Wahab submits that similar is the case of the present petitioners and since the present petitioners were not given the similar and equal right, there is total discrimination in the instant cases and, as such, the respondents violated the provisions of Articles 27,31 and 40 of the Constitution. Article 27 speaks that all citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law. Article 31 speaks that there will be equal right to the protection of law that means to enjoy the protection of the law, and to be treated in accordance with law, and only in accordance with law, is the inalienable right of every citizen, wherever he may be, and of every other person for the time being within Bangladesh, and in particular no action detrimental to the life, liberty, body, reputation or property of any person shall be taken except in accordance with law. Article 40 of the Constitution may also be attracted in the present cases of the petitioners. Considering the above it appears to us that the present action of the respondents, in fact, violated the provisions of Articles 27, 31 and 40 of the Constitution by doing discriminatory treatment between the teachers of one nationalised college and the teachers of another nationalised college though they are, in the eye of law, on the same footing. In support of his contention Mr. Wahab has referred to the case of Director General, NSI vs. Md. Sultan Ahmed, 1996 BLD (AD), 76. In this judgment their Lordships enunciated a principle to the effect that a double standard treatment meted out to different employees by the executive Government is deprecated.</u>

<u>27. Question may arise as to the fact that the salaries and remunerations of the petitioners were stopped from June, 1989, but why they filed the writ petitions in 1993. During this long gap what is the explanation of the petitioners given in their petitions. It appears that they worked in their respective posts in Cheora Government College upto May, 1989 with all the salaries and remunerations from the Government. When their salaries and remunerations were stopped, they made representations to the different authorities of the Government. But they did not get any relief whatsoever from them. Finding no other way the petitioners were advised to file a civil suit, namely, Title Suit No. 32 of 1992 for declaration of their absorption in their respective posts. But, ultimately, the suit was disposed of by a judgment dated 26-9-92 and the learned Judge in the ordering portion observed that the present suit is not maintainable and the petitioners should seek relief in the Administrative Tribunal. Mr. Wahab submits that since the petitioners were not treated as Government servants, the petitioners might not get the appropriate relief in the Administrative Tribunal. Further, he submits that since he has been invoking the fundamental right Nos. 27, 31 and 40 of the Constitution, the petitioners felt that the writ petition is the appropriate, speedy and efficacious remedy. Thereafter in 1993 they moved all these writ petitions and obtained the Rules. Mr. Wahab submits that after issuance of the Rule he tried his best to get these writ petitions heard and ultimately he is successful to get these writ petitions heard in this court. Explanation for delay given by Mr. Wahab appears to be reasonable. So, in our opinion, there is no inordinate delay in preferring these writ petitions in view of the fact that the Government did not give any reply at any point of time to their grievances so long and even before this Court the respondents did not appear with an affidavit- in-opposition denying the allegations or the claims of the petitioners made in these writ petitions. It appears from the aforesaid annexures that even in the year 1992 the Principal of the college wrote to the relevant authorities for absorption of the present petitioners to their respective posts, but without any result.</u>

<u>28. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the legal provisions as we have discussed above on merit as well as on the ground of fundamental rights as applicable in the instant cases, we are of the view that the petitioners are entitled to get relief in the instant cases as prayed for.</u>

29. In the result, the Rule is made absolute in Writ-Petition No. 757 of 1993 and the respondents are directed to absorb the present petitioner Md. Abdur Rahim in the post of Lecturer in Management in Cheora Government Degree College within 60 days from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment.

The Rule is made absolute in Writ Petition No. 758 of 1993 and the respondents are directed to absorb the petitioner Md. Jashimuddin Patowari to his post of Demonstrator of Physics in Cheora Government Degree College within 60 days from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment.

30. The Rule is made absolute in Writ Petition No. 759 of 1993 and the respondents are directed to absorb the petitioner Halima Akhter to the post of Lecturer in Bengali of the aforesaid Cheora Government Degree College within 60 days from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment.

31. The Rule is made absolute in Writ Petition No. 760 of 1993 and the respondents are directed to absorb the petitioner Yasmin Ara Begum to the post of Lecturer in Economics in the aforesaid Cheora Government Degree College within 60 days from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment.

32. The Rule is made absolute in Writ Petition No. 762 of 1993 and the respondents are directed to absorb the petitioner Ratna Rani Das as Demonstrator of Biology in the aforesaid Cheora Government Degree College within 60 days from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment.

33. The Rule is made absolute in Writ Petition No. 763 of 1993 and the respondents are directed to absorb the petitioner Selina Akhter in the post of Lecturer in Political Science in the aforesaid Cheora Government Degree College within 60 days from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment.

34. The Rule is made absolute in Writ Petition No. 764 of 1993 and the respondents are directed to absorb the present petitioner Md. Faizullah in the post of Lecturer in Economics in the aforesaid Cheora Government Degree College within 60 days from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment

35. From June 1989 till the absorption, the salaries and remunerations of the petitioners shall be considered and decided in accordance with the provision of relevant laws and rules applicable to the teachers and staff of the nationalised colleges of Bangladesh.

There will be no order as to cost.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Sirajul Islam J: This Rule under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the plaintiff was directed against the judgment and decree dated 2-5-1994 and 9-5-1994 respectively passed by Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Khulna in Title Appeal No. 156 of 1986 reversing the judgment and decree dated 30-7-1986 and 5-8-1986 respectively passed by Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 89 of 1983.

2. Facts leading to this Rule are that the petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 89 of 1983 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Khulna against the defendant-opposite parties for declaration of title to the suit land described in the schedule to the plaint. The land measuring a total of 30.66 acres of CS Khatian Nos. 54 and 55 to 56 originally belonged to one Banikanti Roy. During RS operation those lands were recorded in RS Khatian Nos. 184, 185 and 186. The land of RS Khatian No.184 belonged to Khirod, Angod, Binoy, Dukhiram, Jogendra Math, Anania, Surendra, Soitya Bala, Trishnaboti, Aswini, Dhoru, Gadadhar, Sipin and Meneka Sundari as tenants. Due to non-payment of rent government started a certificate case No.546 KM/1955-56 and in that certificate case the entire land of RS Khatian No.184 was put to auction. The plaintiff for the purpose of purchasing the said land in auction sent his brother-in-law Krishnapada Mondal to purchase it in auction in the name of the plaintiff but Krishnapada purchased the same in his own name to the extent of 10 anna share and other 6 anna share was purchased by some other persons. The auction sale took place on 25-1-1956 and was confirmed on 3-4-1956 and that Krishnapada took delivery of possession of the land on behalf of the plaintiff and since then the plaintiff has been possessing the auction-purchased land. During SA operation the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of ex-tenants. Thereafter, one Ananta and Trishnaboti filed Miscellaneous Case No. 194 of 1961-62 to set aside the auction sale but this Miscellaneous case ended in compromise and that the auction sale to the extent of 3.22 acres of land was set aside and the auction to the extent of 5.74 acres of land was confirmed, out of which the plaintiffs 10 annas share measuring 3.60 acres of land remained in tact. The plaintiff has been possessing this land through borgadars and paid rent. The plaintiff was the real purchaser-owner of the suit land and Krishnapada was simply his benamdar. Thereafter, this Krishnapada sold the land in favour of defendants on 13-3-1983. This sale to the defendants is a collusive sale and that the defendants did not get title or possession by their purchase. This sale clouded the plaintiff's title and hence the plaintiff filed the suit as aforesaid.

3. The defendant Nos. 9-11 and 16 contested the suit by filing separate sets of written statements denying all the material allegations made in the plaint. Their case is, that they purchased the suit land by registered kabala dated 13-3-1983 from the real owner Krishnapada and since then they have been possessing the suit land through bargadars. Their further case is that Krishnapada purchased the suit land in auction out of his own money, took possession of the same and possessed it in assertion of his own right and title. Krishnapada was never benamder of the plaintiff Angada. While in possession, Krishnapada sold the suit land to these defendants and delivered possession to them. Plaintiff has no right, title or possession in the suit land and hence the plaintiffs suit is liable to be dismissed. The defendant's further case is that the suit is barred by section 21 of the PDR Act and by section 42 of the SR Act.

4. After trial, the learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff vide his judgment and decree dated 30-7-1986 and 5-8-1986 respectively. Against that judgment and decree the defendant- opposite party Nos. 1-4 preferred Title Appeal No. 156 of 1986 which was heard and disposed of by the Additional District Judge. 1st Court, Khulna. The learned Additional District Judge after considering the facts and evidence of the case allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and dismissed the plaintiffs suit by his judgment and decree dated 2-5-1994 and 9-5-1994 respectively.

5. Being aggrieved by this judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, the plaintiff as petitioner has filed this revisional application in this court and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr. Hasan Faiz Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff- petitioner, has submitted that the learned Additional District judge did not consider the plaintiffs case of auction purchase of the suit land in benami of his brother-in-law Krishnapada and the case that the plaintiff was the real owner of the suit land. He submits that the learned Additional District Judge has not also considered the fact that the plaintiff has been in possession of the suit land since the time of his auction purchase in 1956 for more than twelve years and thus acquiring title by adverse possession. The contention of the learned Advocate is that by not considering the facts and evidence of the case in its true perspective the learned Additional District Judge has committed an error of law in his findings resulting in an error in his decision occasioning failure of justice to the plaintiff-petitioner.

7. Mr. Awlad Ali, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-opposite party, on the other hand, has raised a preliminary point regarding maintainability of the suit saying that the suit was not at all maintainable in the form and manner as filed by the plaintiff as because the suit will be hit by section 21 of the Public Demands Recovery Act in view of the fact that the plaintiff claimed the title of the suit land solely on the basis of auction-purchase in benami of his brother-in-law Krishnapada in Certificate Case No. 546 KM 195-56. Mr. Awlad Ali submits that Krishnapada is the certified purchaser of the property in certificate sale dated 25-1-1956 and that the defendants by kabala-purchase from Krishnapada dated 13-3-1983 have entered into the shoes of the certified purchaser and that section 21 of the PDR Act prohibited any suit against the certified purchaser of a certificate sale or any person claiming under the certified purchaser and in view of the provision of section 21 of the said Act, the plaintiff's suit against the defendants will not be maintainable. For better appreciation of the provision of section 21 of PDR Act, we would like to quote below section 21 which runs as under:

Section 21". Suit against purchaser not maintainable on ground of purchase being made on behalf of plaintiff-(1) No suit shall be maintained against any person claiming title under a purchase certified by the Certificate-Officer in such manner as may be prescribed, on the ground that the purchase was made on behalf of the plaintiff or on behalf of someone through whom the plaintiff claims.

8. By a reading of this provision of section 21 of the Public Demands Recovery Act as quoted above, it appears that this section bars a suit by a plaintiff against the certified purchaser on the ground that the purchase was made on behalf of the plaintiff. The present suit as brought by the plaintiff-petitioner is a suit for declaration of his title to the suit land. The plaintiffs claim is that the suit land was put to auction in Certificate Case No. 546 KM/1955-56 and that the plaintiff sent Krishnapada to purchase the same in the name of the plaintiff but that Krishnapada purchased it in his own name on behalf of the plaintiff. Thus as per this averments as made in the plaint the plaintiffs whole case appears to be an auction-purchase made by Krishnapada on behalf of the plaintiff. So, the matter as it stands in the plaint seems to be coming within the purview of the prohibition of section 21. The same provision is there in section 66 CPC that no such suit shall be maintained by a plaintiff against a certified purchaser in a court sale.

<u>9. Mr. Hasan Faiz Siddique, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner, however, submits that this suit will be maintainable in this form because of the fact that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land since the time of auction purchase for more than 12 years and thus he has also acquired title by adverse possession. In support of his contention, Mr. Siddique referred to a decision in the case of Laxman vs. Govind reported in AIR 1920 Nagpur 51 wherein it has been observed by a Single Judge as under:</u>

<u>"A person who has been in adverse possession for a period of more than 12 years, cannot be considered to be a trespasser."</u>

<u>Mr. Siddique cited another decision in the case of Md. Abdul Jalil Khan and others vs. Muhammad Obaid Ullah Khan and others reported in AIR 1929 PC 228 wherein it has been held by their Lordships as follows:</u>

<u>"A suit based on dispossession after an adverse possession of 12 years is clearly not a suit on the ground that the purchase was made on behalf of the plaintiff or on behalf of someone through whom the plaintiff claims" within the meaning of section 66 and does not become so merely because the plaintiff as part of an alternative cause of auction sets up and proves that the purchases were in fact, benami."</u>

<u>10. In the above cited Nagpur case of AIR 1920 the plaintiffs case was that his father purchased the suit field at an auction-sale in benami of one Ambadas and since then they were in possession adversely for 24 years. The defendant subsequently purchased it in a sale in execution of a decree against Ambadas. The plaintiff sued for a declaration that the defendant had no right as auction-purchaser to take possession of the field from him. Hence, the plaintiffs main case was a case of acquisition of title by adverse possession for more than twelve years. The District Judge held him a trespasser. In that context the above cited observation was made that a person in adverse possession for more than 12 years cannot be considered as trespasser and the suit was remanded to decide the question of title by adverse possession. In the Privy Council case as reported in AIR 1929, the plaintiffs' case was that the purchases in court-auctions were made in benami, but that the plaintiffs had been in proprietary possession of the property ever since the court-auction and that by virtue of their adverse possession for more than 12 years they became absolute owners in possession of the property. They prayed for declaration of title by adverse possession and for possession and injunction. Several issues were framed in that case including an issue of adverse possession. In that suit, their Lordships held that the suit did not come within the meaning of prohibitory section 66 CPC.</u>

11. The instant suit before us is not a suit for acquisition of title by adverse possession nor a suit for benami declaration. The whole case of the plaintiff in the instant case is based on a benami-auction-purchase but the plaintiff did not also specifically state whether he paid the consideration money. It will thus appear that the facts and position of the above cited cases were quite different from the facts and position of the instant case. The facts being distinguishable the principle laid down in those cited cases will not be applicable in the instant case before us.

12. Mr. Hasan Faiz Siddique next submits that the learned Additional District Judge did not discuss nor consider the evidence of possession as adduced by the plaintiff to come to a finding of possession in favour of the plaintiff. But the fact remains that there is no averment in the plaint claiming any title by adverse possession by the plaintiff nor is there any issue framed to the effect of adverse possession of more than 12 years. By a perusal of the impugned judgment, it appears that the learned Additional District Judge has discussed all the averments made by the plaintiff in his plaint together with the evidence regarding possession, rent receipts and other matters and has come to the conclusion that the plaintiffs claim of possession has not at all been proved. This finding of the learned Additional District Judge appears to be based on proper discussion and appreciation of the facts and evidence of the case. We are therefore, of the opinion that the contention as put forward by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner that the suit will be maintainable in this form has no substance.

<u>13. Mr. Awlad Ali, the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party in support of his contention that the suit is not maintainable being barred by section 21 of the PDR Act, has referred to a decision in the case of Iswar Chandra Pal and others vs. Kabiruddin Ahmed and others reported in AIR 1934 (Cal) 322 wherein it has been held as under:</u>

<u>"Suit by a person for a declaration that plaintiff is entitled to certain share of property purchased in execution sale on ground that though purchase was made in another's name he contributed to the price in that proportion. It was held that section 66 CPC was a bar to such a suit. The operation of section 66 could not be ousted by the existence of any private agreement or undertaking."</u>

<u>Similar view has been expressed by their Lordships in the case of Hanuman Pershed Thakur vs. Jadu Nandan Thakur reported in 1915 ILR 20.</u>

<u>14. Section 21 of the PDR Act corresponds with section 66 of the Civil Procedure Code in the same language. The section 21 of PDR Act has put a stop to benami purchase in certificate sale and section 66 of the Civil Procedure Code has put a stop to benami purchases in court sale. The object of both the sections is the same to put a stop to benami purchases in auction sale. Both the sections have provided that no suit shall be maintainable against a certified purchaser. It has been held in the case reported in AIR 1920 Nagpur 51 as above mentioned that section 66 applies to the successors-in-title of a certified purchaser.</u>

15. In the instant case, the plaintiffs case is that he auction-purchased ten anna share measuring 3.60 acres of land in the Certificate Case No.596 KM/1955-56 and prayed for declaration of title to that extent on the ground that although the purchase stood in the name of Krishnapada but that Krishnapada auction-purchased the land on behalf of the plaintiff. Thus it appears that Krishnapada is the certified purchaser. The defendant's case is that they are the successor-in-title by purchase from certified purchaser Krishnapada. It thus appears that the principle as laid down in the above cited two cases is applicable in the facts and position of the present case. In that view of the matter and in view of the prohibitory provision of section 21 of the PDR Act, we hold that the plaintiff-petitioner's suit being barred by section 21 of the Public Demands Recovery Act is not maintainable in this form.

16. By a perusal of the impugned judgment passed by the learned Additional District Judge, it appears that the learned Judge has discussed all the facts, circumstances and the evidence of the case quite elaborately and has come to his decision that the suit is not maintainable and that the plaintiff could not prove his case. We find that this findings of the learned Additional District Judge are based on appreciation of law and facts of the case and hence there is nothing to interfere with this definite findings arrived at by the learned Additional District Judge in appeal.

17. Mr. Hasan Faiz Siddique the learned Advocate for the plaintiff- petitioner, made a last submission that the learned Additional District Judge did not consider the evidences of plaintiff's possession in the suit land in its true perspective and that it is a fit case for sending back on remand for the purpose of arriving at a decision in respect of adverse possession. But we have found above that the learned Additional District Judge has discussed the evidences of possession with rent receipts and other papers and found that the plaintiff failed to prove his possession and the case of the plaint and more so, the plaintiff had no clear case of any title by adverse possession and that there was no issue in that respect. Remand is not made to fill up the lacuna. We are therefore, unable to accept this submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

18. In view of the above facts, circumstances and the position of law, we rind that the learned Additional District Judge has not committed any error of law or of facts or procedure in coming to his decision. The impugned judgment therefore, does not call for any interference by this court.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. This revision case having been disposed of, the connected Rule being Civil Revision No. 2920 of 1994, becoming infructuous, is hereby discharged.

End.

parties:
Rupali Bank and another ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Md. Solaiman and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the defendant- petitioner Rupali Bank calls in question the judgment and decree dated 14-2-94 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Cox's Bazar, in Title Appeal No. 95 of 1990 affirming those dated 31-7-90 passed by the Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Cox's Bazar, in other Class Suit No. 26 of 1988.

2. The fact, in short, leading to the issuance of the Rule is that, the plaintiff opposite party Mohammad Solaiman filed Other Class Suit No. 26 of 1988 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar against the defendant-petitioner namely, Rupali Bank for a declaration that the order of termination dated 15-9-81 by the bank is illegal, alleging that he joined the defendant petitioner bank on 1st July, 1974 as guard-cum-peon. During his long tenure of service he never faced any charge of any kind. The Karmachari Union of defendant-petitioner bank was a member of Bangladesh Bank Employees Federation and the said Federation called strike from 10-9-91 in order to realise their 4 points charter of demands. When the plaintiff-opposite party reported for his duty on 9-9-81 the bank executives advised him to go away from the bank and accordingly, he did not report for his duty on 10-9-81. The plaintiff opposite party also could not come to the bank since 10-9-81 as the Police and Ansars were Guarding the bank. After some days the plaintiff opposite party came to report for his duty and wanted to sign the attendance register but he was prevented to do so by the bank authoriy.

3. The defendant-petitioner bank allowed other bank employees to join their duty on 14-9-81 except the plaintiff-opposite party and thereafter the plaintiff- opposite party came to know that he was removed from service. It is also alleged by the plaintiff opposite party that he was neither served with the letter of termination nor he received any termination benefits. It is further alleged by the plaintiff-opposite party that he submitted an application against his removal before the review committee constituted at the instance of the then Martial Law Administrator/ President of the country but without any result. The plaintiff opposite party eventually managed to obtain a copy of the termination letter dated 15-9-81 from the office of the Assistant General Manager of the defendant-petitioner bank on 13-12-87 and came to know that his services were terminated. Since his services were terminated by the defendant petitioner bank in violation of Regulation 13 of the Rupali Bank (Employees) Service Regulations, 1981 without any show cause notice the same was liable to be set aside.

4. The defendant-petitioner bank contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint. The defendant-petitioner bank asserts in its written statement that the order of termination is legal as it was made in terms of Regulation 13(2) of the Rupali Bank (Employees) Service Regulations 1981.

5. Both the plaintiff-opposite party and the defendant-petitioner bank examined one witness each in support of their respective case. The trial Court as well as the appellate Court below by their respective judgment and decree dated 31-7-90 and 14-2-94 decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff-opposite party on the finding that termination was not in accordance with Regulation 13 of the said Regulations inasmuch as he was punished without affording him any opportunity of being heard in the matter.

6. Mr. Miftauddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant petitioner bank submits that Regulation 13 of the said Regulations authorises defendant-opposite party bank to terminate service of any permanent employee on payment of notice pay without assigning any reason. Hence the defendant-opposite party bank having terminated the services of the plaintiff opposite party on payment of the pay for the notice period without any show cause notice has validly terminated the services of the plaintiff-opposite party. It is next contended by the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioner bank that since the plaintiff-opposite party admits in paragraph 3 of the plaint that he was informed about his termination on 24-9-81 he should have filed the suit within six years from that date. But the plaintiff opposite party having failed to do so the suit is barred by limitation in terms of Article 120 of the Limitation Act. It is further contended by the learned Advocate that since the plaintiff-opposite party failed to show that he was ever refused payment of termination benefits, the offer made by the defendant-petitioner bank to receive his termination benefits from the accounts department of the bank after adjustment of any dues amounts to sufficient compliance regarding payments for the notice period as contemplated under Regulation 13(2) of the said Regulations.

7. Mr. Md Ismail, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party, on the other hand, contends that the so-called termination of the services of the plaintiff-opposite party is a kind of punishment and, as such the defendant-petitioner bank was required to provide the plaintiff opposite party with the opportunity to show cause in order to explain his position before the impugned order of termination was made. It is further argued by the learned Advocate that the mere offer to pay for the notice period without, in fact, making any payment thereof is not sufficient compliance of the requirements laid down under the Regulation 13(2) of the said Regulations, more so when the defendant-petitioner bank failed to prove that the letter of termination was, in fact, received by the plaintiff opposite party and, as such, the impugned order of termination is liable to be set aside.

8. Regulation 13 under Chapter III of the Rupali Bank (Employees) Services Regulations, 1981 provides for termination of a temporary as well as confirmed employee of the bank by giving him three months notice or on payment of substantive pay in lieu of such notice. Sub-Regulation (2) of Regulation 13 of the said Regulations providing for termination of the confirmed employees reads as under:

"13(2). The competent authority may terminate the services of a confirmed employee or call upon him to resign without assigning any reason, by giving him three months' notice in writing or on payment of three months' substantive pay in lieu of such notice and the employee shall not be entitled to any form of compensation for termination of service."

<u>9. Similar provisions being Regulation 12(ii) fell for consideration by the Appellate Division in the case of Abdul Hannan Sikder and another vs. Bangladesh Bank and others reported in 31 DLR (AD) 298. In that case it was held that termination of service simpliciter without any stigma or accusation is not a punishment and, as such, the question of giving notice or an opportunity of being heard did not arise. In such case there is also no scope for making any grievance on the ground of violation of principle of natural justice.</u>

10. Decision on the question raised by the present Rule mainly depends on proper interpretation of Regulation 13(2) of the said Regulations, 1981. Contention that the plaintiff opposite party ought to have been given prior notice or an opportunity of being heard does not arise in the present case. Because this position is clear from the language used in Regulation 13 and also other Regulations if they are read together. In the present case there is also no scope for making any grievance that the plaintiff opposite party ought to have been terminated by giving him an opportunity of being heard in the matter on the basis of principle of natural justice. The reason being that the termination of services as contemplated under Regulation 13(2) speaks of simple termination without any kind of stigma. The letter of termination in the present case speaks of termination simpliciter as it does not contain any accusation or stigma.

<u>11. Now, with regard to the next contention made by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party that mere offer in the impugned letter of termination to pay for the notice period without, in fact, making any payment could not be considered to be sufficient compliance of Regulation 13(2) of the said Regulations. It is pertinent to consider that the important objective underlying Regulation 13(2) is to enable the bank authority to get rid of unwanted undesirable employee in the best interest of the bank without taking recourse to long and elaborate procedure involved in case of disciplinary action under Regulation 28, Chapter-IX of the said Regulations. This objective is likely to be frustrated if termination is made dependent on actual receipt of notice pay by the employee. Hence the letter of termination with a request to collect termination benefit from the bank, in my opinion, is a sufficient compliance of Regulation 13(2). To hold otherwise would frustrate the said objective and the scheme of the said service Regulations. If the termination of service is validly made by making an offer to pay termination benefit, payment thereof can be secured at any stage even with compensation if actual payment is refused or withheld by the bank. It is however noticed that this contention was never made in the courts below but raised before this court for the first time.</u>

<u>12. With regard to the contention that the suit is time barred I agree with the submission of the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioner bank that the suit ought to have been filed by the plaintiff-opposite party within 6 years from the date of his knowledge ie 24-9-81. The plaintiff-opposite party having failed to do so the suit is barred by limitation. Plaintiff-opposite party cannot be expected as a reasonable man to wait for long 7 (seven) years to seek his remedy by filing the suit as he did. Since it is a case of termination without any accusation such as illegal strike or abstention from work the review committee had no jurisdiction to consider the application of the plaintiff-opposite party. In this background of the case, both the trial Court as well as the appellate Court below decreed the suit on misconception of the law involved i.e. Regulation 13(2) of the said Regulations as well as misconstruction of the impugned letter of termination. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. Judgment and decree dated 14-2-94 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Cox's Bazar, in Title Appeal No. 95 of 1990 and the judgment and decree dated 31-7-90 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Cox's Bazar, in Other Class Suit No. 26 of 1988 are set aside.</u>

End.

Narayan Chandra Rajak Das ------- Appellant.
Vs.
Md. Amjad Ali Miah and others ------- Respondents.
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 6.7.1989 passed by the High Court Division, Barisal Bench in Civil Order No. 111 of 1989).
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J. : This appeal by the defendant is by leave from Judgment of the High Court Division, Barisal Bench in Civil Order No. 111 of 1989 dated 6.7.89, summarily rejecting the application under section 115 CPC in affirmance of the judgment and decree dated 22.5.89 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Barisal in Title Appeal Nos. 7 and 8 of 1983 allowing the appeals and decreeing the suits in reversal of those dated 25.11.82 passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Barisal in Title Suit Nos. 473 of 1978 and 135 of 1979 dismissing both the suits, heard and disposed of analogously.

2. The two plaintiff-respondents filed Title Suit No. 473 of 1978, against the defendant appellant for his eviction from the suit premises and for realisation of arrear rent and compensation as also for permanent injunction. It was their case that in respect of the suit premises to with a tin-shed measuring 4' X 7' and adjoining bhiti containing 15 bunds of tin, situated within Barisal Paurashava the appellant was a tenant at the rate of Tk. 40.00 per Bangla month. He paid rent irregularly upto Chaitra 1382 BS and has defaulted in the payment of rent since Baisakh 1383 BS in course of which Tk. 960.00 has fallen due to him upto Chaitra 1384 BS. The plaintiffs need the suit premises for their own occupation and for re-building. The appellant refused to accept a registered notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. Hence the suit with the reliefs prayed for.

3. The appellant in his written statement denied the relationship of landlord and tenant between him and the plaintiffs. He claimed settlement of the suit premises from the recorded tenant Rajendra Lal Karmaker who was his father-in-law on the 4th Baisakh 1354 BS at an yearly rent of Tk. 76'00. The appellant has obtained a compromise decree on 19.7.77 from the 2nd court of Munsif, Barisal in Title Suit No.1 of 1977 wherein his right, title and possession in the suit premises has been decreed.

4. The plaintiff-respondents also filed Title Suit No. 135 of 1979 in the same court against the same defendant-appellant for a declaration that the aforesaid compromise decree dated 19.7.77 in Title Suit No.1 of 1977 was illegal, void, fraudulent, collusive and not binding on the plaintiffs on the allegations, inter alia, that an area of 0'080 acres of land of plot No. 3058 appertaining to RS khatian No. 4972 corresponding to SA khatian No. 2994 of JL No. 50 belonging to mouza Bawa Alokanda (of which the suit premises in the other suit is a part) belonged to Rajendra Lal Karmaker who died leaving 3 sons, namely, Dilip Kumar, Hirendra Nath Karmaker and Dhirendra Nath Karmaker. The aforesaid land comprising 0'080 acres shall henceforth be described as the said land. On 8.12.62 Dilip Kumar, claiming to be the sole owner of the said land, sold it to the plaintiffs for Tk. 5,000'00. One Abdul Mannan Khandaker purchased the said land in execution of a rent-decree passed against the 3 sons of Rajendra Karmakar. The plaintiffs pre-empted the sale to the extent of 2/3rd of the said land by obtaining an order of Pre-emption in Pre-emption Case No. 12 of 1964 of the same Court on 15.8.1964. The plaintiffs have since raised new structures after getting a plan passed by the Barisal Municipality. The defendant-appellant and some others, namely Dulal Chandra Karmaker, Sankar Lal Karmaker and Kala Chand Karmaker are tenants under the plaintiffs in respect of the said land. The defendant-appellant has created some fraudulent documents of pattan in respect of the portion occupied by him and has obtained a compromise decree in the aforesaid suit on 19.7.77 without making the plaintiffs a party to the same and suppressing the notices of the suit.

5. The defendant-appellant in his written statement denied the plaintiffs purchase and pre-emption of the said land and termed the plaintiffs papers as forged and fraudulent. He also denied any new construction by the plaintiffs and totally denied that he or the persons mentioned above were ever the tenants of the plaintiffs. As in the other suit he claimed pattan of the entire land comprising 0'080 acres from his father-in-law Rajendra Lal Karmaker on the 4th Baisakh 1358 BS on a yearly rent of Tk. 76'00 and claimed to be in possession thereof ever since.

6. The two suits were tried analogously by the learned munsif. The plaintiffs examined 7 witnesses and the appellant examined 6 witnesses.

7. The trial Court found that the plaintiffs have proved their purchase and pre-emption of 0'080 acres of land and that the defendant-appellant could not establish the forged and fraudulent character of the plaintiffs document by any evidence. The defendant's own pattan is an unregistered document which the trial Court disbelieved, as a lease was required to be executed by both sides and registered in view of the said land being a town property. The trial Court also found that the document of pattan was an ante-dated one. Rajendra Lal Karmakar himself carried on litigations with his neighbours in respect of the said land upto 1959.

8. On the subject of the appellant being a tenant under the plaintiffs the trial Court discussed the plaintiffs evidence and found that there was no reliable evidence of realisation of rent from the appellant. The plaintiffs have no documentary evidence of tenancy. There is no receipt of rent, no averment in the plaint as to from when the tenancy started and no oral evidence either to those effects. The appellant was never a tenant under the plaintiffs and he was in possession of the suit premises long before the plaintiffs acquired title to it. The plaintiffs Title Suit No. 473 of 1978 is barred under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and their Title Suit No.135 of 1979 is liable to be dismissed. Both the suits were, therefore, dismissed by the trial Court.

9. The plaintiff respondents filed Title Appeal No.7 of 1983 against the judgment in Title Suit No. 473 of 1978 and Title Appeal No.8 of 1983 against the judgment in Title Suit No. 135 of 1979. Both the appeals were heard analogously and disposed of by the same judgment dated 22.5.89 by the learned Subordinate Judge.

10. The lower appellate Court concurred with the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their ownership of the entire land of 0'080 acres and that the appellant's pattan was an ante-dated document created for the purpose of grabbing the said land. The lower appellate Court discussed the oral evidence afresh and found that in spite of some contradictions in the statements of PWs the plaintiffs have been able to establish that the appellant was a tenant under them. The lower appellate Court, therefore, set aside the judgments and decrees of the trial Court, allowed the appeals and decreed both the two suits in favour of the plaintiff-respondents.

11. The defendant-appellant then preferred civil revisional application before the High Court Division, Barisal Bench against the aforesaid judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court. The High Court Division summarily dismissed the application on the short ground that the appellant "has made submission on facts" and has "not been able to point out any error of law in the decision" of the lower appellate Court" for issuance of Rule."

12. Leave was granted to consider the appellant's submission that the finding of the lower appellate Court regarding relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties is not based on any clear evidence on record. The lower appellate Court has itself noticed that apart from a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act the plaintiff-respondents did not furnish any documentary evidence of tenancy. The trial Court's findings on the relationship of landlord and tenant have not been reversed by the lower appellate Court, it was submitted.

13. Mr. SS Halder, learned Advocate for the defendant-appellant, submits that the plaintiffs have not stated in the plaint as to from when the tenancy of the appellant started. There was no averment that the plaintiffs were attorned after their purchase of the suit land. There is no oral or documentary evidence of receipt of rent. PWs 4 and 5, who were the ex-tenants of the plaintiffs, admitted in their cross-examination that they did not see the appellant to pay rent to the plaintiffs. The trial Court noticed these deficiencies in the case of the plaintiffs but the lower appellate Court has not specifically reversed these findings. It was, therefore, not a proper judgment of reversal and the High Court Division erred in law in summarily dismissing the application without issuance of any Rule to consider these glaring omissions.

<u>14. It is true that apart from the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act the plaintiffs have not adduced any documentary evidence as to the relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties. The plaintiffs, however, have adduced oral evidence to that effect. While the trial Court noticed the contradictions in the evidence of witnesses and placed no reliance on them, the lower appellate Court also noticed the contradictions, but held that the evidence of witnesses making contradictory statements need not be wholly rejected and the evidence of such witnesses should be considered in the light of all circumstances on record. The appellant's case of pattan was roundly disbelieved by both the courts below. It was, however, accepted that he was living in the suit premises from long before the purchase and pre-emption of the same by the plaintiffs. Both the courts below observed that there was no legal bar in the appellant's becoming a tenant after the plaintiffs purchase. The lower appellate Court considered the surrounding circumstances, namely, that other persons like Dulal Chandra Karmakar, Sankar Lal Karmakar and Kala Chand Karmakar were sued for eviction in Title Suit No. 474 of 1978 and that the plaintiff-landlords obtained a decree for their eviction. A tenancy can also be created by an oral agreement and the PWs who were ex-tenants and present tenants of the plaintiffs depose that no receipts were ever issued to them by the landlords, obviously in view of the fact that the rate of rent in each case was a small amount The fact that no one actually saw the appellant's paying rent to the plaintiffs does not detract from the fact that the appellant was described as a tenant under the plaintiffs by PWs 2, 4, 5 and 6. PW 7 was a clerk of Rajendra Lal Karmakar who was an Advocate since 1934 and the lower appellate Court also relied on his evidence.</u>

15. In the last analysis, therefore, it boils down to appreciation of evidence. While the trial Court could not place reliance on some witnesses, the lower appellate Court did so giving independent reasons. One may differ with the appreciation of evidence by the lower appellate Court but one must grant to the appellate Court the right of differing from the trial Court as far as reliance upon witnesses is concerned, especially when it is backed by adequate reasons.

16. We do not find that the lower appellate Court has not reversed the material findings and observations of the trial Court. Consequently we are unable to accept the argument of Mr. SS Halder that the lower appellate Court's judgment was not a proper judgment of reversal.

For all the above reasons, we do not find any merit in this appeal. Hence the appeal is dismissed with costs.

End.

Vs.
