case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 25th April 1994  passed by. the High Court Division in Appeal from Original Decree No. 266 of 1991 (Dhaka) and 27 of 1988 (Chittagong).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: This appeal by leave has impugned the judgment and order dated 25-4-1994 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Original Decree No. 27 of 1988 allowing the appeal.

2. The plaintiff-respondent Nos. 1-3 instituted Other Suit No. 71 of 1987 for declaration of title to the disputed property and for declaration that order dated 30-6-1986 and 11-6-1987 are illegal, void and not binding upon them stating, inter alia, that one Yakub Seth on 24-2-1932 purchased the property in suit, got mutated his name and paid rent and constructed building and was living thereon peacefully and that father of the defendant No.1 instituted Other Suit No. 929 of 1931 against the said Yakub Seth and plaintiff's grandmother for declaration that the property in suit was waqf property and for recovery of khas possession by evicting Yakub Seth and others. The suit was decreed on contest on 22-8-1934 and the defendant fought up to the then High Court of CaIcutta against the decree of the trial Court unsuccessfully but the decree-holder defendant never executed the decree and Yakub Seth continued in possession till 1965 and after his death the plaintiffs Were possessing the .said property and that plaintiffs acquired title by adverse possession for possessing more than 12 years after passing of the decree in Second Appeal No. 1192 of 1937 which arose from the decree passed in the Suit No. 929 of 1931 (subsequently re-numbered as Other Suit No. 8 of 1934) but defendant No.4, Administrator of Waqfs, issued notice under section 64(1) of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 and on 30-6-86 defendant No.4 passed order for eviction of the plaintiffs . The plaintiffs filed an application for review of the order which was rejected on 11-6-87 by defendant No.4 leading to the institution of the suit.

3. The appellant contested the suit filing written statement stating, inter alia, that the property in suit is waqf property and Mutwalli is entitled to recover possession of the same.

4. The appellant, however, filed an application under Order VII rule 11 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint on the ground that the suit is barred under section 102 of the Waqf Ordinance 1962 and also by res-judicata to which the plaintiffs filed written objection denying the same. The trial Court by its order dated 10-7-1988 rejected the plaint on the ground that the suit is barred under section 102 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 and the same is also barred by res-judicata. The plaintiffs accordingly moved the High Court Division in appeal and upon hearing the same the appeal was allowed setting aside the order of trial Court rejecting the plaint and directing the trial Court to hear the suit in accordance with law.

5. Leave was granted to consider the submissions for the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant as under:

"Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the suit against the orders dated 30-6-86 and 11-6-87, passed by the Administrator of Waqfs, is barred under sections 64 and 102 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962, and, as such, the High Court Division erred in setting aside the order of the trial Court rejecting the plaint. The learned Advocate further submits in view of the decree passed in SA No. 119 of 1937 read with the provisions of section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962, no suit could be instituted under section 64 of the Ordinance by the Administrator of Waqfs in that the remedy against such action lies under section 50 of the Ordinance by the Administrator of Waqfs for a decision regarding title by adverse possession or per se such claim for opposing eviction by the Deputy Commissioner under section 64(1) and failing thereto is to obtain decision from the learned District Judge under section 64(2) on appeal."

6. Mr TH Khan, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant, submits that in view of the provisions under section 102 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 the suit against the orders dated 30-6-1986 and 11-6-1987 passed by the Administrator of Waqfs is barred by law and accordingly, the High Court Division erred in law in reversing the judgment and order of the trial Court rejecting the; plaint. The learned Counsel further submits that even on a plain reading of the plaint showing that the property is waqf property of Amir Ali Waqf Estate and that the appellant's title having been declared in Title Suit No.8 of 1934, the suit is barred under the provision of section 102 of the Waqf Ordinance and accordingly, the plaint is liable to be rejected. The learned Counsel further submitted that in view of the decree passed in Second Appeal No. 1192 of 1937 read with section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962, no suit could be instituted by any person against whom action has been taken under section 64 of the Ordinance by the Administrator and the remedy of the plaintiffs, if there be any, lay before the Waqf Administrator under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance for a decision claiming title to the waqf property by adverse possession, inasmuch as claim of possession by way of eviction by Deputy Commissioner under section 64(1) of the Waqf Ordinance is subject to an appeal under section 64(2) of the Ordinance before the District Judge.

7. Dr Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Counsel appearing for the plaintiff respondent, however, submits that as a general rule it is no denying the fact that a suit is not maintainable for declaration as to whether a property is waqf property or not as is barred under section 102 of the Waqf Ordinance 1962 inasmuch as to challenge the order of eviction passed under section 64(1) of the Waqf Ordinance and that the dispute regarding nature and character of the property as waqf is to be determined under the provision of section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance but in the given fact of the case as detailed in the plaint that the predecessor of the defendants themselves filed a suit for declaration that the property is a waqf property and for recovery of khas possession from the predecessor-in-interest of plaintiff-respondents and that the suit having been decreed but admittedly no delivery of possession in any manner even by execution of the said decree having been taken in that suit the contention of the plaintiffs is that the plaintiff respondents are entitled to a declaration of title in the instant suit on the ground of adverse possession and, as such, the suit is neither barred under section 102 nor under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance.

8. The plaintiff-respondents instituted the suit for declaration of title by adverse possession and a consequential relief for a decree that the notices issued under section 64(1) of the Ordinance for eviction of the plaintiffs is illegal and not binding upon the plaintiffs on the averment, inter alia, that one Peer Box Sawdagar was the original owner of the suit land which was inherited by the predecessor of the plaintiffs Yakub Sawdagar by way of purchase on 24-2-1932 and have possessed mutating his name in the Sherista of the Zaminder and paying rent regularly and constructed a pucca building and planted trees, made pucca wall in the suit land. The father of the appellant-defendant No.1, however, instituted the suit for declaration that the property belonged to and was part of Amir Ali Waqf Estate and also for resovery of khas possession by evicting the present plaintiffs predecessor Yakub Sb. and grand-mother Fida Bibi therefrom. The suit being Title Suit No. 929 of 1931 was decreed on 22-8-1934 and an appeal therefrom being Title Appeal No. 375 of 1935 was dismissed on 19-8-1935. The second appeal being Second Appeal No. 1192 of 1937 was, however, dismissed on 27-7-1939 but the predecessor of the defendant never took possession by way of execution of the decree or otherwise evicting the plaintiffs predecessor and grandmother therefrom. The predecessor of the plaintiffs accordingly, continued in their possession in the suit land as before on payment of rent and after State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the suit land was recorded in the name of plaintiffs father without any objection from any quarter whatsoever and subsequently, the name was recorded in the PS Khatian and the father of the plaintiffs has been possessing on payment of rent and taxes to different authorities. Upon the death of the plaintiff's father in 1965 the plaintiffs as the heirs have been owning and possessing the suit land openly and adversely without any interference or interruption from any quarter and upon amicable arrangement between the plaintiffs and the deceased father, the plaintiff became the sole owner and being in possession mutated the same in his name in the record of right overruling the objections of the defendants upto appellate stage. The defendants. ultimately, took a short-cut measure issuing notices under section 64(1) of the Waqf Ordinance terming the plaintiffs as illegal occupants of the waqf property without serving any notice whatsoever and hence the suit.

9. The appellant though contesting the suit filing written statement but has, however, filed an application under Order VII rule 11 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejecting the plaint on the ground that the said suit is barred under section 102 of the Waqf Ordinance and the plaint is liable to be rejected.

Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as under:

11. The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:

(a) where it does not disclose a cause of action:

(b) where the relief Claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation warren a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so:

(c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so;

(d)  where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law: Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not exceed twenty-one days.

10. Thus the plaint is liable to be rejected where it does not disclose a cause of action, while the relief claimed is undervalued, where the relief claimed for is not properly valued but the plaint is written upon an insufficient stamp paper and where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law.

Thus, it is imperative to reject a plaint which from a reading of the plaint it is manifestly vexatious and meritless, in the sense of not disclosing a clear right to sue, when deficit court fee is not put in or that the suit is insufficiently stamped or otherwise barred by any law.

<u>11. The defendant has alleged that the suit from its own averment appears to be barred under section 102 of the Waqf Ordinance. While considering the application under Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Court cannot take into account materials beyond the plaint to declare the case of the plaintiff as frivolous and vexatious and the Court is not required to take into consideration the defence set up by the defendant in his written statement or written objection. The question as to whether the plaint is liable to be rejected being barred by law must be apparent from the statement made in the plaint itself and not from the written statement or any other material other than that has been put in the plaint. Thus this provision applies when It appears from the statement in the plaint that suit is barred by any law either due to limitation, res-judicata or barred by law providing ouster of the jurisdiction of the Court.</u>

12. The defendant has alleged that the suit is barred by section 102 of the Waqf Ordinance, that is ouster of jurisdiction of the Civil Court, as the suit is sought to be filed against the order of Waqf Administrator ordering eviction of the plaintiff from the suit land. Section 102 of the Waqf Ordinance reads as under:

Section 102. Bar to Suits—Except as otherwise expressly provided in this Ordinance, no decision or order of the Administrator shall be questioned in any suit or other proceeding in any Court.

<u>13. As a general rule, the provision of section 102 of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 is to be viewed excluding those of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Waqfs Ordinance, being a special statute providing a special remedy any relief provided therein shall bar the jurisdiction of the civil Court. Thus under section 102 of the Waqf Ordinance, no decision or order of the Waqf Administrator shall be questioned and any suit or other proceeding in any Court except as otherwise provided in the paid Ordinance. The express ouster is attracted only after the Administrator has given a decision or order. From a reading of the provision it does not appear to us that there is any express or implied bar to the jurisdiction of the civil Court to entertain any suit as to the Waqf character of the suit land. Section 102 is applicable in a situation when the Administrator of Waqf has given a decision or order in relation to the same operating as a bar under section 102 of the Ordinance. Thus, in a suit for declaring the order of eviction passed under section 64(1) as illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff, the plaint of the suit cannot be rejected either under section 64 or under section 102 of the Ordinance as the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the civil Court is not to be readily inferred It is the cardinal principle of law in case of ouster of jurisdiction to examine the case whether provisions of an Act have been complied with or not or that the authority has acted in conformity with the fundamental principle of judicial prudence.</u>

14. Similarly, under section 50 of the Waqfs Ordinance, Administrator of Waqfs is authorised to decide whether a property is waqf property or not and then this decision can be challenged before the District Judge. In the same manner as contained in section 35 which section has been made to apply to an order under the said section subject to challenge of the decision by way of an appeal before the District Judge and any order by the District Judge is appealable to the High Court Division whose decision shall be final.

15. In the instant facts of the case though the previous suit being Title Suit No. 990 of 1931 was for declaration that the property is waqf property and for recovery of khas possession which was decreed but no step was ever taken for recovery of possession by execution of the decree or otherwise and the plaintiffs and their predecessors continued in possession by mutating their names in the record of right on payment of rent and by construction of building and boundary wall allegedly, openly and adversely to the waqf estate or the Motwalli of the waqf estate since then and the plaintiffs have filed the suit challenging the order of eviction claiming title to the property by way of adverse possession.

<u>16. Mr TH Khan has referred to a decision in the case of Masjid Hanifa vs Korhan Shah, reported in PLD 1996 Lahore 314 for the proposition that Mosjid being property of God no limitation operates against it and if somebody is in possession thereof he could not claim any right of ownership thereof how long he had lived therein, his possession would not matter therein. Mr TH Khan has further referred to the decision reported in 1998 2 SCC 642 for the proposition that once a waqf it is always a waqf and the nature of the property is not extinguished by lapse of time. Mr Khan has further submitted that a notice under section 64 of the Waqfs Ordinance is not controlled by any law of limitation or under Article 142 or Article 144 of the Limitation Act.</u>

17. We do not dispute the propositions of law submitted by the learned Counsel for the appellant but in the peculiar facts of the instant case when the suit for declaration that the property is a waqf property with a prayer for recovery of possession has been decreed and subsequently, the decree having been maintained up to the appellate Court but no delivery of possession by way of execution of the said decree having been effected the plaintiffs predecessors who were defendants therein admittedly remained in possession, allegedly adversely, openly, declaring hostile title by mutating their names, paying rent and taxes to the authorities concerned including the Government, raising building and boundary wall and presently have

18. Thus prima facie, from the averment in the plaint we find that for failure to obtain the possession admittedly from the plaintiffs in execution of previous decree in Title Suit No. 990 of 1932 or otherwise, an alleged contention leading to a civil dispute has been raised in the suit as to whether the plaintiff could or did acquire any title by adverse possession in respect of the admitted waqf property and could be evicted by issuance of the notice under section 64(1) of the Waqfs Ordinance which is designed to evict a trespasser and/or a miscreant. Thus, from the averment in the plaint we do not find that plaint is prima facie liable to be rejected as being barred either under section 50 or section 102 of the Waqfs Ordinance.

19. Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure expressly provides that the Courts shall (subject to the provisions herein contained) have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognisance is either expressly or impliedly barred. The nature of the dispute which was being litigated upon is entirely a civil dispute and can only be decided by competent Court of civil jurisdiction.

The appeal is, accordingly, dismissed without any order as to costs. However, any finding or decision in the disposal of the appeal aforesaid shall have no bearing in the matter of disposal of the suit or appeal by the Courts concerned, which would independently dispose of the same on the materials; evidence in the suit and in accordance with law.

End.

lawyer:
Mamtazuddin Ahmed with Saifuddin Ahmed Chowdhury, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners. 
SK Sinha, Advocate  ----- For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Sher Mohammad & another ----- Petitioners.
Vs.
Sarada Bala Sen and another ----- Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
This Rule obtained under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against an order dated 23.3.92 passed by Mr. Md. Aminul Islam, First Additional Assistant Judge, Sadar, Chittagong, in Other Suit No. 7 of 1991.

2. Facts, as stated in the petition, in short, are, that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 instituted a suit, being Other Suit No. 220 of 1978 for ejectment of a tenant, for arrear of rent and compensation. The suit was renumbered as Other Suit No. 40/90 and ultimately when it was transferred to the Additional Assistant Judge, First Court, Sadar, Chittagong, for disposal it was renumbered as other Suit No. 7 of 1991.

3. In the plaint the plaintiff claims that the defendant Haradan Chowdhury has been his monthly tenant since 1st November, 1974, at a monthly rent of Taka 125.00. Since July, 1975 the defendant defaulted in paying rent and as the plaintiff had a bonafide requirement of the premises he served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, terminating the tenancy from July, 1978. The defendant received the notice yet failed to hand over the vacant possession of the suit land. Hence the suit.

4. The defendant opposite party No. 2 contested the suit by denying the relationship of landlord and tenant with the plaintiff. He claims that in 1972 he entered into the premises as monthly tenant of one Parimal Bhattacherjee who later on sold his interest to Abdus Salam and others and from July 1970 he was attorned to the said Abdus Salam.

5. On 9.2.92 the petitioners submitted an application claiming that the plaintiff is not the owner of the suit premises. They purchased it from Abdus Salam and others, and the defendant since then paid them rent which has been increased from time to time. They further claim to have instituted a title suit, being Title Suit No. 52/87, regarding the suit premises in the court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Sadar, Chittagong, in which the plaintiff of Other Suit No. 7 of 1991 has been made the defendant No. 2. The latter appeared in that case by submitting written statement, but did not mention anything in Other Suit No. 7 of 1991 about the pendency of the Title Suit No. 52 of 1987.

6. The petitioners further claim that the plaintiff is not entitled to evict the defendant and the petitioners are entitled to be impleaded as defendants as they are the owners of the suit premises. It the suit is disposed of without their being added as parties it will affect their title and also the result of Title Suit No. 52 of 1987. The petition was rejected by the learned Additional Assistant Judge on the ground that there is no legal basis for adding the petitioners as parties.

7. Being aggrieved by the order the petitioners moved this court and the Rule was optional.

<u>8. Mr. Momtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that the impugned order was passed on wrong conception of law. By denying to add the petitioners as parties the trial Court has excluded necessary and proper parties from appearing in the suit. In their absence there will be no effective and proper adjudication of all questions involved in the suit. More so, when the defendant tenant has denied the title of the plaintiff and set up the petitioners as landlord. He submits that as a result of the defendant's claim the suit has lost its simple character of being an ejectment suit and now" involves adjudication of title incidentally and the court is authorised to go into the title incidentally. " Unless the petitioners are impleaded the plaintiff who has no title may get a decree and thereby prejudice the petitioners title to the suit premises. In support of the petitioners claim that they are necessary and proper parties the learned Advocate has cited the cases of Mst. Jahanara Begum Vs. AL Md. Shamsul Haque reported in 27 DLR (AD) 129 in which the general principles of who is a necessary party has been discussed.</u>

9. Mr. SK Sinha, the learned Advocate for the appellant opposite party, submits that, on the other hand if the petitioners are allowed to be added then it will result in a multiplicity of suits involving numerous questions of law and fact, and the transformation of a simple suit into a title suit, in which case there will be no end to the dispute. He also submits that an eviction proceeding under section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance is more or less a summary proceeding in nature and in such a suit a third party should not be added. In support of his above submissions he has cited the following cases; 1977 AIR, Orissa 184, 1925 AIR Calcutta 26, AIR 1960 Bombay 238, 1978 AIR Jammu and Kashmir 85, AIR, Nagpur 234, 42 DLR page 72 and 1983 BLD 274.

10. Order 1 rule 10 sub-rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides:

"The Court may at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party, and on such terms as may appear to the court to be just, order that the name of any party improperly joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, be struck out, and that the name of any person who ought to have been joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, or whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit, be added."

11. This confers a discretion upon the Court and which discretion should be exercised taking into consideration the facts and circumstances of a particular litigation, subject to the general principle that the parties cannot be added if it actually changes or alters the nature of the suit. Hingu Lal Vs. Baldeo Ram 1902, 24 All ER 53.

12. Besides, only in two cases may a person be added as a party to a suit. First, when an effective decree cannot be passed without making him a party and secondly, when the suit cannot be effectively and completely decided without his presence. Mst. Jahanara Begum Vs. ML Md. Shamsul Hoque, 27 DLR (AD) 129.

13. The relevant passage from Dicey on Parties to an Action (R 113 P 495) as quoted in UG Sukhare Vs. VCG Gawande 1960 AlR Vol. 47 Bombay 238, relevant para 7 reads:

" A person who has a right to defend any action of ejectment is any person named in the writ and any person who is in possession by himself or his tenant. The object of the plaintiff in ejectmnet is to obtain, not damages but possession of the land. He brings his action against the person actually in possession."

14. This passage is actually referring to a case where the precedent title of a third party is not disputed. Apart from that, the passage strictly speaking, will imply that only all those persons who are in physical possession of the suit property should be made defendants and others are neither necessary nor proper parties.

15. From the above discussion it appears that in an ejectment suit, if the plaintiff can make out a legal title to land, he is entitled to maintain a suit against the person in actual juridical possession of such land as such person is the only necessary and proper party. A third party will not be added if it transforms the nature of the suit from a simple rent suit into a complex title suit. But it does not mean that the question of title may not be investigated incidentally, as for example, it may be investigated in a suit for arrears of rent where the tenant defendant disputes the extent of title of the plaintiff to the arrears demanded, making it incumbent on the court to determine the point before the claim is allowed or disallowed.

16. In the instant case the petitioners are neither proper parties nor necessary parties. Nowhere in the plaint the cause of action against them has been disclosed. I do not see any allegation that prior to the suit filed by the plaintiff in 1978, the petitioners set up a claim in the suit premises. The Title Suit No. 52/87 comes after the ejectment suit was filed by the petitioners in 1978. Then again their application to be added as parties was made at a stage when the case was ready for argument after closing of evidence. If the petitioners' claim to be the land owners is genuine then naturally they would have known about the suit from the defendant-tenant earlier and would not have waited till such a late stage to apply to the court to be added as parties.

17. Moreover, if the petitioners are now allowed to be impleaded then the plaintiffs simple suit for recovery of rent and eviction of the defendant-tenant will be transformed into a complex title suit between the plaintiff and the defendants along with the petitioners, and the relief asked for in the original suit will pale into secondary importance. In this connection I have also considered the decision held in the case of Nurul Akbar and others Vs. Saifur Ahmed and others BSCR 1979 page 3 referred to by Mr. Momtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, wherein a stranger is allowed to be added as a party in an ejectment suit. But that decision, in my opinion, is not attracted in the instant case as the facts are quite different in the said case the plaintiff filed an ejectment suit against the sole defendant claiming her to be a temporary monthly tenant and alleged that the defendant was holding over the property even after the expiry of the lease. The defendant denied a landlord-tenant relationship and claimed adverse possession from the time of her predecessor, Ram Chandra Roy, from whom she has purchased the suit land, then had her name mutated in the Municipal Register and later on sold the suit land to the third party who filed an application to be added in the suit. The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court allowed the third party to be added as party as the court below came to the findings that the third party had purchased the property and had been in possession. But in the instant case the petitioners are neither in possession of the suit premises nor have their ownership been established. The ownership has remained very much a disputed fact and therefore I am of the opinion that they are not necessary and proper parties in this suit for ejectment.

<u>18. Apart from this consideration, the petitioners have themselves filed Title Suit No. 52 of 1987 in the court of the Subordinate Judge, First Court, Sadar, Chittagong, claiming title to the suit premises. The plaintiff has been made a party in that suit. Even if the petitioners are not impleaded in the instant case any decision held therein will not in any manner bind or affect the right, title or interest of the petitioners in the suit premises. The petitioners' right in Title Suit No. 52 of 1987 will be decided without being prejudiced or influenced in any manner by the decision in Other Suit No. 7 of 1991.</u>

19. Mr. Momtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioners then submits that the impugned order is not a speaking order. It only states that there is no "legal basis" for allowing the petitioners to be added as parties under Order 1 rule 10 of the CPC and therefore, he argues that the case should be sent back to the trial Court on remand. In this connection he has cited the case of Moyenduddin Mondal Vs. Sushil Kumar Kundu & others, PLD 1960, Dhaka, 734 where the case was sent on remand to the trial Court without any reason being given.

20. No doubt the impugned order is a very sketchy one. It merely states that the application stands rejected as there is no 'legal basis' for adding the petitioners' as parties. There should have been more application of mind by the learned Additional Assistant Judge. Under Order 1 rule 10 the court has first to be satisfied as to the conditions mentioned in the said Order before an order is given as to whether a person is to be added or not The learned Additional Assistant Judge is required to express his opinion, one way or the other, as to whether addition of the petitioners as parties would be necessary in order to enable the court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit. However because of the nature of the suit i.e. it is an ejectment suit under section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance I am not inclined to send the case to the trial Court on remand. Moreover, the learned Additional Assistant Judge has at least given a reason for rejecting the application, however sketchy it may be, and the reason is that there is "no legal basis" for adding the petitioners as parties. I do not think it will serve ends of justice if the case is sent to the trial Court on remand on this point alone.

21. Mr. Momtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, further argues that the defendant has denied the title of the plaintiff even before the notice under sec. 106 of the Transfer of Property Act had been served upon him. By such prior denial the defendant has caused the determination of tenancy by forfeiture, consequently the ejectment suit is not maintainable. But I do not have any evidence before me which supports the claim that such prior denial of tenancy was made. The defendant appears to have denied the title of the plaintiff for the first time in the written statement.

<u>22. In view of the decision in Ahmed Hussain Vs. Zakia Khatun, 20 DLR 1157 it will appear that denial of the title of the plaintiff landlord in the written statement of a suit is not available as a ground for forfeiture, obviously for the reason that the suit was filed before the written statement and disclaimer or the challenge of the title of the plaintiff was made in the written statement. Therefore, the denial of the title of the plaintiff in the written statement will not be available under section 111(g) (2) of the Transfer of Property Act, causing the determination of tenancy by forfeiture.</u>

23. Accordingly the Rule is discharged. The stay granted earlier is hereby vacated.

Communicate this order to the lower court at once.

End.
